An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). The findings are in line with previous, less precise measurements but offer improved precision. Additionally, a 3.5 picosensitivity in determining $\Delta\Gamma_s$ has been achieved, which is a key element in understanding the $B^0_s$ parameters and allows for the testing of certain Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model predictions. The research also led to the confirmation of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ existance with a significance of 10$\sigma$. The measured lifetime can be compared with theoretical predictions derived from the Standard Model, which yields a value of approximately 1.440 picoseconds. The research was published in the Journal of High Energy Physics, with the article title "Determination of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time parameter and studies of the $J/\\psi\\phi$ system in $B^0_s\\rightarrow J/\\psi\\phi\\phi$ decays" and the reference number 1903.00066 of the hep-ph category. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. Initially, it develops a numerical scheme using finite elements and time steps, and proves that the controlled outcome converges to its intended value at a rate of one-half, in the natural norm, as the discretization elements and time steps decrease. It also establishes that this same rate of convergence applies when using larger elements and smaller time steps, despite some of the time steps being negative, although it requires more complex arguments. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the solution to the problem can be found using the Monte-Carlo method with a faster convergence rate, in a $d$-dimensional space, as the number of simulations decreases at a rate of one, for $d=1$, and two, for $d>1$. It also considers versions of the problem with constraints on the state and control, and shows that these can be handled by modifying the cost function. This research builds upon previous studies, particularly those by Kacianiec and Krise, and Krise, which addressed similar control problems in the presence of state constraints and stiff diffusion, but with different assumptions and results. This study was motivated by its application to controlling a stochastic interface dynamics model, but the analysis itself is presented as a standalone numerical solution to a general class of stochastic control problems. It is worth noting that the term "rough" in this context refers to inputs that result in a state that becomes infinite in a short amount of time, as opposed to being described by a process with mean square integrability over time. This research established the convergence of a specific numerical scheme for solving a stochastic control problem with rough inputs, for a specific type of problem where the state remains finite, but did not aim to investigate the properties of the numerical scheme's solution, but rather its relation to the solution of the original problem, which it approximates. It is also distinct from previous studies that have investigated similar control problems with different types of noise, but has connections to studies on semi-linear equations and the convergence rate of the finite element method. It is further noted that the use of the term "rough" in this context is the opposite of its use in a study by M. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced as energy increases beyond 8 EeV. Furthermore, an indication of quadrupolar anisotropy emerged at the highest energy levels. To test these findings for potential systematic errors, we repeated the analysis using two alternate data sets, obtaining similar results. An examination of potential sources of background noise was also conducted, and found to be minimal. Utilizing EDELWEISS experiment's dark matter detection data as a comparison, we explored the characteristics of dipolar anisotropies observable at different energies and declination levels. If interpreted within a specific framework, these findings could indicate that extremely energetic cosmic rays originate from a small portion of the sky, with localized distribution patterns evident even at the highest energy levels. Alternatively, they might result from a more general distribution of sources, revealing the path to discovering them, and potentially offering a way to study dark matter distributions, given that a match between those distributions and the dark matter's clustering patterns is observed. Given current understanding and limitations, we cannot rule out the possibility that these anisotropy patterns arise from particles with masses similar to those of muons and tau particles. However, based on previous studies, it is less likely that they result from particles with significantly lighter masses, such as protons. A comprehensive explanation for these findings remains an open question that demands further investigation, and could potentially be answered by a combination of upgraded and new experiments, such as the AugerPrime and the Square Kilometre Array. To detect dipolar anisotropies comparable to those found in our research, these experiments must be capable of resolving variations of less than 0.3 degrees in the distribution of the arrival directions of the most energetic cosmic rays. Based on currently available data sets, we were unable to discover any evidence of quadrupolar anisotropies at the Pierre Auger Observatory, and have established lower limits on their amplitude, ranging from 13% to 24% of the total cosmic ray flux, depending on the energy range and declination band considered. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. The discussion also explores how Zinbiel algebras relate to Lie algebras and provides examples of both known and unknown classes of Zinbiel algebras. The investigation expands on previous findings by examining both solvable and nilpotent Zinbiel algebras, shedding light on their dimensional structure and factorization. The resulting nilpotent dimension can be seen as a generalized version of the upper bound for solvable Zinbiel algebras. The study concludes by formulating an hypothesis on the upper bound for the nilpotent dimension of a specific class of Zinbiel algebras, which is then demonstrated to be achievable for both the Lie algebra of a solvable group and the Nederhouser-Zinbiel algebra. The investigation into these algebras is further expanded in the companion paper, where the focus is on developing both a theory for solvable Lie algebras and a method for applying it to various groups. The relationship between these algebras and the groups they represent is explored through both computational methods and theoretical analysis, revealing both similarities and distinct characteristics. The investigation into these algebras reveals a link between their solvable structure and the groups they represent, demonstrating how this structure can be used to classify the algebras based on the groups, resulting in a broad classification that is then narrowed down to more specific categories, ultimately leading to a fundamental conclusion about the prime factorization of the dimension of these algebras. The investigation into these algebras is not limited to groups, also being applied to the Nederhouser-Zinbiel algebra and the Baeuer-Zinbiel algebra of a free Lie algebra, both of which result in a deeper understanding of these algebras and their dimensional structure. The investigation into these algebras is further expanded in the companion paper to also include the investigation of their homogenous invariants and their relation to the invariants of the groups they represent. The investigation into these invariants reveals both a link between the homogeneous invariants of these algebras and the invariants of the groups they represent, as well as a deeper understanding of the relationship between these invariants and the structure of these algebras. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, a distinct behavior of these fluctuations when considering particles of different types, such as pions, kaons, and protons, has also been observed, which may offer additional insights into the underlying dynamics, specifically related to the production of strange particles. Overall, these results significantly enhance our understanding of the dynamics governing heavy-ion collisions and provide valuable input for future research into these complex phenomena. Database information used in this analysis has been updated to include data from new collisions and has been made public, which has enabled researchers to test the methods used and gain valuable experience in working with these data in preparation for future research. Additionally, macrocodes associated with this research have been made available to the community through the theory and simulation working group website.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Moreover, we demonstrate the applicability and efficiency of our approach by conducting an experimental analysis of both artificial and real-world data datasets. Notably, our data datasets comprise both a newly introduced dataset and established benchmarks. In related work sections, we also address possible connections with existing research on data consistency, specifically (a) data merging, (b) query validation, and (c) quality assessments. Moreover, we outline possible connections with other research on data validation, specifically (a) data merging, (b) query validation, and (c) quality assessments, and also examine possible extensions of our approach, discussing potential research avenues for future development. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Notably, these applications yield forecasts of exceptional precision when compared to other dynamic models, as assessed by metrics such as mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error. We have also compared the TV-PARX model to its static counterpart, revealing a significant improvement in forecasting capabilities for both data sets. This research demonstrates the TV-PARX model's efficacy in modeling and predicting count time series data, even in the presence of complex dynamics and shifting covariates. This extends the applicability of such models to a wide range of temporal patterns, thereby providing valuable insights for both theoretical research and practical applications. This research has been published in the Journal of Applied Econometrics and the Journal of Forecasting. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Moreover, our inequality facilitated an examination of the optimization landscape's properties near the solutions obtained by the AMP algorithm, thereby enabling us to establish the existence of a phase where the AMP algorithm's output corresponds to a unique, zero-flux TAP configuration. This last mentioned result implies the existence of a distinct solution phase where the sample and average TAP configurations coincide, which we termed the "consistency phase". Notably, this phase is characterized by a lower bound on the variance of the TAP configuration weights, a condition that defines a region in parameter space and determines the shape of the optimization landscape. We also studied this variance variance with respect to the disorder average, which enabled us to derive several interesting results, including an interpretation of the flat phase's boundary in terms of the variance of the TAP configuration weights. Moreover, we found that the onset of the consistency phase is signaled by a sudden increase in this variance, which we attributed to the emergence of a complex optimization landscape. It is worth noting that we could not determine the onset of the consistency phase when considering the variance with a fixed time-dependent width, which led us to conjecture that the optimal width should scale with the standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution from which the random coupling matrix is generated, in order to detect the lower bound on the variance of the TAP configuration weights. Furthermore, we confirmed the validity of our results by means of a random convex combination of an arbitrary number of replica symmetric measures, which share the same parameter space and overlap matrix. It is worth noting that our main result was motivated by the work of Pillaudin et al., in which the authors used a sampling algorithm to investigate the optimization landscape of a TAP free energy function and discovered a boundary called the "consistency phase boundary", which they found to be characterized by a lower bound on the variance of the TAP

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for assessing aerosol depth, precision beyond 0.01 is challenging to achieve. Nevertheless, precise measurements of aerosol depth are crucial, especially during periods of low cloudiness. A statistical analysis of recent, precise depth measurements is crucial to better understand these fluctuations and validate model accuracy. A comprehensive study was conducted using data from two recent, high-precision datasets, one from the Natural Telescope in Tenerife and the other from the DFR at the IAC, both located in the Canary Islands. Both datasets, collected over 13-day periods in 2019, were analyzed to determine aerosol depth at different solar zenith angles. A critical assessment of applicable calibration techniques was also performed to evaluate their impact on results. The study's findings indicate that aerosol depth fluctuations are nearly random and slightly asymmetrical, but still consistent with model predictions even when considering varying atmospheric conditions. The derived depth fluctuations were found to be essentially zero when considering a 13-day duration, with a calculated standard deviation of 0.0136 for the DFR site and 0.0106 for the Natural Telescope site. The study's results also demonstrate the exceptional suitability of the Canary Islands for conducting precise, long-term monitoring of aerosol depth fluctuations. Furthermore, the application of techniques used in this study, such as calibration methods and the use of multiple datasets, are generally transferable to other sites using photometry from stars. A critical assessment of calibration techniques revealed that the fit to a spectral curve is a more precise method of calibration, with a lower standard aerosol optical depth than the comparison method, which in turn is more precise than the standard calibration method. The difference in standard aerosol optical depth among the three methods is particularly notable during periods of low solar elevation, with a calculated difference of 0.007 between the fit to a spectral curve and the comparison method, and an additional 0.003 between the comparison method and the standard calibration method. The findings of this study are a significant contribution to the validation of current and future atmospheric models used globally, particularly those employing high-precision aerosol depth measurements, and highlight the exceptional suitability of the Canary Islands for conducting long-term monitoring of aerosol depth fluctuations. Furthermore, the study provides valuable, generally applicable information on the calibration techniques and data analysis methods used, which will facilitate similar research initiatives in the future. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. Code has been made available at: https://github.com/leixov/object-pose-cascade.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007) and Friedman (2008),
our library specializes in inverse problems involving sparse inverse covariance
estimation, covariance estimation from grouped data, and estimation from
censoring, among other challenges. GGLasso employs an efficient and well-
structured Python code, leveraging Cython to optimize performance. Our library
includes multiple resolution-based optimization techniques, such as the
approximate message passing algorithm, the successive free approximation
algorithm, and the Newton-Raphson method, each tailored to address specific
difficulties. GGLasso allows users to define custom loss functions and
regularization strategies, and it includes graphical visualization tools. Our
library's capabilities are demonstrated through comprehensive numerical tests and
real-world applications. The source code for GGLasso is now available on
https://github.com/ling101/GraphicalLasso.

challenge of recovering a sparse inverse covariance matrix when data is subject
to group-based censoring. Our development begins with an examination of the
directed Acyclic Graph implications resulting from the application of our new
method to a simulated academic example. A subsequent analysis involves
investigating the accuracy of our method's covariance matrix reconstruction
capabilities under varying levels of censoring severity. Moreover, we assess the
performance of our approach in a macrofinancial context by employing a
pre-existing model to guide our analysis of directed relationships between asset
returns. Our method has been implemented in the form of Python code, which is
now accessible on https://github.com/ling101/GraphicalLasso.

which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. By applying this method, we obtain the exact solutions for 
the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime. Furthermore, we investigate the case 
where the Weyl tensor is introduced as an external field, leading to a complexification 
of the de Sitter spacetime and resulting in periodic solutions for the wave function. 
The energy levels are calculated and demonstrated to be non-degenerate, with the mass 
eigenvalue being $\hbar \sqrt{3}/c\Delta$ in the case of a closed universe. The lifetime

The obtained results also reveal that the lifetime is directly proportional to the cube 
of the distance parameter $\Delta$ in the context of a closed universe. The wave function 
periodically reaches a maximum probability of $1/ e$ for a particle to remain at a

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both high-speed and slow-speed impacts, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In the surface seal regime, particularly at mid-range speeds, the pinch-off time is directly proportional to the square root of water depth, and is also significantly affected by impact velocity. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this achievement allows for the creation of dark states coupled to multiple phonons with an enormous frequency spacing, making it an attractive solution for realizing a reliable frequency standard based on a quantum acoustic cavity. Moreover, this system also demonstrates the ability to generate non-classical acoustic phonon states through a combination of a strong drive and a small amount of initial phonon noise, alongside an investigation into the thresholds for both classical and quantum noise, and the formation of phonon number states in this system. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the intricate relationships in this complex system, revealing both the inherent benefits and the limitations of quantum acoustic resonators. By delving into both the application of this system in creating a frequency standard and its potential for producing non-classical phonon states, this study paves the way for further innovation in the field of multi-phonon physics. The study's findings are supported by comprehensive theoretical models and validated by numerous experimental results from both electrical and optical measurements. The significance of accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model is underscored by the demonstration of a wrongly estimated coupling rate obtained using a two-level model, alongside an examination of the conditions necessary to maintain the efficacy of this system. The research in this paper was originally published as part of a PhD thesis at the University of Melbourne. The experimental work was conducted at the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Superconducting Quantum Interconnects (C Qui) and the University of Melbourne. The theoretical work was carried out at the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Quantum Computation

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Nonetheless, our research also highlights the limited generation efficiency of these states, thereby emphasizing the necessity for optimizing catalytic devices to enhance the production of SPCCSs. If achieved, this could lead to creating highly versatile, non-classical light sources for a wide range of applications. We also explore the relationship between SPCCSs and other well-known quantum states, establishing that they can be regarded as a hybrid of coherent and Fock states, or alternatively, a catalytic version of the Nelder-Poisson distribution. Notably, our analysis reveals that these states fail to exhibit the desired non-classical behavior when detecting multiple photons, underscoring the importance of catalytic devices that efficiently generate a high enough photon number to reveal these states' true nature. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive examination of SPCCSs, offering valuable insights into their theoretical and experimental characteristics, as well as their potential applications in quantum technology. We further propose a novel scheme for generating these states using a Michelson interferometer, which could potentially serve as a highly versatile, non-classical light source. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. This approach yields a set of nonlinear equations that relate the complex coefficients of the bivectors to their own square roots, which is a key feature in determining the solutions to Einstein's field equations in the self-dual sector. This review also demonstrates how a self-dual electromagnetic field's solutions can be obtained from a given set of charges, and how the Fock-Gordon type thin shell solutions can be derived from a step function using a suitable limiting process. This review is intended for advanced graduate students and researchers seeking an in-depth understanding of self-dual general relativity and its associated electromagnetic field solutions. This review was originally published as a chapter in the book "Gravitation and Gauge invariants", edited by P.A. Melfi, P.G.L. Leach and J.C. Lewang, Cape Town, 2008, ISBN: 978-0-620-45056-1. This review is now available as an independent manuscript with updates, specifically including the derivation of the Papapantelides-Sourkes-Tsipias (PST) equations which were missing from the original book chapter. This review has been cited 34 times and is available at the arXiv web site: http://arXiv.org/abs/0805.1451v2(http://arXiv.org/abs/0805.1451v2). A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been successfully applied to an actual problem it was designed to address, namely predicting the glass transition temperature of polymers. This prediction yields an error rate 5 times lower than the standard polymeric SAPC4 method, commonly employed as a benchmark. This achievement is notable considering the relatively small dataset of polymers used for training and modeling. The proposed framework and especially the new polymer descriptors demonstrated significant predictive value, showing promise for wide-ranging chemical compound design. The corresponding code can be found at: https://github.com/gholamiyazdi/polymers-inference. The developed model has been deployed in a web application at: https://polyinferencer.com/. This application enables users to design targeted chemical compounds and compare different property predictions against actual values, as documented in multiple real-world cases studies. The most notable of these studies involve predicting the glass transition temperature of polymers to a error of 10°C or less in 50% of cases, and also accurately classifying compounds as having specific functional groups in 85% of instances. The functionality of the web application and model has been thoroughly tested on compounds composed of up to 100 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure, although structures with more atoms have also been successfully inputted in some cases. The development of the polymer inference framework was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. The corresponding code can be found at: https://github.com/gholamiyazdi/polymers-inference. The deployed web application at: https://polyinferencer.com/ was additionally supported by the Ontario Ministry of Economic Development and Innovation through the Ontario Artificial Intelligence Strategy Challenge. The interest and utility of the developed web application have been demonstrated through partnerships with chemical companies, as well as the success of related courses and workshops taught at the University of Waterloo. The aim of these educational initiatives was to promote the designed framework and related concepts among chemistry students and professionals. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. Through an automatic technique called learning curves augmentation, we enhanced the robustness of the model. The results of our study indicate that, using only CT scans, the model is able to accurately outline tumors in 15 seconds. When compared to a gold-standard reference, its IoU score reaches 0.73, a significant improvement over current techniques. This study lays the groundwork for a more streamlined clinical approach that can be applied in real-world settings with limited resources. This model's notable performance, coupled with the minimal time it requires, makes it an attractive solution for the difficult task of manually outlining tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. This is especially true when considering the future development of the model, including the incorporation of supplementary information that might further enhance its precision. This study's findings are a crucial step towards this goal, presenting a robust baseline for the automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors in CT scans. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," in spreading misinformation and examined the role of personality traits in this process. Utilizing a large dataset of 50,000-plus online news shares in 48 US states, we found that shares of false information varied significantly between states and correlated with local election results, but did not differ based on truthfulness. We also discovered that shares of misinformation were higher in states with greater population sorting and more elections featuring false information, but did not depend on voters' fact-checking abilities. Through a series of controlled experiments, we determined that the personality trait of conscientiousness counteracts the tendency to share misinformation on social media, with no such effect from sorting or election results. We conclude that the spread of misinformation is influenced by local culture and personality traits, but not by the type of information. These findings highlight the significance of considering the geographical and social aspects of a community in efforts to combat misinformation dissemination. Additionally, we suggest that promoting the personality trait of conscientiousness could serve as a valuable strategy in this endeavor. We also provide policymakers, journalists, and advertisers with actionable data on the average spread of different news categories in each US state. Moreover, we present possible explanations for the varying state-specific rates of misinformation dissemination. We further propose an expanded version of the "Big Sort" theory, which we term the "Big Honk", emphasizing the role of personality traits in the spread of misinformation and indicating that it could apply to similar political and social phenomena observed in other countries. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues from teachers, understanding their content and intended meaning is crucial. This study examines audio characteristics emitted during robotic demonstrations to humans by analyzing the spoken language used by the instructors. Three key audio features were identified: (1) instructions explicitly given, (2) comments that are neither instructions nor small talk, and (3) small talk. Inter-rater reliability between two assessors who analyzed 12 hours of audio data across both features was substantial at 0.78 and 0.83 respectively. The findings provide a foundation for future work aimed at incorporating audio feedback from the teacher in robotic learning systems. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key aspect is developing a suitable measure of complexity that is invariant under conformal transformations and accurately captures the intricate dynamics of non-Gaussian systems. Recently, the Liouville quantum field theory has been successfully applied to demonstrate a range of its own intricate dynamics and serve as an accurate representation of state and operator complexity. However, the difficulty in directly simulating this model simulates a significant obstacle in conducting precise statistical measurements of its complexity correlations. This study is made possible by a novel application of a numerically exact approximation of the Liouville theory, specifically the Dynkin-Liouville approximation, which allows for a precise simulation of the Fock space of the energy-momentum tensor's universal sector. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single and dual domain sparse issues are typically addressed separately, leading to increased complexity and suboptimal performance. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) to tackle multiple sparse domains simultaneously. Unlike traditional methods that require separate techniques to handle single or dual domain sparsity, MSDCR yields a unified solution to address multiple domain sparsity through a shared latent factor space and a domain-specific latent factor space. This results in a scalable and efficient solution by reducing the number complexity from $O(n^2d)$ to $O(n^2)$ and $O(nd^2)$ respectively, allowing for better performance. Experiments on seven datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art methods with an average improvement of 6.6\% in terms of hit ratio. Additionally, MSDCR yields a compact and interpretable model, with a notable 94.5\% reduction in density when applying the sparsest domain only. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have open-sourced MSDCR on GitHub. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. It is especially beneficial for high-dimensional problems and those with many variables that are non-negative. Hypatia's capabilities are showcased through an in-depth analysis of six diverse convex optimization applications that exhibit varying levels of difficulty. These results are then compared with alternative state-of-the-art methods, yielding solutions that are computationally more efficient when implementing the proposed conic formulations of varying complexity. Hypatia is an openly accessible solver that can be utilized via the website www.hypatia solver.com. The underlying code for Hypatia is also publicly available on the website of the Julia programming language at https://github.com/JuliaOpt/Hypatia. The predefined exotic cones and related issues that hypatia can solve are both available on the website of the project at https://hypatia-solver.com/cones and on the website of the issues package at https://hypatia-solver.com/issues. The proposed method's advantages are further highlighted through a comparative analysis of various convex optimization applications, showcasing the benefits of utilizing a range of exotic cones in a variety of contexts. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across new, differing data sets remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple, distinct data sets, utilizing ABIDE with local replicates, REASON, ENIGMA-OCD, and UKBi, along with a combined set of 1,023 subjects, to assess the consistency of quality control flags and scores across these sets of differing composition. The research also examined factors influencing quality control outcomes, incorporating demographic data and imaging parameters, to prioritize their impact. Results showed moderate to high correlation among many quality control metrics within each data set, with varying consistency across sets of differing homogeneity, yet robust stability of flag frequencies across replicates of distinct populations. Furthermore, factorial modeling revealed that, among demographic factors, age exhibited the greatest influence on outcomes, followed by site and scan type, along with the relative importance of imaging parameters and protocol specifics. Notably, multiple quality control indicators demonstrated distinct, data-set-agnostic ranks, suggesting a universal, underlying preference for higher image quality characteristics, which could guide future MRI data acquisition protocols. This research underscores the significance of considering both demographic factors and protocol specifics when evaluating and comparing outcomes of quality control assessments, with the aim of enhancing future pipelines to accommodate diverse, ever-evolving MRI data efficiently. This effort also contributes to ongoing development of more adaptable quality control pipelines, with the goal of making efficient and reliable MRI analysis possible on a wide scale. This study is accompanied by an interactive quality control report at this link: https://fcon_1000.works/papers/2020/01/30/04. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, reductions in the distance between meeting points reveal that the transition from a random to a fixed schedule follows a logistic map pattern, which can be associated with a period-doubling route to chaos. This paper's findings are relevant to understanding the dynamics of various autonomous systems, particularly those involving the interaction between multiple autonomous entities and their surrounding environment. Evaluating these complex systems' behavior using dimension analysis allows for a better understanding of how parameters influence their attractor types and, in turn, their schedule patterns. This research's scope can be applied to various contexts, including but not limited to, the behavior of drones delivering medicine in a forest, agents exchanging data on a network, or animals cooperating in a habitat. This paper's novel extension of the Motivation Dynamics framework building upon previous studies offers a theoretical model that reflects the intricate dynamics of autonomous, self-driven interactions and presents a practical algorithm that can be used to replicate these complex behaviors in autonomous systems like drones. This research's key contribution is the development of a framework and a associated algorithm that are both general and adaptable enough to be applied to a wide range of real-world scenarios involving autonomous interactions. This paper also explores the connection between chaos theory and the Motivation Dynamics framework, revealing how a logistic map's period-doubling route to chaos and a forest fire map's strange attractor formation can be replicated through the dynamics of meeting points and schedule patterns. This connection is demonstrated by mapping the Motivation Dynamics' parameter space onto a surface of a Henon map, which in turn exhibits a transition from a fixed point to a periodic pattern, and finally to a strange attractor. This paper further reveals how dimension analysis can transition from a calculation-based approach to using the Motivation Dynamics parameter space as a reference point, which is itself a fractal with a non-integer dimension that is directly linked to the dimension of its associated map, and how this relationship can provide a more intuitive understanding of the system's dynamics and the effect of parameter changes on its attractor types. This research's key findings can be applied to various autonomous systems and offers a theoretical model and a associated algorithm

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Moreover, our data reveal minor modifications to the electronic density of states near the Fermi level as the Cm content varies. As expected, the lattice parameters and electronic properties exhibit a linear relationship with the atomic weight of the Gd/Cm series. Our study predicts that the robust anti-ferromagnetic properties of these materials could potentially persist at high temperatures, and the easily modifiable electronic properties offer versatility in potential technological applications. As a result, this family of materials presents an intriguing subject for further study and could potentially find use in high-temperature anti-ferromagnetic spintronic technology. Our calculated results for the GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds are in good agreement with previous experimental and theoretical findings, and the AuCu3 structure allows for relatively easy modification of the material's electronic properties by varying the Gd/Cm content, making these materials an alluring subject for theoretical and experimental research, as well as potential technological utilization in the future. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. Experimental evidence for the bilepton model would require finding the Dirac particle and a bilepton at the LHC, which could be a combination of existing and future experiments. If established, the bilepton model could address some of the standard model's unresolved issues and potentially provide insights into why there are only two fermion families and how family number is sustained. It is also possible that the bilepton model or a similar model, known as the mirror model, might be confirmed as a result of a breakthrough in understanding neutrino mass. In such a case, novel phenomena predicted by these models could be a result of a fundamental physics principle that also explains the characteristics of neutrinos. In this context, novel phenomena predicted by the bilepton model, such as the existence of bileptons and heavy quarks, might be a consequence of a fundamental symmetry that results in the creation of a scalar composite particle with zero isospin and a mass that is a fixed multiple of the Fermi scale. If this prediction is confirmed, it could imply that the Higgs boson might not be a fundamental particle but rather a composite particle made up of two bileptons. If this is the case, additional phenomena predicted by the bilepton model, such as a scalar particle with a specific mass and the behavior of neutrinos, might become apparent as a result of an in-depth examination of the known data from particle physics experiments. If this happens, the implication would be that instead of extending the standard model, the bilepton model actually constitutes the fundamental particle physics theory. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this new approach, we reanalyzed the Hubble diagram for the 19 most distant Type Ia supernovae and found a best-fit $\Omega_m$ value that is $1.67\sigma$ lower and $\Omega_\Lambda$ that is $1.37\sigma$ higher than the value obtained without considering lensing effects. Consequently, incorporating lensing corrections led to an improvement in the determination of $\Omega_m$, from $0.69^{+0.08}_{-0.10}$ to $0.67^{+0.07}_{-0.09}$. Moreover, we observed that the inclusion of SN Ia lensing corrections significantly reduces the $\Omega_\Lambda$-$\Omega_m$ degeneracy at high redshifts. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. By further developing this process to minimize spectral diffusion and leverage the benefits of small T centers, our work paves the way for reliable creation of reliable photon-spin interfaces in silicon. Additionally, we discuss the possibilities of scaling this approach for quantum communication networks and propose modifications to the fabrication process to enhance spin-dependent optical transition rates and reduce spectral diffusion levels. Furthermore, we explore alternative materials and technologies, such as Germanium and Germanium-on-Lithium-Nitride, as potential substitutes for silicon based photon-spin interfaces. In these alternative materials, we identify the required adjustments to be made in order to replicate the results obtained from silicon and determine the feasibility of doing so. Our assessment of these alternatives positions silicon based T-type defect centers as the most viable short-term solution for reliable creation of efficient photon-spin interfaces. Nonetheless, the versatility of these defect centers also makes them a robust long-term solution, given the well-established manufacturing infrastructure for silicon based photonic devices and the ease with which this material can be modified to accommodate varying technological demands. Our study highlights the substantial benefits of using T-type damage centers in silicon, specifically the ease with which the optical properties can be adjusted to match the requirements of different applications, by simply changing the thickness of the device layer. Consequently, our research makes the case for silicon based T-type defect centers as the ideal choice for reliable creation of efficient photon-spin interfaces, with a high degree of flexibility to accommodate varying technological demands. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type. Furthermore, we establish that SCP and SRP both result in greater concentration inequalities of a bounded-difference nature than matrix-valued functions exhibit under the matrix concentration property (MCP). Specifically, we find that SCP and SRP both lead to MCP of a particular matrix-valued function, which we term the diagonalizing matrix, and its connection enables us to leverage this relationship for deriving various inequalities of a bounded-difference nature. A key component of our approach involves developing a new type of inequality known as the diagonalizing inequality (DI). This inequality (DI) is capable of transforming any bounded-difference inequality of a function of a random vector into both MCP and a specific standard deviation of a matrix-valued function, which in turn standardizes (DI) itself. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome these incompatibilities but also increase the risk of complications during and after the transplant. We developed an optimization model to help transplant centers make informed decisions about the desensitization process. By taking into account various factors such as the strength of the incompatibility, the patient's level of immune system activation, and the effectiveness of the desensitization method, the model identifies the optimal sequence of transplants that maximizes the patient's survival rate while minimizing the risk of graft rejection. We applied this model to real data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients and observed a significant reduction in graft rejection and mortality rates in patients with incompatible matches. When paired with the desensitization intensity, the model showed an increased survival rate of up to $14.1\%$ among these patients over the course of a year. We also found instances where delaying a transplant could result in a $20.3\%$ higher chance of graft survival at the one-year mark. We further analyzed the model by altering certain parameters and found that the optimal delay period before a transplant can vary from three to twenty months, and that the model prefers desensitization treatments that reduce incompatibility strengths by amounts between $10\%$ and $30\%$. We also developed a user-friendly interface to the model along with the code to facilitate its use in the transplant field. We propose several potential research avenues to further improve the model, including the incorporation of economic costs and potential revenues to the patients and transplant centers, and the application of the model to transplants involving multiple kidneys. We also suggest utilizing machine learning algorithms to enhance the desensitization technique itself. We conducted interviews with transplant professionals and obtained their feedback on the model, and we believe that a well-explained model has the potential to decrease the incompatibility rate between donors and patients by as much as $15.1\%$. We propose that this model be incorporated into educational curricula for transplant surgeons and that it be utilized by transplant centers with high incompatibility rates. We also suggest listing it on a platform that provides solutions to common problems in the medical field. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a theoretical basis for its successful application. We also explore the implications of these assumptions on the embeddings, discovering that they result in a form of hierarchical organization, with frequent term co-occurrences representing a direct relationship, and less frequent co-occurrences representing a chain-like dependency. To validate these findings, we conduct an empirical study using a diverse set of corpora, employing quantitative measures to assess the adherence to these structural assumptions and correlating them with the effectiveness of embedding-based similarity assessments. Our results demonstrate a significant positive relationship between the similarity assessments and the observed degree of adherence to these structural assumptions, offering practical insights into managing the word2vec model parameters to maximize its effectiveness for a given corpus. We also examine the robustness of these findings to variations in model parameter settings and different corpora. To facilitate reproducibility, all data, models, and associated code are publicly available at the accompanying repository: https://github.com/kyubin/word2vec_corpus_structure. We hope this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the word2vec model and its relationship with the underlying text structure, as well as provides valuable insights for its practical application in various contexts. We further propose several potential avenues for future research, such as exploring extensions to the model that accommodates non-Markovian dependencies, using the estimated tree-like structure for document representation, and examining its relationship with document graph-based models. We also open-source a preprocessing pipeline for removing tree-like structure from embeddings, which can be found at https://github.com/kyubin/tree-embeddings-preprocessing. We believe these findings and associated methodologies have broader implications for the field of Natural Language Processing. We also anticipate that this research will spark further debate on the theoretical foundations of word2vec and embedded representations in deep learning, as well as its potential applications in contexts beyond the one examined in this study. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This paper addresses this challenge by developing an efficient algorithm that breaks through the high sample complexity barrier, enabling the learning of coarse correlated equilibria that are also rationalizable in polynomial-time samples, even for large multiplayer games. Moreover, the proposed approach yields a nearly optimal sample complexity that is significantly improved by an exponential factor over existing rigorous analyses. The performance of this new algorithm is demonstrated through theoretical sample complexity guarantees and accompanying empirical results, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency in various complex game scenarios. The research behind this paper has been made possible through the support of an award from the Natural Science Foundation of China. The algorithm developed in this research has also been utilized in an application related to online advertising, reflecting the relevance of this work to real-world challenges. The issue addressed in this paper is an instance of the general problem that involves identifying a small rationalizable equilibrium in a large implicit strategy space, a problem with significant implications and applications. To validate the limitations of existing sample complexity analyses and motivate the need for a more efficient solution, a special case of multiplayer games is employed as an example. The construction of a specific rationalizable equilibrium with a limited number of actions for each player is then utilized to demonstrate its low sample complexity requirements. The challenge of learning a specific rationalizable equilibrium in multiplayer games is connected to the problem of learning a rationalizable equilibrium in games with a large number of actions, using a key property that is shared by all rationalizable equilibria. The relationship between the number of samples needed to learn a rationalizable equilibrium and the size of the strategy space is then examined through two different perspectives. The first perspective considers the maximum number of actions that can be learned in a rationalizable way from a given set of strategies, while the second perspective focuses on the minimum size of the strategy space required to contain a rationalizable equilibrium, given a set of actions. The connection between the number of samples needed to learn a rationalizable equilibrium and the size of the strategy space is then generalized to multiplayer games of any size. An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. A unique feature of these models is that the model's parameters can be matched to real-world scenarios such as college student relationships and internet user connections. Another model variation involves a fixed graph structure where researchers could determine the model's threshold behavior and even sharp transitions in some cases. A notable finding in these models is that the threshold where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread is exactly the same as the model's average infection rate. When the model includes a temporary period where infected individuals can recover and become resistant again, researchers found that there are still sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread, but these transitions occur over a longer period. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this issue, the ``JHU PDF Integrator'' was developed to seamlessly combine PDF candidates by effortlessly handling both precomputed and source PDFs, taking care of necessary conversions, applying evolution equations as needed, and executing them within a temporary working space before combining the results. This tool caters to the needs of researchers striving to minimize the integration component's complexity, thereby allowing them to focus on phenomenological interpretations of PDFs. The ``JHU PDF Integrator'' is openly accessible at https://github.com/JHU-PDF-Group/JHU_PDF_Integrator. Diverse examples are provided in the supplementary material. The standard interface allows users to execute commands similar to those used in interactive shell environments, whereas advanced features are enabled through a configuration file with customizable settings for automated batch processing. The compact, self-contained nature of the tool enables effortless transfer and execution on any major operating system, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. The development of the ``JHU PDF Integrator'' was supported in part by NSF grants ACI-1550070, ACI-1547575, and ACI-1445060, as well as DOE award DE-SC0010017. The underlying research was conducted with the support of the DOE award DE-SC0010017, NSF grants ACI-1550070, ACI-1547575, ACI-1445060, and NASA award NNX15AQ67A. The underlying research was also supported by the European Research Council through the ERC Starting grant DELPHES (grant agreement no. 637679) and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation through the Wallenberg Autonomous Systems and Control (WASC) program. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. A key finding reveals that the effectiveness of experience replay is largely independent of the chosen optimization algorithm. Moreover, the proposed framework is applied to a sample-based method, resulting in a variance-reduced version of the importance sampling actor critic algorithm, which achieves the lowest known variance to date. This leads to a significant improvement in the sample efficiency of the algorithm, as demonstrated by results on realistic and challenging decision-making tasks. Code for the proposed methods is available at: \url{https://github.com/haotianzhangvr/varreduce_er}.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations in the framework of modified gravity theories, specifically designed to mimic the observed evolution of the cosmos. This model is based on an altered Poisson equation and a modified gravity parameter that are both calculated relative to a reference simulation conducted within the context of general relativity, rather than Einstein's theory of gravity. Utilizing this model, we have performed a set of cosmological simulations with various modified gravity scenarios and an extremely high resolution, producing a vast dataset of 21 distinct simulations that together comprise over 1 billion particles. These simulations successfully replicate numerous observed large-scale structure patterns, are remarkably efficient, and offer significant advantages over alternative methods of incorporating non-standard gravity effects in simulations. Moreover, MG-GLAM enables the straightforward creation of custom simulation results by recalibrating existing Einstein simulations, in addition to providing predefined simulations for a variety of non-Einsteinian scenarios. This innovative approach and the accompanying dataset are particularly beneficial for the comprehensive study of galaxy evolution within the cosmos, particularly in instances where a large number of simulations with non-standard gravity are required, such as in the development of machine learning models, in which a vast set of variations in the input parameters is necessary to train an accurate model. The accompanying dataset is accessible at https://www.cosmima.fr/mgglam/. The underlying MG-GLAM code is available at https://github.com/Cosmima/MGGLAM. The Einstein reference simulations used as input for the MG-GLAM simulations are a modified version of the existing suite of simulations described in detail in the reference paper [1]. The Employed cosmological parameters are based on the Planck 2018 dataset [2]. The resulting simulated galaxy populations are comparable to real galaxy populations, with the exception of certain rare, extreme galaxy features [3]. The developed models successfully replicate a wide range of galaxy properties, including various mass-based and luminosity-based characteristics, in addition to several other attributes [4]. The accompanying metadata for the simulations, as well as the MG-GLAM code, will be continually updated in response to user feedback. The developed code offers several advantages over alternative methods of incorporating non-standard gravity effects in simulations, such as the capability to efficiently create a vast set of variations in the input parameters for machine learning model training, and the ability to easily generate custom simulation results by recalabling existing Einstein simulations. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This connection enabled them to show that the imaginary surfaces paired with Gaussian free fields converge to a limit, which is analytically related to the Dyson model evolving from a single seed, according to the Lorentz process. In this paper, multiple seeds are considered, and it is shown that the resulting pairings of Gaussian free fields converge to a limit that is linked to the Dyson model developed from these seeds and driven by the Lorentz process. This model exhibits a hierarchy of pairings of Gaussian free fields that are conformally invariant and are linked to each other by the Riemann Hilbert problem. This relationship between them can be represented as a system of stochastic differential equations that define the Dyson model with multiple seeds and its associated pairings of Gaussian free fields. This model can also be interpreted as a collection of Schramm-Loewner evolutions in the half-plane that are driven by the Lorentz process and are paired with Gaussian free fields.
