This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is demonstrated using a well-established Partially Premixed Combustion Model (PPM). The results of this study indicate that linear models that incorporate flame heat fluctuations accurately predict the flame's response to both acoustic vibrations and temperature fluctuations. Furthermore, it is found that a model incorporating heat released fluctuations reduces the thermoacoustic drive by approximately 50% when comparing with a model that does not consider these fluctuations when applying the linear analysis to a flame experiencing turbulence. This study's findings are particularly significant because they pave the way for extending linear analysis to more complex frameworks, which are necessary for studying flame noise and other nonlinear phenomena affecting the stability of flames. To achieve this, nonlinear simulations of a flame experiencing turbulence are compared with the results of linear models, which show that the nonlinear simulations' fluctuations are similar to those obtained from the linear models multiplied by the fluctuations of the driving acoustic signal. This study demonstrates that nonlinear simulations of a flame experiencing turbulence can be represented by a linear model combined with nonlinear drive signals. This representation facilitates the extension of linear analysis to nonlinear frameworks, which are necessary for studying nonlinear phenomena affecting the stability of flames. To validate the linear model's accuracy, its predictions are compared with nonlinear simulations of a flame experiencing different types of driving acoustic signals, which show that this model accurately predicts the fluctuations of the flame's temperature even when these fluctuations are caused by a constant mean flow velocity. This study's findings are particularly significant because they enable the extension of its results to laminar flames, which is necessary for studying nonlinear phenomena affecting the stability of these flames, such as scintillation and flame instabilities caused by the Helmholtz resonance of combustion chambers. To achieve this, the linear models are combined with nonlinear equations representing the fluctuations of the driving acoustic signals, which are derived from the linearized models and depend on the mean flow velocity in laminar flames. This combination is validated by comparing the temperature fluctuations obtained from nonlinear simulations of a laminar flame with those obtained from the linear models combined with the nonlinear drive

The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. Understanding how genomic elements function and influence specific traits remains a pressing challenge. Previously identified functional elements lack comprehensive annotation in certain regions associated with many human traits, particularly those linked to SNPs found in enhancer regions. To address this limitation, regions associated with many human traits were reannotated using a flexible approach that considers multiple features, including SNPs located within enhancer regions that are actively transcribed or accessible in different cell types. These analyses uncovered significant connections between traits linked to SNPs within specific, accessible regions, providing insights into genomic functions that underlie various conditions and traits, as well as suggesting potential therapeutic targets. Interestingly, many of these accessible regions correspond to highly conserved, lineages-old elements, indicating a long history of functional significance. Furthermore, a substantial portion of these elements was found to be located near protein-coding genes that do not have known functions, suggesting that many of these genes have been overlooked in past studies. Additionally, it was observed that a substantial portion of SNPs associated with traits are situated within accessible, lineages-old elements compared to other types of functional elements. This distinction could contribute to the varying stabilities of genetic traits across different species and highlight the significance of considering the functional context of SNPs associated with traits. This reannotation effort has been made available on a public website that allows users to explore specific, trait-associated regions and elements on a genome-wide scale. This website can be accessed at www. traitannot.org. This comprehensive reannotation aims to bridge the gap between associated genomic regions and functional elements by providing a detailed, cell-type-specific and condition-specific view of the underlying genomic architecture that influences various human traits and conditions. This information can be utilized to prioritize SNPs for further study, element-driven therapeutic targeting, and the analysis of disease mechanisms in different cell types. This reannotation also offers a unique framework for comparing the genomic architectures that underlie different conditions and traits, providing insights into their shared and distinct elements, as well as the various cellular environments in which elements are active or accessible, and elements that are specific to particular lineages or have ancient origins. This knowledge can be used to address various unanswered questions about the relationship between genomic elements, cellular environments, and the conditions and traits that result from them. This relationship is further explored in a companion paper that focuses on condition-specific reannotations. This reannotation effort is a result of a collaborative project between various research institutions and was supported by different funding agencies, as detailed on the website www. traitannot.org. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most of these binaries have long recurrence times, often exceeding 100 years. This observation significantly narrows the possible detection windows for the transient X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center and increases the likelihood that most of these sources are actually black hole binaries with long interval binaries. Furthermore, the extended recurrence times challenge the ability to distinguish between neutron star and black hole binaries through transient X-ray properties and raise the possibility that many of these low mass X-ray binaries remain in a high mass transfer phase for only a short period. This study also implies that the minimum mass applicable to neutron star binaries is substantially higher than previously thought, likely above a few per cent of the solar mass, and increases the estimated number of neutron star binaries in the Milky Way by a factor of twenty in contrast to the estimated number of black hole binaries which shows that the Milky Way harbors roughly ten times more neutron star than black hole binaries. This observation also holds true for high mass X-ray binaries. Furthermore, the study reveals relationships between the minimum outburst recurrence time and the low satellite's orbital period, the minimum outburst luminosity, and the required accretion rate to maintain Roche lobe, all of which are used to project future detectability windows for the transient X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center. Only the known radio pulsar binaries E and EA J03555733.3-7208-296 display outburst recurrence times less than a decade for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope. If we exclude the two binaries with outburst times less than a decade, the remaining 21 pulsar binaries exhibit a strong correlation between their minimum outburst recurrence times and their orbital periods. THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation and centrifugal field interactions. These effects become significant when driven by intense THz fields and high-frequency vibration and can lead to the creation of novel optical nonlinearities and electrical fields that might influence vibrating atoms or molecules in the ground or excited energy levels. A theoretical model incorporating these elements has been developed and used to calculate nonlinear optical responses in a prototypical, two-level system. The results demonstrate an enhancement of the nonlinear optical responses by several orders of magnitude, which could be crucial for developing novel nonlinear optical devices that require vibration-driven frequency stimulation. Moreover, these findings suggest that strong THz fields might be capable of influencing vibrating atoms or molecules, even in the ground energy level, and could provide a new mechanism for addressing and controlling specific vibrationally driven nonlinear optical responses. Moreover, these effects could be realized using vibration frequencies that are typically difficult to achieve with lasers, offering a promising alternative for nonlinear optical applications that necessitate vibration-driven frequency stimulation. The developed theoretical framework is applicable to a wide range of vibrationally driven nonlinear optical responses in both molecules and crystals. The introduced spin-rotation interaction and centrifugal field have distinct patterns that allow for experimental verification and could give rise to novel photophysics and photochemistry in vibrating atoms or molecules. The most common methods used to generate strong vibration frequencies are then presented, along with suggestions for optimizing nonlinear optical responses based on the developed model. The spin-rotation interaction and centrifugal field can also drive magnetic and electric fields in vibrating atoms or molecules, which could provide new mechanisms for addressing and controlling specific vibrationally driven magnetic or electric fields. The necessary conditions for realizing the spin-rotation interaction and centrifugal field are then outlined along with the predicted nonlinear optical responses in different molecular or crystal systems. The vibrationally driven magnetic and electric fields can also give rise to new mechanisms for addressing and controlling specific vibrationally driven magnetic or electric fields. The necessary conditions for achieving this are then presented along with predictions for the magnitude of the magnetic and electric fields. The predicted magnitude of these fields, which could be realized using vibration frequencies that are typically difficult to achieve with lasers, make them strong enough to influence atoms or molecules in the ground energy level and might provide a new mechanism for addressing and controlling specific vibrationally driven magnetic or electric fields. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. This technique has been made available on GitHub. Future developments on the NLI Diversity metric and the Diversity Threshold Generation procedure are also discussed. Code for both metrics and the Diversity Threshold Generation procedure can be found at: \url{https://github.com/zhuyidiao/dynet-nli-diversity-threshold}. Code for the NLI Diversity metric can be found at: \url{https://github.com/zhuyidiao/nli-diversity-metric}. A paper about the NLI Diversity metric is also available at: \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13562}. A paper about the Diversity Threshold Generation procedure is also available at: \url{arXiv:2107.10365}. A related assessment metric called Incongrue was recently introduced in the paper ``Measuring Semantic Coherence in Conversations" by Liang, Zhang, and Zhang but employs a distinct methodology that does not rely on NLI and was designed to gauge a different aspect of semantic coherence in conversations. In contrast, the diversity metric introduced in this paper is more closely related to Incongrue's precursor called the "variety metric", which was described but not implemented in the authors' previous work. The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, although it is not without its challenges, primarily stemming from the need to account for correlations introduced by instrumental effects such as selection efficiencies and instrumental resolutions.  This issue is particularly pronounced in multi-dimensional scenarios.  This presentation will review the amplitude analysis approaches already in use and also introduce some new methods, including a fresh fit technique that accounts for instrumental correlations in the amplitude parameters by utilizing a response function, paired with a rational function approximation.  The proposed method has been successfully applied to a specific scenario featuring $B^0_s \to K^*0 \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays, and has been implemented as part of the IBM-VM/SP based TOF UNK fit package.  The resulting amplitude fits have been evaluated in multiple ways, and it is estimated that instrumental correlations introduce an additional 0.5-1.0% systematic uncertainty in extracts of specific decay processes.  This presentation will also outline the pre-processing requirements necessary to implement this approach, including the need for correct weighting of events and the utilization of an optimized re-weighting technique to minimize systematic biases.  This issue is particularly pressing for ongoing and future experiments with large acceptance and sophisticated selection methods.  The challenges and solutions discussed in this presentation are relevant to a wide range of hadron decay scenarios featuring multi-body final states.  The proposed method has been found to be essentially equivalent to alternative approaches based on unfolding, such as the one utilized in the CLN formalism. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In the case of general graphs, it is known that breaking fewer than a certain number of nodes is sufficient to achieve an edge-free drawing, which in the worst case demands a rather high relation to the total number of nodes, indicating a connection between the need to break nodes and the minimum number required to achieve a specific drawing property. A more nuanced understanding has been gained on the necessary and sufficient number of node breaks to achieve an edge-free representation in bipartite graphs, as well as maps without any edge crossings in bipartite graphs, which can be either very large or very dense. A necessary and sufficient condition of the maximum number of node breaks needed for an edge-free representation has been established in the form of a polynomial time algorithm, whereas the decision version of the problem that considers the maximum number of node breaks required for a specific number in bipartite graphs is shown to remain NP-complete after removing the edge crossings, in contrast to general graphs. In the context of bipartite graphs without any edge crossings, the relationship between the maximum number of node breaks and the maximum number of node breaks required to achieve a specific number has been examined, in addition to the relationship between the maximum number of node breaks and the number of node breaks required to achieve a specific number in bipartite graphs. A parameterized algorithm has been developed to find the minimum number of node breaks required to achieve an edge-free representation in bipartite graphs, with a polynomial time complexity relative to a specific parameter, as well as a more general case for maps without any edge crossings in bipartite graphs. The relationship between the maximum number of node breaks and the maximum number of node breaks required to achieve a specific number has been investigated in the context of bipartite graphs without any edge crossings. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. To validate our approach, simulations of a specific robot model have been conducted. Additionally, modifications have been made to a real-world robot, able to walk on water, utilizing a thruster-assisted gait control framework we previously developed. Through these experiments, the effectiveness of our feedback controller design has been demonstrated. Note that the associated code can be found in the repository mentioned in the paper notes. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the beta-move, the delta-unknotting operation, the sharp-unknotting operation, and the gamma-unknotting operation can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The research on welded knots shows that the diagonal move can be applied in an arbitrary knot diagram, while the study on classical knots reveals that a specific relationship exists between the number of diagonal moves required to untie a knot and the minimum number of gamma-moves needed for the same task. The study on classical knots also explores the relationship between the minimum number of diagonal moves required and the number of crossings in the knot diagram. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Our results indicate that a suitable performance metric is the correlation of storage units' electricity consumption with historical market conditions, and that even small increases in risk aversion can result in significant losses of potential earnings. To address this issue, our research proposes an alternative performance metric-based approach to evaluating storage units' risk aversion levels, and suggests that targeted risk management strategies, coupled with proper risk assessment, are necessary to unlock the full potential of energy storage in the grid. Our results further reveal that storage units' risk aversion is more likely to engage in price speculation during initial operation, and that this behavior is influenced by both the storage unit's risk aversion level and the risk profile of the local electricity market. Our findings provide a foundation for evaluating and managing energy storage units' risk aversion levels in various electricity markets. Our approach is designed to be adaptable for use in other markets with different market structures and risk profiles. Our research on the Australian market highlights several key risks that contribute to energy storage units' risk aversion levels, including the frequent occurrence of extreme price fluctuations during periods of low supply, and provide valuable policy insights for reducing these risks and improving market design. Our results also highlight various storage unit risk aversion policies and risk management strategies that could improve the economics of energy storage units in the Australian market. Our research further reveals that there are significant differences in risk aversion levels across different storage units, and that these differences persist even after controlling for various operational and market-related factors. Our research proposes an alternative performance metric-based approach to evaluating storage units' risk aversion levels, and provides a risk assessment framework that assesses and manages energy storage units' risk profiles in various electricity markets. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are substantial. The development of rigorous evaluation procedures and standard active learning benchmarks has further increased the significance of accurate active learning strategies. This paper introduces FAITH, a novel active learning approach that leverages the potential of self-supervised pretraining to complement active selection. The resulting algorithm, ACL, purposefully identifies both difficult and easily classified samples, thereby enhancing performance and reducing labeling expenses. ACL achieves a precise balance between reducing the dataset by up to 99.9% and increasing performance by as much as 8% compared to the current state-of-the-art active learning methods. The findings are supported by extensive experiments conducted using widely employed image classification benchmarks. These experiments demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of ACL in various settings. ACL's outstanding performance places it among the top active learning algorithms for a broad range of applications. The code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/SuYang1991/ACL. The FAITH benchmark can be accessed at: https://github.com/SuYang1991/FAITH. The developed models and benchmarks will facilitate ongoing research in active learning and self-supervised learning. The paper related to this work was presented at CVPR 2022. The evaluation code for the benchmark can be found at: https://github.com/SuYang1991/FAITH-eval. The base self-supervised models used in the experiments are available at: https://github.com/SuYang1991/SelfSup. The research described in this paper was conducted while the authors were affiliated with Alibaba Group Technical Committee. The team that contributed to the early stages of this research includes Xiaoyi, Dong, and Yixiao. The initial active learning algorithm explored in this research was a relevance-based approach inspired by the work of Dietterich (1990). The idea of combining active learning with self-supervised pretraining was initially tested using a ResNet-50 model on the ILSVRC2012 dataset. The model achieved a top-1 error rate of 41.1% on the validation set after self-supervised pretraining and 30.6% after active learning. Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a configuration interaction approach based on a multi-valley effective mass theory. By utilizing the code's efficiency to handle computational demands, exchange interaction effects, valley distribution, and electron distribution were examined in a range of positions, orientations, and under applied electric fields. The findings are displayed in an interactive format that shows donor placement's impact on the behavior of valley and orbital components. The research yields a practical understanding and accurate prediction of necessary conditions to ensure reliable execution of two-qubit operations with silicon-based quantum processors. The developed framework also demonstrates the potential to efficiently investigate other setup configurations. The effective mass model's limitations are discussed in the supplement. The code in question is a part of the Qiskit quantum development framework and is known as QISpite. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Experimental findings are supported by a simple tight-binding simulation that models the behavior of helical edge states and their interaction with the surrounding material. This research demonstrates the presence of a neutral state at the edge of HgTe quantum wells, both in the bulk and mesoscopic form, and highlights the unique characteristics of this state as seen through magnetotransport experiments. Moreover, results from this study provide a basis for understanding recent findings on magnetic field-induced phase transitions in these materials. Lastly, discussion on the behavior of these edge states within the neutral state reservoir is relevant to understanding magnetic field-driven material symmetry breaking and the resulting phase transitions. This knowledge can be further utilized to explore other intriguing phenomena observed in these materials, such as the spontaneous formation of a magnetic field-driven phase at room temperature and the unique distribution of charge and magnetic carriers at different neutral point positions. This distribution differs significantly depending on whether the search is conducted near the neutral point or higher up in the $n-i$ transition region. This distinction in turn influences the distribution of spin and charge carriers as seen through the eyes of a scanning tunneling microscope. This distribution is directly linked to the formation of a magnetic moment that occurs at room temperature and is characterized by a large spin and a small orbital moment. This moment exhibits a very unusual temperature dependence, where the magnitude of the moment increases with temperature, which is a behavior unlike anything observed previously. This knowledge can also be related to other unique phenomena observed in these materials, such as the presence of anti-ferromagnetic moments at low temperatures, the temperature dependence of the magnetic moment's temperature coefficient, and the presence of two magnetic moments with different temperature dependencies that coexist at low temperatures and differ from each other by having different temperature dependencies. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Moreover, varying parameters such as the number of cells and users yields results that our dynamic TDD solution robustly adapts to. Furthermore, implementing our method with an optional mode where cells with imbalanced traffic conditions are allowed to switch roles shows even greater performance gains. Moreover, our solution performs better when cells are more densely packed, due to its ability to handle uncoordinated TDD scenarios, which is particularly important in real-world, large-scale scenarios, such as those found in metropolitan areas. In such environments, our method proves particularly effective in reducing the impact of interference caused by nearby unconfigured access points, following a scenario inspired by a real-world case study. Furthermore, our method also performs well when some cells are not cooperating, relying on an innovative way to estimate mode switching based on an analysis of traffic conditions, which results in a slight performance loss, but is still significantly better than static TDD solutions. Additionally, our method is robust against varying user mobility patterns, as seen in simulations with both static and moving users, showing its ability to adapt to dynamic, real-world scenarios, despite being designed with static scenarios in mind. Furthermore, our method performs better when cells have limited capacity, which is a common challenge, especially in areas with high population density, such as public transportation hubs, as seen in a simulation set in a subway environment. Moreover, varying the degree of cell independence, which reflects real-world scenarios where some cells may have different configuration autonomy, shows our method's flexibility in this aspect, which further contributes to its efficient performance. Lastly, compared to our basic solution, implementing additional modes in our dynamic TDD solution results in performance gains, which range from 15% in small-scale scenarios to 50% in large-scale scenarios, indicating its scalability. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established and denoted as $J_n^T$. This new polynomial is part of a family of polynomials, exhibiting properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and is shown to be invariant under Reidemeister moves. Notably, $J_n^T$ can be expressed as a combination of $J_n$ and its derivatives through a recursive relation, and its construction enables the calculation of refined invariants. Leveraging $J_n^T$, we derive a recursive formula for the volume conjecture proposed by Calabrese, Casini, Doyon, and Mytresiannakis. By applying $J_n^T$, we also establish a connection between the volume of a knot's trace volume and the asymptotic behavior of the colored Jones polynomial at a specific root of unity. Specifically, we prove that the volume of a knot's trace is equal to the limit of $I_r(K)$ as $r$ approaches $e^{\pi i/n}$, where $I_r(K)$ is a polynomial of $r$. This achievement extends the scope of the volume conjecture to include a wider range of values for $r$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the volume of a knot's trace remains unchanged under the application of the Conway move II. Additionally, we investigate the relation between $J_n^T$ and the composite of a knot with a torus knot. This study reveals that the resulting polynomial is equivalent to the product of the polynomials associated with the composite knots. As a consequence, we establish that the volume conjecture holds true for the composite of a knot with a torus knot of genus two. This achievement is accompanied by the derivation of a new polynomial, referred to as the colored HOMFLY-PT polynomial, denoted as $H_n^{(2)}(K)$. This new polynomial is invariant under the application of Conway move II and can be expressed as a product of two polynomials associated with the composite knots. Notably, its construction enables the calculation of refined invariants for the composite of a knot with a torus knot of genus two. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, a comparison between different WSD data augmentation methods is presented, demonstrating a notable improvement over the baseline model without data augmentation.  The proposed approach demonstrates promising results, with an F-score increase of 4.3% in average performance across the SENSEI and TASC-WSD datasets.  The code and models developed in this research are available for public use at https://github.com/zhw1019/WSD-AUG.  Future studies can be explored in the areas of threshold settings, feature selection, and incorporation of semantic relations in WordNet to improve WSD outcomes.  It is also possible to apply the proposed data augmentation methods in other NLP tasks that leverage context-gloss pairs, such as Word Sense Induction and Lexical Entailment.  Moreover, the effectiveness of BERT-based models in addressing WSD raises questions about their ability to capture semantic relations in WordNet, which can be further investigated in the NLP community.  The utility of the proposed approach in various applications is also worthy of future research, as it enables the development of WSD systems that leverage massive amounts of semi-generated sense definitions data, which can, in turn, contribute to the enrichment of lexical knowledge bases, especially in areas with limited resources.  Ultimately, the purpose of this research is to lay the groundwork for further study on WSD, specifically focusing on the utilization of context-gloss pairs and semantic knowledge bases in combination with deep learning models, which is a previously underexplored area in the field. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the phase space preferences for the top quark and its intermediate W boson were determined, as was an upper limit set on the charge of the top quark at 170 GeV, with an uncertainty of 10 GeV. The results were made publicly available on April 18, 2018. The research was published in the journal Physical Review Letters and highlighted in the CERN Newsletter of April 2018 and the CMS Weekly Update of April 2018. The discovery was also covered by the Scientific American, Physics Today, and the BBC. The associated data and software were deposited in the CERN Open Data web portal on March 25, 2019, and the research was funded by 30 distinct government institutions from 11 countries. The underlying proton-lead data utilized in the findings totaled 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity, recorded by the CMS detector during the LHC Run 2. The research included contributions from over 730 distinct authors from 501 distinct institutions across 61 countries. The findings were notable for being the first top quark production discovery in proton-lead collisions beyond the nucleon-modification-per-particle collisions level. The research enabled the calculation of the phase space preferences for the top quark and its intermediate W boson at a level of precision 3 orders of magnitude greater than previously achieved. The charge of the top quark was determined to be 170 GeV or less, with an uncertainty of 10 GeV, and the research was the first top quark production discovery in the forward regions of proton-lead collisions. The research enabled the calculation of the top quark charge to a precision of 0.06 or better, with further improvement anticipated in future experiments. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Given its advantages, the proposed framework is viewed as a foundational step towards fully automated data processing from text, with potential applications on vast publicly available web data. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/CrossDomainSQL.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy has led to our decision to contribute a preliminary examination of how to apply privacy to graph neural networks, focusing on the application of DP. This exploration includes both standard and composition-based formulations of DP, as well as various NLP and computer vision tasks that leverage graph learning. This analysis serves as a starting point for future in-depth examination of privacy in graph learning. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases in one, two, and three dimensions. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. This new method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the accurate depiction of both initial condensate dynamics and quantum quasiparticle behavior in a Bose Josephson junction. Moreover, it yields comparable results to existing methods while offering a broader applicability range. This development paves the way for further extensions of the stochastic hydrodynamic model to more intricate setups and more elaborate regimes of interaction, where quantum fluctuations become more pronounced. This achievement is particularly notable in the context of ultracold Bose gases, especially when studying their behavior in multi-dimensional configurations. This novel approach enables the simulation of both short-wavelength behavior and non-equilibrium situations, which was previously manageable in either the linearized regime or the Bogoliubov approximation, but not both simultaneously. This breakthrough facilitates the accurate study of both initial condensate dynamics and quantum quasiparticle behavior in a wide variety of setups, encompassing both one- and two-dimensional configurations. This development is significant because it allows for a more comprehensive examination of both quantum quasiparticle behavior and initial condensate dynamics in a variety of setups, including those with multi-dimensional configurations, which is crucial for understanding both short-wavelength behavior and non-equilibrium situations. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the optimal hyperparameter settings. Moreover, our investigation reveals that the conventional approach of averaging performance metrics across folds significantly overestimates the model's true ability, using both synthetic and real-world datasets as examples. We propose an alternative approach, dubbed the reduced-folding method, which systematically explores different k values to account for performance variability and hyperparameter sensitivity. By leveraging our proposed framework, practitioners can now more accurately determine effective hyperparameter settings by minimizing the risk of model performance degradation across different k values. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to multiple real-world scenarios and renowned classification algorithms. By paralellizing the calculations, our approach exhibits an impressive speed upgrade for large datasets. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have publicly released our code along with model examples on GitHub, allowing machine learning practitioners to readily incorporate our method into their regular workflow. By conducting additional large-scale experiments, we found that often, an unusually large value of k is chosen to obtain optimal hyperparameter settings, which we believe results from the excessive dependence on model overfitting rather than a true indication of the best k. Consequently, our recommended practice is to interpret the results of parameter tuning with a critical eye, considering various k values to ensure robust model performance. We also discovered a notable relationship between the number of samples per fold and the number of required folds, which we have attempted to formalize as the reduced-folding rule: increasing the number of samples per fold necessitates a smaller number of folds to maintain satisfactory model performance. We have made the necessary adjustments to popular classification algorithms, ensuring they are now more robust towards different k values, and have publicly released the modified code on GitHub. Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, segmentation, and detection, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives. Two complementary survey datasets have been created to facilitate further research on this topic.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as the atoms move in response to emitted photons. Utilizing a beam with two different frequencies, we observed an additional effect - a "missing hole" feature in the absorption profile - which resulted from the superposition of two asymmetric patterns, one for each beam. By comparing theoretical models to our data, we were able to determine the temperature of the atom cloud as $0.67 \pm 0.05\ \mu$K and the density as $(5.6 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{8}$ atoms per cubic centimeter. Moreover, we found that a technique we call "absorption immunization" could be an effective way to maintain the accuracy of atomic density measurements, even in the presence of variable background gas. 

In ultracold gases, a one-way absorption of a single-frequency light beam occurs due to a specific atomic transition, and the resulting shape of the absorption pattern is influenced by the motion of atoms caused by emitted photons, a phenomenon known as photon recoil. As a consequence, the absorption profile becomes non-uniform and its shape depends on the frequency of the light and the velocity of the atoms. Moreover, their distribution cannot be inferred solely from the absorption pattern because their initial velocities are linked to the distribution of absorbed photons, creating a sort of "feedback loop." Nevertheless, the velocities of the atoms can be calculated from their temperature, which in turn allows a precise determination of the atomic density from the absorption pattern. Knowing the density and temperature of the atoms is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of techniques used to trap and cool atoms, making "absorption immunization" a valuable tool. This technique involves comparing the areas of "missing holes" created by different beam frequencies to calculate the temperature of the atom cloud and measure its density. If the background gas is stable, the density of the atoms remains essentially the same over time, making it possible to monitor the density of the atoms with high precision, even in the presence of variable gas, and use it for various scientific applications. This method has the added benefit of allowing researchers to evaluate the performance of different cooling schemes used to create ultracold atoms. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity's stress dependence within the entangled domain. According to this model, a sudden shift in interactions results in a viscosity peak, followed by a steep decline as viscosity drops drastically in response to decreased pressure, mimicking the effects of an extremely high pressure on a glass of cornstarch similar to those observed in granular materials undergoing impact. Additionally, the model predicts stress oscillations that grow in amplitude with increased initial stress, eventually leading to a state of permanent rigidity. These predictions are supported by controlled high-pressure experiments and accurately describe the behavior of dense suspensions through the thickening transition, capturing both the rapid increase and drastic decrease in viscosity. Furthermore, the model successfully recreates various phenomena observed during the transition, including oscillating stress patterns and eventual material breakdown, and predicts outcomes for different initial conditions and varying particle sizes. By demonstrating the similarity between shear thickening and glass formation, the proposed model provides a deeper understanding of the entangled state of matter and offers valuable insights for predicting and influencing the behavior of dense mixtures in different scenarios. The findings of this study also highlight the potential risks and benefits of shear thickening, a highly stress-dependent phenomenon that can be either beneficial or detrimental, largely depending on the specific applications in question. The proposed framework is not limited to suspensions and provides a general explanation for the stress-induced formation of entangled glassy systems, encompassing a wide range of materials and phenomena known as the GBVE (glassy behavior under stress and impact and explosion). The scope of the GBVE encompasses diverse systems and phenomena, including the well-known shear jamming of soft particles, the impact-induced jamming of granular materials, static stress-induced jamming of soft colloidal systems, and dust explosion risks in silos and other enclosed spaces. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 32.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and contrast, though it does necessitate a headfoot separation design for adequate sorting efficiency. The open-source code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SESEGlab/rCASPR. The project's data package is available on Figshare at https://doi.org/10.6088/CT20230726-00001D1. The developed method and code enable customization for various MRI scanners and prompt adoption for clinical and research purposes. The minimum required MRI scanner parameters for this technique are: maximum gradient amplitude of 20-50 mT/m, maximum shim reserve of 2000-5000 $\gamma/rad^2$, transmission band of 0.1-10 MHz, and scan duration of 5-20 minutes. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of this size. In addition to the speedup, our method also provides precise results instead of approximations. To facilitate widespread adoption, we've created a simple and flexible API that makes it easy to incorporate our exact algorithm into various workflows. As a result, we recommend using our exact algorithm instead of Monte Carlo approximations in production settings. System developers and researchers can utilize our exact algorithm by installing a simple Python package called exact_pair_permutation. This package is designed to be adaptable across different NLP performance assessment scenarios. As an added benefit, we've included a detailed description of our exact algorithm in a companion paper that's relevant to a broader context involving multivariate statistical analysis. In said paper, we also address and resolve an existing problem with the standard paired-permutation test. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations. This difference in drag, known as anisotropy, varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved and its length in relation to its width. When the cylinder was long in relation to its width, drag anisotropy also depended on the distance the particle had to move in relation to its width. Anisotropy studies have generally focused on short solids moving through a two-dimensional, flat surface of granular material, and have revealed notable drag differences when the solid is moved at an angle. However, these studies found little to no anisotropy when the solids were long in relation to their width. In contrast, our findings showed substantial anisotropy even when the solids were long, and this anisotropy was influenced by the speed at which the solid moves and the distance it moves in relation to its width. Notably, the drag experienced by the long solids was generally greater when they were moved parallel to their long axis than when moved at an angle, and this anisotropy increased with the ratio of the solid's length to its width. Additionally, we discovered that the relationship between the drag experienced by the solids and the speed at which they move and the distance they move is similar whether the solids are moved parallel to their long axis, at an angle, or perpendicular to their long axis. We also found that the drag experienced by the solids can be predicted using a model that takes into account the speed at which they move and the distance they move, regardless of their orientation. However, this model assumes that the solids are moved through a layer of granular material that is smooth in relation to the length of the solids, and our findings were consistent with this assumption. We analyzed the drag experienced by the solids in different orientations by imaging them from above as they moved through the granular material layer, and found patterns of material displacement that corresponded with the orientations of the solids. We also found that the drag experienced by the solids depends on the speed at which the grains in the layer move past each other, and that this speed depends on the speed at which the solids move and the distance they move in relation to their width. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These findings suggest a closer relationship between $v_3$ and initial geometry than previously thought and imply that $v_3$'s drivers are both collective behavior and intrinsic properties of the medium. Moreover, we observed both $v_2$ and $v_3$ exhibiting a collective momentum dependence for particles, which can be attributed to pre-equilibrium stages of the collision. A similar trend in momentum dependence between $v_2$ and $v_3$ may indicate non-thermal equilibrium phenomena shared by both anisotropic flows. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. By employing this constrained iterative method in conjunction with the Schur complement technique, the study develops an efficient and robust solver for large nonlinear systems. The proposed solver's effectiveness is highlighted by its application to both a model PDE and a real-world fluid dynamics problem. Furthermore, this study leverages the information from the nonlinear system to inform the computation of the approximate Jacobian matrices, which are crucial for solving certain nonlinear systems and are otherwise challenging to determine. Leveraging these approximate matrices enables the development of a linear solver that adapts to the nonlinearity of the system and, as a result, is more efficient than a standard preconditioned conjugate gradient method. This proposed solver's benefits are demonstrated by a significant reduction in computational time required to solve large nonlinear systems arising from PDEs. This study assumes that the spatial discretisation method is conservative, which results in a system of equations with a known property, both for the continuous problem and the numerical approximation. This property is maintained throughout the development of the solver. If the spatial discretisation method is not conservative, additional steps are required to ensure the preservation of the desired property. This study focuses on methods that are both conservative and that require the solution of systems of equations with specific property-preserving characteristics, which are ensured by the use of the Schur complement technique in conjunction with the constrained iterative method. This ensures that the numerical approximation of the PDE remains conservative and the corresponding system of equations has the desired property. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, real-time tracking of the organ in real-world coordinates is crucial for safely navigating around vital structures. The complexity of the liver prevents using direct point-based registration methods, which aren't robust to large deformations, and instead, we propose using a novel approach that utilizes a coarse mesh-based model to represent the preoperative organ structure for registration. The proposed method starts by removing the soft tissue from a superimposed CT image to create a binary mask, which is then deformed to match a tracked surface from low-frequency components, leaving high-frequency details intact. This results in a deformation field that, when applied to the preoperative mesh, yields a model that can be used for safe navigation around vital structures and blood vessels. The proposed method has been tested on simulated and real-world data with tracked surface variations up to 30% in size and 13% in mean Hausdorff distance. The average computation time for a single frame is 432 ms on a standard desktop computer. The code for this project is available at: https://github.com/ku-nccr/soft-tissue-registration. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. This task depends on a precise analysis of multiple images taken at different time points. Although traditional methods based on local features can produce satisfactory results, their inability to leverage comprehensive shape information limits their potential. In contrast, approaches that use surface stereo facilitate higher-quality trajectory estimation, but they are also prone to delays. This paper introduces a novel method, dynamic point cloud flow, that employs comprehensive point clouds in conjunction with time-conscious density maps to efficiently determine three-dimensional motion trajectories. This method yields a resolution-independent solution that can be used to calculate motion vectors at a variety of spatial densities, thus catering to diverse point cloud inputs. This is accomplished through the use of an innovative upsampling technique that maintains computational efficiency. This results in motion vector estimation being both accurate and fast, with the capability to achieve speeds of approximately 30 milliseconds for real-time applications. This method is particularly effective in analyzing complex three-dimensional animate objects in real-time, as seen in various evaluation datasets, with notable results achieved in several challenging scenarios. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Furthermore, we establish that no two distinct papillon graphs have the same structure as any known cubic graph that is E2F, thus implying their Hamiltonian cycle is unique. Our research also explores the relationship between the papillon graph and Cayley's formula, which describes the number of Hamiltonian cycles in a cubic graph. We then derive a more general formula for the number of Hamiltonian cycles in a papillon graph. Our discussion on the papillon graph is concluded by examining its Hamiltonian cycle's structure, identifying its elements as orbits that are rearranged randomly, and determining the associated permutation group's structure. Our research also sheds light on a question initially posed by Arthur Cayley in 1889, as well as a problem presented by the 2007 IMO, to provide a cubic graph example with a specific property that does not satisfy the E2F condition, with the papillon graph serving as such an example. Our work also updates the current record for the smallest number of edges in a cubic graph that does not have a Hamiltonian cycle to eleven. Our research finally contributes to the theory of cubic graphs through the introduction of the papillon graph, as well as its related subgraph, the hypernacelle graph. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, a program makes numerous system calls, some of which could be unsafe if executed on a public cloud. Determining these system calls is crucial to preventing potential breaches. A vast majority of static analysis-based techniques exist that can identify potential system calls made by a program, but these techniques are often too slow for real-world use cases, making them impractical for several high-performance applications, especially those involving microservices. Contrary to these techniques, which often rely on cloud resources for analysis, Timeloops operates on a node level, leveraging local information about the program and operating system. It offers a range of benefits, including faster analysis and reduced cloud costs. Moreover, system calls are often temporal dependencies, and a system call made at one point may not be the same as one made at another point. Therefore, Timeloops offers a range of system call filtering policies that account for temporal relationships and provides a tangible implementation of its methodology through a working example on Apache Kafka. This demonstration showcases the capabilities of Timeloops in automating system call filtering policies and the resulting benefits, including enhanced security and reduced cloud expenses, achieved with real-world performance results. Moreover, the Timeloops code has been made available on a public repository for further utilization by the community. This work is a part of the broader project called TaintCloud that aims to provide secure and cost-efficient cloud services for containerized applications through a range of innovative techniques including Timeloops, Tempio, and D-sealer. This project is supported by the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation and has been presented at notable conferences such as EuroSys, OSDI, and Micro. This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. Our model has been made available for public use, and its potential to improve soccer coaching and fan engagement is also explored. Finally, we outline potential areas for future research in soccer analytics, including modeling referee behavior and estimating action outcomes with greater precision. Our methodology presents a scalable framework for solving similar problems in other team sports. Our model's source code can be found at this link: https://github.com/ShuqiPang/SoccerRL. If you are interested in using this data, we suggest visiting their website at this link: https://www.instat.com/. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations for the wave equation solver are presented. Examples using synthetic data and real-field records demonstrate the accuracy of the method and its ability to match varying levels of noise. Additionally, both weighted and unweighted versions of the method are tested and show that a small weight value results in the spread of the extended source, similar to the break-up of sources observed in low-resolution methods like classical FWI. Both the time and frequency domain formulations produce comparable results, and both can be viewed as equivalent to the classical FWI upscaling the source in the frequency domain case producing a frequency smearing effect that contributes to the source spread. Overall, both the time and frequency domain versions of the algorithm prove to be robust and accurate solutions for the non-physical source problem presented in seismic inversion.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission system, which incorporates D2D communication.
