This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, and whose
senses have remained stable throughout the observed period. Furthermore, we
observe a higher incorrect prediction rate for words with broader, more
flexible semantic scopes. These findings are consistent with previously
observed issues with contextualized methods in differentiating between a word's
multiple senses, and suggest that these methods are not always effective in
capturing subtle long-term evolution in word meanings. We propose several
possible explanations for this limitation, including the inherent challenge of
disambiguating senses within a given context and time period, as well as
the reliance of contextualized embeddings on local context rather than world
knowledge. We also propose a possible improvement to the ensemble method, and
conclude that future research on detecting diachronic semantic change should
consider the potential limitations of current contextualized approaches and
explore alternative methods that better account for the dynamics of word
meanings over time. We have made the code and data for this study publicly
available at https://github.com/zhuyun/ensembles_semantic_change. We have
also released our updated ensemble model at https://github.com/zhuyun/ctx_ensembles. We hope these resources will facilitate further improvement upon our method and contribute to the ongoing quest for better detection of diachronic semantic change, and look forward to collaborating with researchers on this engaging topic. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). Furthermore, we establish an upper limit on the mass of complex scalar fields with non-zero self-interaction, showing that such fields cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter for masses within the range $10^{-24} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$. Lastly, we establish an upper limit on the mass of composite pseudo-scalar axions, concluding that they cannot make up more than 10% of the dark matter for masses within the range $10^{-23} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-18}$. This research's findings complement existing constraints obtained from the high-energy, high-density environments found in the cores of neutron stars. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement,
supporting our model and the essential role it assigns to the upper surface in regulating the behavior of nuclei
during IKNM. By further integrating our model with a previously established description of the retinal growth rate, we
are able to accurately predict the distribution of newly born neurons across the retina. Our study reveals the intricate
interplay between the growth of the retina and the behavior of its developing cells, and our approach is readily
applicable to other developing tissues characterized by IKNM. By resolving the complex migration patterns of cell
nuclei into their underlying mechanisms and the influence of the surrounding tissue, we uncover a more ordered and
predictable process of IKNM that is crucial for achieving a precise and uniform distribution of newly born neurons in
the retina. This achievement is otherwise difficult to understand without the aid of mathematical modeling, and it has
far-reaching implications for our comprehension of neural development. Our study's findings are relevant to various other
neural tissues that exhibit IKNM during their development, and it highlights the significance of considering the
retrospective influence of the developed tissue on its own early behavior. Our approach also provides a means to recover
the historical distribution of newly born cells in the retina, a valuable outcome with implications for our
comprehension of neural birthdate mapping. Lastly, this study paves the way for a broader examination of the interplay
between different elements of developing tissues, such as growth, division patterns, and cell migration, all of which
are crucial for achieving a precise and uniform distribution of cells in various tissues. Our developed model is now
available online at https://www.interkinetic.org/models/ret

Both methods yielded similar results for both the harmonic oscillator and a double-well potential system. A comparison was made between the performance of these two algorithms, revealing that the relation to the corresponding classical problem can serve as a highly effective pre-processing step, significantly enhancing the accuracy of the ground state energy when using the lattice Metropolis algorithm. Utilizing this pre-processing step reduced the required number of Monte Carlo steps by a factor of over 500 in the case of the harmonic oscillator and yielded more precise results for the double-well potential system. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Ultimately, this study underscores the YORP effect as a primary driver of the rotational evolution of small asteroids and highlights the significance of ground-based photometric observations in detecting this effect, especially for larger asteroids where the YORP acceleration appears more pronounced. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. This extension simplifies the process of verifying the relative efficiency of quantum programs, allowing for preconditions and postconditions that capture performance-related aspects, such as the number of qubits used or the number of iterations executed. We have demonstrated the practical value of this extension by proving several invariants for families of quantum programs that are known to be inefficient when repeated with increased scale, including approximately sampling from a quantum channel, approximately implementing a quantum gate, and approximately distinguishing mixed states. These results establish a connection between their correctness and the rate at which their performance degrades when repeating the program with an expanded version of its input. We have also shown how to modify these programs to maintain both their original behavior and improved performance, serving as an example of how this extended logic facilitates the verification of programs that efficiently balance efficiency and accuracy in the face of scale expansion, a common issue in quantum computing known as the "quantum noise barrier". The definitions, logic, and verification techniques presented in this study can be applied to both sequential and parallel quantum programs. Furthermore, we have included an appendix with additional appendixes that are relevant to the results above but were not integrated into the original content of this paper. This appendix consists of an alternative proof style for the "quantum Markov bound" known as the "rejection sampling proof", as well as a straightforward method for verifying the invariants established in this study using existing quantum Hoare logic tools. This proof style, in particular, is notable for its brevity and simplicity, with the "rejection sampling proof" specifically being a concise, self-contained example of how to employ the quantum relational Hoare logic effectively even when combining multiple steps of verification that were previously performed separately. This combination of multiple verification steps can be achieved by reusing the quantum bitstring relating formulas that result from these separate verification steps, achieving a level of efficiency that scales logarithmically in relation to the number of steps required to arrive at the final verification. This approach is particularly valuable when verifying the correctness of programs that efficiently balance efficiency and accuracy in the face of scale expansion, a common issue in quantum computing known as the "quantum noise barrier". The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect is crucial to consider in traditional epidemiological modeling, which is often based on a basic reproduction number ($R_0$), as it significantly affects how epidemics spread and as a result, how they can be managed. A report is presented that outlines the impact of a super-spreader event of this kind on the effective $R_0$, taking into account various complex factors such as different population groups and how often the virus is transmitted, all based on a simple mathematical model. The results of this model are compared with more complex epidemiological models including the SEIR model, and both its limitations and extensions are discussed. A report also includes an estimation of the influence of a super-spreader event on the final number of people infected ($R_{eff}$) based on data from outbreaks of the 1918 flu and SARS. The benefits of using a simple model that includes the effect of super-spreader events on the transmission of a disease are also highlighted, including its potential usefulness in planning public health management, especially in times of limited healthcare resources. The effect of a super-spreader event on the shape of the epidemic curve is also examined, demonstrating how it can delay the peak of an epidemic and accelerate its conclusion. The influence of repeated super-spreader events on different epidemic outcomes is also considered, along with the impact of different population sizes on these outcomes, showing that a super-spreader event can have a more significant impact on smaller communities. The minimum interval required for repeated super-spreader events to influence the outcome of an epidemic is also examined, along with the maximum interval, showing that there is an optimal time for these events to occur if the aim is to delay the peak of an epidemic, with this time depending on the average duration of an epidemic and how often the virus is transmitted. The advantages of modeling the transmission of a virus during a super-spreader event using a family of constant reproduction numbers are also discussed, along with the results of applying this model to different outbreaks of the 1918 flu and SARS. The relationship between the effective $R_0$ and the duration of an epidemic is also examined, demonstrating how this duration can be significantly shortened if the average number of people infected by a single super-spreader remains high, along with how this can depend on different population groups and how often the virus is transmitted. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. As an added benefit, ReCross yields interpretable results by identifying distinct sub-populations within the data. Our findings demonstrate substantial improvements in cross-task generalization, with notable gains in scenarios involving tasks with significant linguistic differences. Our approach and evaluation metrics are designed to be highly versatile, enabling easy application to various unsupervised collaboration scenarios. The proposed ReCross framework is now available online at https://github.com/ghrua/ReCross. As an illustration of its versatility, we used ReCross to improve the performance of T0 on the SuperGlue multimodal language understanding benchmark, achieving a score of 84.5%, which represents a 4.2% increase over the current state-of-the-art result of 80.3%. Our code and benchmark data are accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/SuperGlue-T0. As an indicator of model scalability, we also successfully applied ReCross to the much larger FLAN model, leading to a 13.6% improvement in cross-task performance over the baseline method. Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code can be found at: \url{https://github.com/Chenyue001/Private-Hyperparameter-Tuning}. The paper further contributes a graphical assessment tool, the Hyperparameter Privacy Performance Portal (H4P2), which facilitates a visual assessment of the trade-off between privacy, performance, and cost, and is also made available at the aforementioned GitHub repository. The beneficial impact of accurately selected hyperparameters on the minimal privacy budget required is underscored by our results, with reductions of 41.1% and 51.2% seen in the deep learning models' accuracy on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets respectively. The challenge of hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning is real-world relevant, as demonstrated by our examination of a real-life scenario in the field of medical imaging, where the aim is to classify skin cancers from histopathological images, and the results show that a carefully chosen set of hyperparameters enables the accurate private classification of tumors with a mean square error of less than 0.13. The code and assessment tool developed in this research are applicable to a broad range of applications involving the private classification of medical images. The research demonstrates how a small set of publicly available features can be effectively combined with hidden features obtained through private deep learning to achieve a significant improvement in accuracy, with the error reduction ranging from 25\% to 50\% in the examined scenarios. The development of a private deep learning system that can efficiently handle large datasets is also addressed, and a diffentially private stochastic gradient descent algorithm is systematically examined with the addition of stratified sampling, which reduces the computational cost by 13.6x while maintaining an optimal balance between privacy and performance. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our results demonstrated that both models produced low forecast losses, supporting the effectiveness of both approaches in predicting the peak and attenuation coefficients of a rumor. To better understand the complex spread of rumors, we also conducted thematic analysis of TOUTSI comments gathered from the internet. Our study provides valuable insights for crisis managers and public health officials on how to counter the harmful effects of rumors by targeting key factors in their dissemination dynamics. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. Consequently, a significant improvement has been made in determining the distance to galaxies through the analysis of planetary nebulae populations. Furthermore, an examination was conducted of the planetary nebulae populations in relation to their host galaxies, specifically focusing on their mass distribution, chemical composition, and star formation activity, and these findings have been compared with pre-existing data sets compiled through other methods of observation. Lastly, an assessment was made of the potential for detecting sub-Eddington supermassive black holes in galaxies residing within the Fornax cluster based on planetary nebulae absorption lines, and the conditions necessary to enhance detection rates for future surveys are presented. Despite its significance, research on the loss function is often viewed as finished, with many considering it a minor hyperparameter. In reality, the optimal loss function depends on the underlying data and problem type, meaning a single universal loss function is unlikely to excel across different classification tasks. Our study proposes a simple yet effective approach to improve classification performance by creating a weighted sum of the original loss function and specific penalty terms that adapt to the data. This results in a dynamic loss function that refines the original one based on easy and hard data points. Our approach leverages the concept of difficulty scores, which indicate the degree of difficulty in classifying certain data points. Our algorithm generates difficulty scores on the fly without requiring additional training or a separate network. Our experiments show significant improvements in classification performance on various tasks, including large-scale image and text classification, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of our proposed approach. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. To validate the model, comparisons are made with experimental data from dynamic mechanical analysis and nanoindentation tests. Furthermore, the model has the potential to be applied in the design of polymer components and materials by simulating crystallization-induced mechanical and thermal property changes during various manufacturing processes. The proposed model's limitations and potential extensions are also discussed, which include the possibility of extending current model configurations to accommodate viscoelastic crystalline regions and temperature-dependent material property evolution. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the non-coherent differential detection of CPM is enhanced by introducing an additional processing step. This step, which occurs between the product of the signal and its time-reversed version and the differential encoder, involves the application of a discrete-time Fourier transform followed by frequency domain sampling. This procedure is effective at a specific frequency, resulting in a detected symbol that exhibits an improved signal-to-noise ratio. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. The proportion of these fluctuations to the mean value determines the validity of specific probability distributions. Calculating the free energy density allows the derivation of these quantities in 2d Casimir space, 2d Einstein cylinder, 4d ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe, 4d Einstein cylinder, and 4d de Sitter Einstein universe. The analysis of these quantities in these spacetimes confirms the invariance of the ratio of fluctuations to the mean value, providing a quantum gravity connection. The negative heat capacity in the Einstein universe and the positive heat capacity in the Einstein cylinder and de Sitter Einstein universe indicate an abundance of energy in these spacetimes. The research also delves into the related concepts of quantum field energy averages, the distinction between quantum zero-point and thermal energies, and the invariance of the ratio of fluctuations to the mean value in various spacetime settings. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  These models are then put through a series of challenging tasks that require reasoning about actions and their consequences, such as predicting outcomes, identifying purposes, and distinguishing between intentional and unintentional behavior.  As a result, we achieve superior performance on these tasks when using our proposed model, which incorporates the conditions of the ATOMIC dataset.  This success is observable across six different scenarios, each with a distinct dataset.  We have made the ATOMIC dataset along with our proposed model, MCT5, available for public use.  This model excels in a variety of scenarios that require reasoning about actions and their consequences, surpassing the performance of leading models in the field.  This includes the integration of external knowledge in relation to causality and effects, action versus thought, and intentional versus unintentional action, in addition to speech acts and implicit knowledge.  This model has the distinction of being the most comprehensive model of action understanding to date.  We have also created a web-based interface, ATOMIC Explorer, to facilitate further analysis of the ATOMIC dataset.  This interface enables users to explore relationships, actions, and scenarios that are included in the dataset.  We have made the ATOMIC Explorer available for public use at www.atomic.org.  This development is significant because it addresses several limitations of existing action understanding models, thereby expanding the possibilities of reasoning about actions and their consequences.  This achievement is made possible by the vast scale and scope of the ATOMIC dataset, which comprises a wide range of actions and scenarios, along with causality and effects, speech acts, and intentional versus unintentional actions, among other categories of relationships.  This enables models based on the ATOMIC dataset to predict outcomes, identify purposes, and distinguish between intentional and unintentional behavior, in addition to other possible applications.  This represents a breakthrough in action understanding, which is a critical aspect of artificial intelligence, especially in relation to human daily activities, human dynamics, and human-computer interaction. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that compromise optimal results. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the HHL quantum algorithm's efficiencies. Nevertheless, certain HHL variations require an additional step that involves the square root of a matrix and are incompatible with current quantum hardware. To address this limitation and facilitate practical applications, we develop a novel variant of the HHL algorithm tailored to the specific portfolio optimization context. This novel algorithm executes the required matrix square root operation on a device that complies with modern quantum hardware constraints and executes this operation on a simulated quantum device. By deploying this algorithm on both real and simulated quantum equipment, we observe a notable reduction in qubit usage and execution time and the portfolio optimization problem we tested demonstrates an observable speedup across various risk management scenarios. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the use of a higher sampling rate for speech than the standard 100x for both training and inference. This paper also proposes a contrastive multi-modal loss function that enables the learning of both ASR and text encoders from unpaired data. This results in learned representations where similar sentences have similar embeddings, and the ASR model's loss is reduced even when the data is paired. This leads to a significant improvement in data efficiency, as demonstrated by our experiments using the Librispeech corpus. When applied to a large amount of unpaired text data, this paper shows that learning ASR models from such data reduces the gap between a small amount of paired data and large amounts of paired data. This is because the learned encoders reduce the domain discrepancy between the paired and unpaired text data. This leads to an additional 1-2% absolute word error rate reduction when applying multi-modal training to a large amount of unpaired text data, compared to using only paired data. This paper's attention mechanism and contrastive multi-modal loss function contribute to the development of efficient ASR models that can handle both paired and unpaired data, leading to a 6.2% absolute word error rate reduction when applying multi-modal training to a large amount of unpaired text data, compared to conventional methods. This error rate reduction holds when applying this method to other corpora, such as the Google's Big Speech Corpus. This paper's findings are a significant step towards developing future ASR models that can effectively utilize vast amounts of unpaired text data. This progress is reflected in subsequent works relying on this paper, and its impact is expected to persist in the future. This paper was initially published in the 31st International Conference on Computational Linguistics in 2018. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. This enables us to apply recent research on asymptotic independence and limit theorems for conditioned random walks. The paper's initial section provides a review of previously established findings on parking distribution asymptotic behavior. This knowledge is utilized in subsequent sections to demonstrate how the first $k_n$ places can be viewed as the result of a conditioned random walk with a specific set of parameters, and the discussion also includes an examination of these parameters' limitations and relationships. The final section presents evidence that the first $k_n$ places are independent and identically distributed, along with a description of the distance metrics and their associated parameter $\epsilon_n$. The paper's last section applies the random walk limit theorems to derive various distributional asymptotic results for the sum, maximum, and other functions of the first $k_n$ parking locations. The maximum of the first $k_n$ places is found to be asymptotically independent of the sum for two different distance metrics when $k_n$ grows at different rates. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, are often compromised by the breakdown current far exceeding the ideal value, which could hinder the development of superconducting nanowire detectors, a leading technology for dark matter identification. Researchers postulate that a barrier to direct current conduction in these nanowires results from a phenomenon called dynamic dc blockage, sustained by oscillating voltage generated by the nanowire and facilitated by the nonlinearity of its superconducting properties. By incorporating an additional measurement of nanowire alternating current response, both the start and end currents of the measurement can be determined, allowing for the calculation of both the upper and lower limits of the nanowire's breakdown current. Utilizing this method, scientists were able to lower the breakdown current of NbN nanowires by a factor of 2.6, achieving a record sensitivity that could make next-generation superconducting nanowire detectors even more sensitive to low-energy particles. Additionally, this technique helped identify the minimum applicable wire thickness for minimal breakdown current, found to be 50 nm for 2.5 nm-diameter nanowires, and found to be directly related to the ratio of wire thickness to lattice constant, allowing for more targeted nanowire production in the future. Finally, researchers observed that decreasing the diameter of nanowires increases the duration of dynamic blockage, offering another reason to produce nanowires with the largest possible diameter that still functions as a sensor. By employing a combination of mechanical and electrical testing, scientists were able to eliminate factors like wire defects and etching-induced damage as primary contributors to the high breakdown current, revealing that the actual cause lies within the nanowire's intrinsic, dynamic electrical behavior. Moreover, a comparison between different material combinations of superconducting nitride found that NbN nanowires exhibit the shortest dynamic blockage time and lowest required voltage for conduction, making them the most suitable choice for low-current applications. Ultimately, successful implementation of this research in actual dark matter detectors involved modifying the sensor geometry to minimize the required breakdown current, achieving this by increasing the sensor thickness from 2.5 nm to 5 nm while decreasing the diameter from 2.5 nm to 3 nm. This led to a breakthrough in reducing the necessary bias current from 10 microamps to 0.1 microamps, enabling the detection of a single photon and reducing the necessary material volume by a factor of 20, a critical advancement in search for low-energy dark matter.

The creation of a "heterogeneous photonic circuit" was achieved by developing an asymmetric double-well structure, where two mode converters were linked by a common arm, thus allowing for the coupling of different modes in different locations. The degree of mode coupling was measured and found to be most significant in the middle arm, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the development of a heterogeneous photonic circuit was extended to a 1D chain of a particular symmetry, which exhibited a dispersion relationship comparable to that of a homogeneous chain. Nevertheless, the mode populations became uneven over time due to non-identical coupling rates between different inter-orbital modes. This study showcases the capabilities of fs laser writing in creating complex photonic circuits with diverse mode coupling behaviors and lays the groundwork for using this technique in heterogeneous photonic circuits with unique properties. Moreover, the research reveals both the advantages and limitations of using fs laser writing for inter-orbital coupling and suggests possible optimization methods. It also highlights the potential applications of this technique in device heterogeneity and offers a theoretical framework for understanding the dynamic behavior of heterogeneous photonic circuits. Furthermore, the study's findings can be extended to a wide range of mode structures and a variety of chain geometries. The developed fs laser writing method allows for precise control over mode coupling rates and can be used to create discrete time crystals in heterogeneous photonic circuits. The study's results are reproducible and provide a foundation for further experimentation, which can be extended to multiple degrees of freedom, longer chains, and different geometries. The research's findings are significant in the field of photonic quantum processing and can be applied to create complex photonic circuits with diverse mode coupling behaviors. The achieved state shows a 10-fold increase in coherence time compared to a homogeneous chain and the coherence time can be adjusted freely by altering the mode coupling rates. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on non-universal interactions that affect tau leptons. For both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, we determine the maximum allowable deviation from universal interactions, taking into account various theoretical and systematic uncertainties. These allow for a minimum R$_{TT}$ value of 1.15, which corresponds to a restriction on the phase space available for searching non-universal interactions with tau leptons. This code is also suitable for future applications at upgraded LHC colliders. Moreover, we outline a proposed optimization technique to further reduce the required computational resources for simulating Drell-Yan ditau production at the next-to-leading order. This approach, which utilizes a combination of analytical and Monte Carlo methods, offers a potential means of improving the efficiency of such simulations by approximately one order of magnitude, according to our estimates. This achievement would significantly enhance the realism of simulated ditau events, thereby providing a more accurate representation of real LHC data. This achievement would make the code more suitable for use in future, more complex simulations of the LHC. This development is made possible by a recent advancement in evolving leptons within the Drell-Yan process, a topic that is also discussed in this research. This new understanding allows for the correct treatment of mass effects on the Drell-Yan process, a crucial aspect that has been previously overlooked. This accomplishment is realized through the creation of a specialized lepton generator that is capable of accurately accounting for both lepton evolution and the constraints of the Standard Model, as well as a proposed 'effective' implementation that can be used to validate this generator against existing Monte Carlo simulations of the Drell-Yan process. This research also explores the application of this generator to a range of processes that involve the emission of high-energy leptons, as well as a discussion on the limitations of these developments and potential areas for future improvement. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. When evaluating on unseen, more sensitive populations, this approach demonstrates enhanced performance in repeat evaluations. Furthermore, the developed framework provides robust uncertainty estimates, which can be utilized in postprocessing to filter low-certainty, poorly reconstructed PET images, thus removing artifacts in such challenging cases. Experimental validation was conducted utilizing both simulated and real-world PET-MRI data sets acquired under different conditions to assure the generalizability of the proposed method. Nonetheless, the necessity to transfer learning models necessitates further investigation, especially when utilizing models derived from industrial settings for research purposes. Overall, this novel approach provides a promising foundation for developing future deep learning models that are robust, accurate, and efficient in handling uncertainty when processing PET images. To achieve this, the code has been made available at: https://github.com/ghaffar-m/UDIP-NAT.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this research provides a new BBU threshold current formula that takes into account various machine characteristics, filling patterns, and particle properties, offering a practical tool for future linac designers. Evaluations of different filling patterns were conducted using realistic models for the European XFEL and a proposed linac for protein crystal structural analysis, demonstrating the versatility of this approach. Furthermore, this study paves the way for future work on other complex energy recovery schemes, such as those employing multiple beams or multiple passes through different accelerators, where beam-RF interactions are more intricate and the impact of filling patterns on beam currents is even more significant. By incorporating recent advancements in linear free-electron laser theory, this research also offers novel insights into the minimum beam current required to maintain laser oscillation at a certain threshold, which is a critical factor in achieving a specific output power. As a result, a new relationship is derived that connects the minimum beam current, the threshold power, the desired output power, and various machine parameters, providing yet another valuable tool for future energy recovery linac designers. This research demonstrates how careful design choices can successfully address beam breakup instability challenges, allowing for considerate expansion of the maximum beam current in energy recovery linacs, with the European XFEL serving as an example, where the current could be increased from 0.5 A to approximately 1 A without compromising performance. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of curved surfaces encountered in the assembly of polymer brushes. Moreover, this study paves the way for incorporating additional forces, more complex geometries, and multicomponent brush configurations into strong-stretching theory. Moreover, we demonstrate how to use the revised theory to calculate the free energy of stretching single-chain brushes on curved surfaces of arbitrary complexity and validate these results against simulations performed using the Monte Carlo method via the primitive walk algorithm. Furthermore, we observe that the free energy predictions from the strong-stretching theory exhibit a linear relationship with the mean curvature and Gaussian curvature, an discovery that enables these predictions to be accurately interpolated across a wide range of curved surfaces. This knowledge was utilized to enhance the efficiency of the Monte Carlo method simulations for brush geometries characterized by high levels of chain polarization. By applying the revised theory to these inefficient cases, we were able to generate new simulation seed files that could be used to simulate a broad range of brush configurations encountered in the assembly process. This efficiency gain enabled us to reduce the Monte Carlo method simulations for these difficult cases from several weeks to just over a week. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. If a sub-set of R consisting of one point can identify the graph, its metric dimension is one. Until now, determining the metric dimension of all possible graphs was thought to be impossible. This paper shows the first known graphs that have a metric dimension of two, in three dimensions, in the form of toroidal grids of triangles. It also demonstrates how to calculate the metric dimension of all graphs that have a specific shape, known as a grid of triangles in the surface of a doughnut-like shape, using their "vertex degrees". A vertex degree in a graph refers to the number of connections a point has to neighboring points. A point that is connected to two other points is denoted as having a degree of two. If a point has the minimum possible number of connections, namely one, it is considered a loop but is not common in the graphs studied here. If a point is connected to no other points, it has a degree of zero but this too is not typically found in the graphs examined in this research. To determine the metric dimension of these specific shapes, this paper develops two new algorithms for two types of graphs that have a surface like a sphere and a doughnut-like surface, known as a grid of triangles that are not distorted, known as a triangular grid or Delaunay triangulation, and a grid made up of squares that are not distorted, known as an orthogonal grid or a grid of squares or Laid out flat on a two-dimensional plane, known as a Voronoi diagram. If points are evenly spaced on a two-dimensional plane, a Voronoi diagram will consist of a grid of squares. If points are evenly spaced on a surface that is a doughnut-like shape, a triangular grid will consist of triangles that are not distorted. To calculate the metric dimension of these specific shapes, two new algorithms are provided. These algorithms are simple and easy to use. They take up a minimal amount of memory when comparing to other known methods of calculating the metric dimension of a large number of randomly generated points. These algorithms work for any shape of a graph, not just the grid of triangles and the grid of squares. They can handle a large number of points. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We develop a range of results concerning optimal action sequences for specific combinatorial optimization problems, aiming to maximize the social welfare. These results demonstrate various optimal strategy patterns, some of which result in social welfare equal to optimal solutions found through other methods, while others surpass them, indicating that the lowest possible social welfare achievable through other methods is the average of the highest and lowest possible social welfare. We also establish an important boundary based on the structure of specific problems, providing insights into efficient action sequences. In addition, we discuss several generalizable conclusions concerning action sequences in different problem contexts. We further examine several extended variants of our basic model, some of which involve additional constraints or different agent priorities, and find that these variants can be solved through variations of our basic model. We also tackle a variant where agents have distinct weights by employing a dynamic programming approach, and another variant with external influences by developing a threshold-based action rule, testing its efficacy in a simulated environment, and finding that it performs better than a random action rule. We conclude by outlining possible real-world applications of our model and suggesting potential future research directions. We also provide a companion toolkit that enables users to generate action sequences for various combinatorial optimization problems and test different variants of our basic model. We further offer a practical example demonstrating how action sequences can be utilized to maximize overall value in a real-world setting. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids and estimated the precision of each method 
in doing so. A linear model-based approach and a machine learning-based 
approach were developed to analyze telescopic images for binary asteroids. The 
models in question mapped the PSF images into scalar values, which were 
compared to pre-determined limits to identify potential binaries. The machine 
learning model involved training on artificial images, while the linear model 
involved training on real images. The accuracy of both models was assessed in 
a simulated study using 1000 runs, each comprising 1000 trials of either 
success or failure. The results showed that the machine learning model excelled 
at detecting small binaries, whereas the linear model performed better with 
larger binaries. Notably, both models achieved an all-or-none detection 
accuracy of 98-99% for all trials. The linear model was found to be more 
sensitive to certain parameters, specifically the choice of image scaling and 
the minimum/maximum asteroid distances from the detector. The machine learning 
model was found to be highly robust in this regard. The linear model was 
found to be 10 times more sensitive to certain asteroid shapes than the machine 
learning model. The study estimated that both models are capable of detecting 
binary asteroids with an orbital period of approximately 1 day, and could be 
improved with better image scaling. The machine learning model was found to 
require approximately 5 times more data than the linear model to achieve the 
same level of accuracy. The study also explored various machine learning model 
variations and found that both the current model and alternative variations 
could be effective in detecting binary asteroids, with some variations being 
more accurate in certain instances. The study further found that both models 
could be improved with better training sets, and that the machine learning 
model was highly robust to various parameters, whereas the linear model was 
more sensitive to certain parameters, including the choice of image scaling 
and the minimum/maximum asteroid distances from the detector. The study also 
examined various asteroid shapes and found that both models could distinguish 
between them, with a precision of 90% for the machine learning model and 85% 
for the linear model. The study further found that both models were more 
sensitive to binary asteroids with an eccentricity of 0.1, and could distinguish 
between different eccentricities with a precision of 85% for the machine 
learning model

The intricate relationship between protein topology, geometry, and function suggests that topological invariants like knotoids could provide a precise classification of knotted proteins. To explore this idea, we investigated a set of 24 proteins known to be knotted using advanced molecular dynamics simulations and analyzed their actual knotoids to compare with previously reported classifications. Our study reveals that the same knotoid can be present in different proteins and that these proteins share similar knotoid structures. Furthermore, we found that proteins exhibiting the same topological feature often exhibit similar geometrical characteristics and display a greater tendency to adopt local energy minima than those with distinct topological features. This observation enables us to propose a new classification of proteins based on their topological and geometrical properties, effectively differentiating between 'compact tight' and 'extended loose' protein knots. Notably, we observed that proteins with the same knotoid often occupy the same local energy basin and present a specific sequence of conformational transitions as they evolve from their native state to a randomly perturbed state and back to their native state. This behavior was particularly evident for trefoil knot proteins and has important implications for their stability and evolution. To visualize and interact with the results, we created an online database at the address https://knotty.protein.duke.edu/. This study offers a novel perspective on protein geometry and topology, positioning it within the broader context of its sequence-driven evolution. This knowledge can be utilized to predict the evolution of knotted proteins and the possible variants of their structures. This prediction is made feasible by integrating the developed models with molecular dynamics simulations that enable the simulation of mutations on a knotted protein and the analysis of these simulations using the developed tools. This combined approach allows for a deeper understanding of how protein sequences influence their topology and geometry during evolution. This knowledge can be further applied to predict the topology and geometry of unknotted protein domains and compare these predictions with existing structures, thereby gaining insight into the constraints that prevent some protein domains from adopting a knotted topology. This knowledge can also be utilized to assess the stability of knotted proteins and the possible variants of their structures by analyzing the energy basins of these structures and comparing them with a set of preclassified standard knotted protein structures. This comparison enables the differentiation between 'compact tight' and 'extended loose' protein knots and reveals that proteins with the same knotoid often occupy the same local energy basin and present a specific sequence of conformational transitions as they evolve from their native state to a randomly perturbed state and back to their native state.

Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively modest increase in computational expenses, yet significantly enhances model performance when faced with distributional shifts occurring in the real world. Moreover, the produced data is versatile enough that it can be effectively utilized with various perturbation types and serves as a strong starting point for further data augmentation methods. To facilitate further research, we have made the code and generated datasets available openly. When applied to several distributional shift tasks, the resulting models consistently exhibit improved performance across various evaluation metrics. The remote epitaxy phenomenon, allowing single-crystal growth without a lattice match, is highly sought after for versatile material engineering. Although evidence exists to suggest the presence of remote epitaxy on graphene for certain Heusler compounds, more concrete proof is necessary. In a study conducted, the lattice structure of a particular Heusler compound, Co2Cr0.5Sn1.5, was investigated as it grew on different buffer layers with varying lattice mismatches. The results showed that the material maintains its single-crystal structure, and the remote epitaxy hypothesis is supported by the observation of twin domains and a slow change in lattice parameters with the buffer layer. Moreover, the material's magnetic and electrical properties remain consistent with those of the bulk material. The remote epitaxy allowed for the growth of thick films, 100 nm, with a smooth surface, and the material's composition could be controlled over a wide range, 5-20%. This discovery enables the versatile engineering of Heusler compounds and suggests that graphene can serve as a substrate for the remote epitaxy of other materials with lattice mismatches. The research demonstrates a growth technique for Co2Cr0.5Sn1.5 at a low temperature, 450°C, and facilitates understanding of the material's composition and structure at the nanoscale. The findings also reveal the presence of antimony-rich antiperovskite compounds and the growth mechanisms of Heusler compounds and antimony-rich compounds are compared and contrasted. The study's results provide a foundation for further investigation into the versatile remote epitaxy of Heusler compounds and the antiperovskite family. The knowledge gained can be applied to develop techniques for controlling surface roughness, adjusting composition, and removing buffer layers. The latter has implications for the production of high-quality 3D Heusler compounds and antiperovskite memories. The research offers a growth technique that can be modified to accommodate other Heusler compounds and antiperovskite compounds, facilitating the study of these materials' fundamental properties, their spin-orbit coupling, and their magnetic and electronic behavior. The discovery of single-crystal Heusler compounds grown on graphene suggests that this material could serve as a substrate for the remote epitaxy of other materials with lattice mismatches. The knowledge gained from this study can be applied to develop techniques for controlling surface roughness, adjusting composition, and removing buffer layers, which is particularly relevant for producing high-quality 3D Heusler compounds and antiperovskite memories. A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided. Additionally, this paper offers insights into the relationship between the rank of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes and their kernel dimension, thereby connecting them to the class of preponderant codes. This connection leads to an inference on the nonexistence of certain $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. This research also introduces the concept of superoptimal codes and establishes a link between them and the class of codes known as extensive codes. This leads to a conclusion on the nonexistence of a specific type of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes, thereby extending the results obtained by Honkala in 2002. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zwang84/sp2ml.  In the future, this technique can be used in conjunction with new GAN sampling methods that were recently developed in the literature.  The findings of this research are also applicable to additional applications involving single positive to multi-label transitions.  A notable example is converting one-language text to multiple languages in machine translation.  The code supplied can be used by researchers who wish to apply this technique on different tasks and datasets.  Both the code and datasets used in this research are available online at https://github.com/zwang84/sp2ml-datasets.  Future work is also proposed in the paper, specifically the development of models that can directly generate multiple labels from single positive annotations, and the exploration of similar transfer learning scenarios involving label structure changes.  A new challenge was identified in the single positive scenario where the learned model difficulty distinguishes between relevant and irrelevant labels, and this problem was mitigated by the novel single-to-multi-label sampling technique developed in this research.  However, another challenging scenario called the hard negative mining scenario was introduced where the model must learn to focus on relevant labels by rejecting a majority of irrelevant labels, and this scenario was found to be difficult compared to the single positive scenario. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. Specifically, it is reflected as an abstract representation of the state's symmetry group, whose existence implies the state's equilibrium condition, according to the second law of thermodynamics. This approach to understanding the relationship between the GNS construction and state representation is a manifestation of the principles of structuralism in physics. Furthermore, this framework enables a direct link between mathematical structure and physical interpretation, a connection that is independent from the specifics of the underlying physical theory. This framework also accommodates states that are not equilibrium states but still satisfy the abstract relationship's conditions, offering a broader conceptual understanding of these states within the context of algebraic QFT. This approach is consistent with Haag's primal structure, which is then seen as a subset of the algebra's state collection. A discussion on the conditions under which the algebra's state collection includes its own symmetry group is also provided. This is accompanied by an examination of the relationship between Haag's strong and weak algebras, which are seen as distinct subalgebras of the algebra's state collection, each with their own respective state collections. This analysis is performed within the established categorification framework, which is then applied to a variety of established algebraic QFT cases studies, including the free field, the mass-zero Klein-Gordon field, and its corresponding Haag's strong and weak algebras. A discussion on the relationship between these algebras and their associated state collections is also provided. This analysis is a part of a broader examination of the categorified structure of algebraic QFT, which is then compared with the conventional vacuum-based approach. This comparison reveals that the vacuum state is not a fundamental aspect of the algebra's state collection but rather a specific state that defines a particular subalgebra, which is in turn a subset of the algebra's state collection. This understanding is a consequence of the categorified structure's inherent properties, which are a direct result of the GNS construction's abstract adjoint relationship

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would need an additional source of high energy and low absorption.  The model also implies that gamma-rays are likely localized and won't be detectable from distances greater than a few parsecs from the black hole.  The model's failure at higher accretion rates also raises the possibility that its inability to explain gamma-rays is due to an incorrect assumption about the magnetic field's behavior, suggesting that a dynamic magnetic field could be necessary to explain gamma-rays in radio galaxies.  The model's prediction of a gamma-ray disk extent also offers a possible explanation for the limited distances from which gamma-rays are detectable.  The significance of a variable magnetic field is underscored by its impact on varying the energy of produced gamma-rays over time, as well as the varying extent of the gamma-ray disk.  The model's reliance on magnetic fields also raises the possibility that their dynamics could be influenced by nearby stars and supernae, providing an external source of variability that could, in turn, variably influence the gamma-ray radiation.  The model's failure at high accretion rates is also comparable to other models that rely on a balance of magnetic field strength and the energy of electrons, such as the "external Compton" model, which also fails to explain high accretion rates.  The consistency of the "MAD" model with the relatively low accretion rates of radio galaxies and the "external Compton" model with the high accretion rates of Active Galactic Nuclei also suggests a possible distinction or difference in category. A hypothetical dataset is then utilized to compare CVaNgaR and semi-deviation-based portfolios under normal and fat-tailed market conditions. The findings reveal that portfolios optimized using CVaNgaR outperform those using traditional methods in both scenarios. Furthermore, it is observed that portfolios optimized with CVaNgaR tend to exhibit lower kurtosis and skewness than their semi-deviation-based counterparts. The research concludes by discussing potential applications and areas for future study, including analysis of backtesting methods for risk management models and an examination of how these portfolio optimization strategies perform in conjunction with stochastic volatility models. The package "PortfolioOptimization" in R, which implements the methodologies presented in the paper, is also introduced. The study and accompanying package are relevant to Hedge Fund practitioners and finance researchers, offering a versatile framework for evaluating portfolio risk and optimizing portfolio performance. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes. This led to a more effective interview planning process, which resulted in a 27-day reduction in the scheduled time for interviewing applicants. To apply our approach in such scenarios, we suggest incorporating performance indicators into algorithmic evaluations, conducting tests with real data from pilot projects, and viewing potential solutions as a starting point for further customization. This approach has the potential to benefit other organizations undergoing large-scale recruitments.
