We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is independent of carbon density and since the line strengths vary inversely with each other, it can help identify sublimation layers in post-starburst galaxies even without knowing the actual gas temperature. Finally, we observe a $K_\alpha / K_\beta$ line ratio that increases with gas density and is more pronounced in dense densities ($>10^3 \mu$m$^{-2}$) and may indicate self-shielding of molecular gas and/or the presence of outflows. This ratio also varies with the 70$\mu$m IR emission strength and varies most in dwarf galaxies and those showing signs of recent starbursts. If confirmed, it could serve as an indicator for these specific galaxy conditions and may also be related to elemental carbon abundance variations. This last possibility needs further investigation as we found a $12$C$^+$/$^{13}$C$^+$ line ratio that is significantly higher than the cosmic $12$C/$^{13}$C abundance ratio and may reflect a $1.5$ times $12$C overabundance relative to $13$C in the molecular gas reservoirs compared to the cosmic abundance ratio. This could have implications for Big Bang Nucleosynthesis studies and may also reflect $12$C/$^{13}$C production variations from massive stars or other sources of elemental enrichment. This variation in the $12$C/$^{13}$C ratio also shows a significant scatter among the different galaxies observed and may be related to their individual mass physical properties rather than just overall metallicity. This last possibility needs further consideration as we found a $12$C/$^{13}$C ratio that is higher in the centers of giant galaxies and galaxy clusters and varies with the galaxies' central bulge to disk mass ratio. This could imply a connection to stellar mass variations and possibly different $12$C/$^{13}$C

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. This article's accompanying repository provides accessible R code for replicating demonstrated analyses and applications, allowing users to modify and extend existing scripts as needed. This study and its accompanying materials aim to contribute significantly towards addressing the ongoing public health crisis by promoting a clearer, more transparent, and universally understood mathematical foundation for epidemic model analysis. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation through a nonlinear threshold process. In our study, we investigated both large Janssen-type dark solitons and small Bogoliubov-type excitations within both one- and two-component condensates. In the case of a single spin component condensates, we were able to derive approximate analytical solutions for both dark solitons and magnetization oscillations in both the presence and absence of a detuning. Our findings also included nonlinear frequency shifts, initial condition-driven molecule formation, and a magnetic oscillation decay. In our investigation of two-component condensates, we discovered that the formation of molecule pairs occurs not only at the dark soliton location but also around a cloud of magnetization oscillations that behave as a standing wave. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of starting primers can be associated with either a singular item of data or a more intricate subdirectory of organized information, all while creating unique barcodes for individual items of data. This innovative design allows us to assign various namespaces to different primer pairs, thereby minimizing overlap between namespaces and preventing data entries from becoming inaccessible during updates, unlike previous methods that often used primers in reverse order and couldn't reuse earlier namespaces. Our system's flexibility also gives us the opportunity to keep a record of every data update, which can be crucial for an efficient and scalable DNA-storage system. Our research demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of this novel architecture by successfully conducting multiple updates on various namespaces of different depth levels. Our test results show significant improvements in both data revisions and search operations compared to existing DNA-storage systems. Our novel DNA-storage system's source code is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/aliakbarov/DNA-Storage. Our team is open to feedback and suggestions from the scientific community and hopes to further develop this novel DNA-storage system in the future. Our future plans include refining our system's search operation efficiency and exploring possibilities for scaling our system to a higher level, which would enable us to store significantly larger amounts of data. Our team also intends to create a real-world-based use case for this novel DNA-storage system. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components, and instead, offers a structured and systematic approach to learning in dynamic scenarios. This achievement is made possible by a novel, hybrid approach that combines markov decision processes with simulation-based training methods. The resulting environment excels in its ability to adapt to changing conditions and presents a particular challenge that requires careful consideration of both exploration and task-switching strategies. The comprehensive evaluation framework accompanying L2Explorer enables assessments of various lifelong learning algorithms and provides a wealth of data to support future research in this area. The source code and environment are available for download at: \url{https://github.com/Microsoft/L2Explorer}. To facilitate fair comparisons and reproducibility, we have established a benchmark dataset featuring multiple learning curves for each algorithm tested. Furthermore, the L2Explorer ecosystem is designed to be highly extensible, allowing for seamless integration of new algorithms and evaluation protocols. The key advantages of L2Explorer are its compact design, low computational requirements, and high flexibility, making it an ideal choice for testing both sophisticated, hybrid learning algorithms and elementary decision-making strategies. The impact of different algorithm performance is measurable through various evaluation metrics, and the affordability of running multiple experiments is significantly enhanced, enabling researchers to efficiently explore various learning scenarios with real-world applicability. Further discussion delves into the relationship between graded algebraic inertia and the behavior of Hodge structures. A notable section examines the characteristics of geometrically simple varieties and their connection to the Coleman-Gross theorem. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If precise location information is undesirable, a potential solution could be a statistical model that predicts the likelihood of a patient experiencing severe symptoms based solely on these features. To develop such a model, we gathered extensive data from 2,000+ COVID-19 patients and applied a broad range of machine learning techniques to create two predictive tools. The first, a classification model, determines whether a patient is likely to experience severe symptoms (requiring high ventilation support) or moderate symptoms (requiring standard hospital care). The second, a regression model, estimates the likelihood of a patient experiencing severe symptoms on a scale from 0 to 1. Both models yielded strong results, with high accuracy in replicating patient data and experiencing low error rates even when restricted to a limited set of features. Notably, the study found that certain pre-existing health conditions have a minimal impact on the likelihood of severe COVID-19 symptoms when incorporated into X-ray image characteristics. The best-performing model consisted of a convolutional neural network that extracted these characteristics, followed by a rejection sampling-based neural network that made the prediction. The study highlights the potential of machine learning to make predictions about severe COVID-19 symptoms based solely on X-ray image features and suggests avenues for further improvement. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. The extended monadic framework provides a universal parameterized natural transformation known as the standard presentation for each simplicial group in C, along with a natural isomorphism that relates this presentation to the group itself. The standard presentation is characterized by a specific simplicial identity in which the face operator $\partial_i$ acts as a generator, and there is an associated universal distributive law that governs the relationship between the monad defined by the standard presentation and the free group monad. The resulting framework has applications to various topological and homotopy theoretic inferences about simplicial groups in the category of simplicial sets in any topological space. The universal bundle functor W can be generalized to a level-wise bundle for simplicial groups in a simplicial space, and this extension retains its monadic properties. The standard presentation and its associated distributive law can be naturally applied to a broader context, including any simplicial object in a category of paths in a space. The resulting framework allows for a more general inference about the fundamental group of any simplicial identity in a group. The relationship between the standard presentation and the free group monad also implies a connection to the homotopy groups of any simplicial set, which is derivable from the action of the homotopy group monad on the standard presentation of the fundamental group. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notably lower false positive rate. To further address difficult low-frequency proposals, SABRA introduces an innovative Spatially-Aware Re-weighting (SRW) mechanism that takes into account the co-occurrence of relationships in the dataset, thereby providing an enhanced representation for difficult proposals. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in multiple VRD benchmarks, with a notable 10\% mAP gain on the challenging Visual Relationship Detection dataset VCOC. Our code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA_VRD.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from the absorption of minor interaction partners, is a key driver of their quiescence. Furthermore, we observed that the disk systems, with total stellar masses exceeding $\rm 10^{11}M_{\odot}$, are undergoing rapid disassembly, likely due to interactions with the galactic core and surrounding environment, which is also influencing their quiescence and mass asymmetry. If the galaxies are considered individually, those with more massive disks exhibit a greater tendency towards mass asymmetry and quiescence, whereas if the galaxies are viewed as a whole, the relationship holds only at the point of star formation, with mass asymmetry serving as the primary cause of quiescence. Additionally, these galaxies fit the low-luminosity extension of quenching predictions, with their IR luminosities being significantly lower than expected given their total stellar masses. If these galaxies are compared to their counterparts in the early universe, those with more massive disks are less quiescent and more massive, also exhibiting more irregular shapes but less massive cores. Nonetheless, the core characteristics remain unchanged, with mass asymmetry being a key driver of quiescence in these galaxies as well. If the galaxies are considered over time, we observed a notable decline in their quiescence and mass asymmetry in just a billion years, with their total stellar masses also increasing substantially. We believe that the unique characteristics of these galaxies are a direct result of their position within a galaxy group, which is subject to varying gravitational influences, with the group's center serving as the primary source of gravitational forces that are strongly affected by the galaxies' irregular shapes. We propose a theoretical framework that incorporates this variation in a `gravitational tapestry' to better understand these complex interactions. Typically, less massive stars retain a rapid rotation rate throughout their main sequence, and a notable discrepancy in core and surface rotation rates isn't observed until they reach the giant stage. Nevertheless, precise measurements of several eigenfrequencies in the $\ell=2$ rotationally induced pattern of HD 43845 challenge this expectation. To explain the observed frequency spectrum, we used three different models of integral spectra and a detailed investigation of various input parameters. Ultimately, a specific combination of a rapid core rotation rate, a slightly asymmetrical core, and a substantial amount of elemental helium in the core successfully replicated the observed frequencies. This discovery opens up possibilities for exploring distinct rotational states of low-mass giants and highlights the potential for uncovering rotational states through a combination of seismic and spectroscopic analysis. Furthermore, this research suggests that a rapid core rotation rate in a less massive giant might result from angular momentum conservation during external mass loss, a theory that we plan to investigate in the future. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing the identification of false information on unexpected events with no need for retraining or labeling new data. This system leverages the strength of its own hyperparameters and the structure of the data to learn a context-invariant fake news detection mechanism, which can be applied to a wide variety of contexts. Experimental results indicate that MetaFEND outperforms conventional approaches, even when applied to new, unrelated domains, with a 12% improvement in metrics used to evaluate its performance. Moreover, it demonstrates the ability to detect false information on unexpected events with no need for additional data, resulting in a 10% increase in metrics used to evaluate its performance when compared to the conventional method of retraining the model. This achievement holds true across different models, including the widespread use of LSTMs, despite their decline in popularity in recent years. Notably, MetaFEND was developed using a large corpus of information with 32 million participants, showcasing its effectiveness in this large-scale setting. To facilitate further research, the code and the proposed approach have been made publicly available. In summary, the proposed system addresses the key limitation of current methods in detecting false information on unexpected events with no need for retraining, and its applicability in large-scale settings makes it a significant contribution in its own right. In these large-scale settings, often found in real-world scenarios, the system's ability to reduce data requirements significantly, by learning a context-invariant detection mechanism, is particularly valuable. This is because it enables the detection of false information on unexpected events with no need for additional data, thus making it a valuable tool for various applications. In addition to its scalability, the proposed approach has been found to be highly effective in detecting false information on unexpected events, surpassing conventional methods in multiple evaluations. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we investigate the well-posedness and stability of this transport equation in $H^{3}\left(S\right)$. It is demonstrated that for $\kappa>0$ and specific range of $\alpha$, where $0\leq\alpha<1$, this transport equation has a unique global weak solution. Furthermore, under the additional condition $\alpha<\frac{1}{2}$, we establish that this unique solution converges to $0$ as time progresses. The research also reveals that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ can counteract the destabilizing effects of the non-local flow. This phenomenon is further highlighted by the formation of singularities in a modified version of the transport equation in a finite time period. The investigation into the transport equation is accompanied by the study of a related linear model, known as the fractional Burgers equation. This fractional Burgers equation is found to exhibit a unique self-similar solution. The research paper also delves into the relationship between this fractional Burgers equation and a corresponding stochastic process, specifically fractional Brownian motion. The relationship is utilized to determine the suitable space in which the solution to the transport equation exists. The contribution of this research paper is the establishment of specific conditions under which the solution to the transport equation exists in $H^{3}\left(S\right)$. This achievement is made possible by employing stochastic analysis in conjunction with classical methods of partial differential equations. The research paper offers a unique blend of transport equations, fractional flows, and nonlinear dissipation, coupled with the employment of robust mathematical tools. The research it encompasses provides a framework for examining various transport equations that feature non-local flows. These equations have been utilized to model diverse physical phenomena, including the propagation of ocean currents, the behavior of biological populations, and the movement of fluids in the Earth's mantle. The paper also presents directions for possible future extensions to its findings. These potential extensions are marked by the challenges they pose, such as addressing the well-posedness issues of transport equations characterized by non-monotone flows and researching the dynamics of fractional Burgers equations in the presence of external forces

The results show that incorporating quantum tunneling effects from a surrounding dopant cloud can either hinder or facilitate coupling between a quantum bit's drain node and its gate, depending on the extent of tunneling. 
This discovery is crucial for developing reliable and coupled quantum devices and also highlights the significance of considering quantum tunneling in interpretations of data from local quantum systems and devices. 
Furthermore, this research paves the way for a broader understanding of the interplay between Coulomb interactions, quantum tunneling, and Josephson coupling in superconducting quantum systems.

By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we created a synthetic dataset comprising various tree-based scenario variations and found that our approach enabled the generalization capability to similar, previously unseen systems. When the training data consisted of only a single system, learned representations demonstrated the ability to recover the underlying structural patterns, effectively bypassing the need for explicit input. Our research provides a unique understanding of how graph neural networks generalize to similar complex systems and sheds light on the relationship between their learned representations and the underlying dynamics. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. By applying these formulas, we are able to determine the graded components of these homology modules and demonstrate that they conform to a specific pattern. As a consequence, we are able to reestablish and improve upon previous findings regarding the vanishing of low-degree components of these homology modules. Additionally, we establish that the higher-degree components form finite-dimensional vector spaces of specific ranks, and we develop a recursive formula to compute these ranks. Leveraging these findings, we are able to describe the behavior of the ranks in relation to their position in the family of binary integer partitions and illustrate that they are determined by a sequence of binomial coefficients. A noteworthy aspect of this structure is that it results in overlapping patterns of decreasing ranks, which we demonstrate are equivalent to the ranks found in a sequence derived from the values of Bernoulli numbers. Moreover, we find that the application of these recursive formulas enables us to extend the analysis from a limited sequence of binary integer partitions to a more comprehensive family defined by a set of modular conditions, thereby providing a means to study various phenomena in the context of stable homotopy theory. As an related observation, we note that these recursive formulas yield a distinctive pattern of integer sequences that are interconnected, reflecting the interdependent nature of the coefficients that define them. As a notable consequence of this analysis, we observe that the application of these recursive formulas results in a sequence of coefficients that gives rise to another sequence of coefficients, which in turn defines the same family of binary integer partitions, thereby establishing a sense of "self-similarity" within this system. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a further contribution, the GP 2 framework, along with BigArray, is being made available to the academic community through an open-source licence. As a result, other researchers can leverage and modify these tools for related purposes of program analysis and verification. To facilitate seamless integration, both the original Bak's compiler and BigArray are implemented using Scala, a versatile and widely adopted programming language. In order to validate the novel compiler and array structure, a set of rigorous tests has been created, ensuring the integrity and reliability of these developments. This test suite, consisting of both unit and functional tests, is also contributed to the academic community through an open-source licence, allowing other researchers to modify and update these tests as necessary. With the GP 2 compiler's performance enhancement and associated developments now publicly accessible, other researchers can leverage a more efficient compiler, a tailored development process, tested source code, and a sophisticated data structure, facilitating further advancements in the verification and analysis of programs utilizing graph transformation rules. As further proof of these developments' advantages, the accompanying paper has been successfully applied to analyse specific properties of binary graphs using linear time complexity, an improvement over the original linearised time complexity of the GP 2 compiler. In the process of making these developments open-source, multiple opportunities for improvement were identified, demonstrating the potential for further evolution of these tools and associated methodologies. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. Furthermore, our contributions update the star twisted wreath classification for dihedrals and wreaths (features already known but now incorporated into a unified framework) and introduce a new twisted wreath structure example derived from cubic extensions of complete graphs. A key aspect of our research involves developing a twisted wreath construction that can be viewed as a cubic extension of a graph obtained from a twisted wreath structure, a concept initially observed in the sector of group theory known as permutation group theory. This achievement allows us to connect our findings to a theoretical permutation group framework, specifically within the class of groups that act on sets defined by root structures of a field with a non-zero characteristic, a phenomenon observed by Burnisland, Giudici, and Spiga. We also identify the parameters under which a twisted wreath construction results in a group with a specific property of acting on sets defined by root structures of a field with a non-zero characteristic, a feature initially discovered by Burnisland, Giudici, and Spiga. A final aspect of our research involves establishing that a class of twisted wreath structures, which include our star twisted wreath examples, do not admit automorphism groups with a specific property called high rank, a characteristic that can be beneficial in resolving the Cayley-Hamilton theorem for the associated polynomial rings. We achieve this by applying a recently introduced theorem by Delgado, Stepanov, and Vyshercv that provides a condition for a polynomial ring to avoid the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. A benefit of this condition is its connection to polynomial rings defined by root structures of a field with a non-zero characteristic. We further explore this relationship by applying the star normal quotient twisted wreath structure to derive results for polynomial rings that do not adhere to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, a characteristic initially discovered in a more limited form by Giudici and Li. We also establish and prove the necessary and sufficient conditions for a polynomial ring that does not adhere to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to have a specific property of acting on sets defined by root structures of a field

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique are capable of outperforming the baseline T5 model in various knowledge-intensive tasks, including QuAIL's quatrains and the FactIQ dataset. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by categorizing sequence elements into two distinct groups based on their distance from the current position. This technique significantly shortened calculation time without compromising performance. Building upon this work, a new model is presented that utilizes a dual-path RNN in the frequency domain to enhance modeling of sequence distances for an inter-frequency speech separation task. Experimental results indicate that this model yields a notable speed bonus and maintains the efficacy of the time domain approach, also offering a higher reduction in calculation time when compared to other long sequence modeling methods. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/parsonson/fd_dprnn.

A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending fluid driven by a thermal instability mechanism. By adjusting various model parameters, it is demonstrated that this model is capable of reproducing the basic characteristics of dry convection. The results obtained from the multi-fluid model are compared to those produced by a traditional dry convection model. The study reveals a higher level of accuracy achieved when using the multi-fluid model to simulate certain aspects of convection, particularly in relation to the distribution of temperature and humidity within the ascending fluid. Nonetheless, both models yield comparable levels of accuracy in terms of simulating the rate of convection. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm for determining the Wigner function from its "tomographic snapshots" and apply it to demonstrate the entanglement generation in a quantum membrane-based optical parametric amplifier. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for eavesdropping protocols based on optical tomography in continuous-variable quantum communications. Moreover, we show that quantum synchronization of two discrete-frequency modes is achievable, offering a versatile means of quantum memory with continuous frequency tuning. These outcomes pave the way for developing quantum protocols based on optical tomography in continuous-variable quantum communications. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm in recovering the Wigner function following a quantum state's dynamic evolution, effectively serving as a diagnostic tool for post-processing quantum state trajectories. Ultimately, our research highlights the utility of combining quantum state reconstruction with machine learning techniques, suggesting the development of a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both methods to enhance the reliability of continuous-variable quantum technologies. Such an hybrid framework, which we refer to as quantum learning tomography, is showcased by successfully recovering a Fock state from its optical tomogram using an initial guess obtained via machine learning. This hybrid method also demonstrates improved accuracy in comparing the dynamics of quantum state trajectories, indicating its potential for facilitating the development of quantum technologies by serving as a diagnostic tool for both theoretical and experimental quantum state trajectories.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve uniform composition over large areas using current manufacturing methods, which limits the availability of these materials for practical use. This study demonstrates a novel and scalable integration method of highly uniform, nanosized alloys with varying composition, exhibiting unique magnetic properties, into a large area substrate. This achievement is made possible by tailoring a nanostructured interface to sort rare earth elements into distinct regions with different compositions while maintaining strong magnetic interactions. The resulting material shows exceptional sensitivity to weak external fields and rapid magnetic decay, which could be beneficial for magnetophotonic applications. By combining this material with a gold nanoantenna array, researchers achieved significant magnetic field-induced optical responses in a wide field and demonstrated controlled, rapid magnetophotonic switching of a plasmonic mode with multiple stable states. These findings open up possibilities for developing ultrafast magnetophotonic devices and switching schemes that require minimal magnetic energy and have multiple stable states. Furthermore, this discovery enables the rapid induction of optical scars and enhances magnetic near-field induction in plasmonic systems. This breakthrough also reveals that rare earth transition metal alloys can serve as an adaptable 'active medium' for nonlinear magnetic photonic phenomena exhibited by the integrated system, allowing for the demonstration of optical rogue waves in a plasmonic system. This innovative technology paves the way for rare earth transition metal alloys to be integral parts of sophisticated magnetophotonic devices and nonlinear photonic systems that exhibit extraordinary behavior under weak driving forces. This achievement is featured as the cover image of this issue. A discussion of the techniques used to synthesize and characterize the rare earth transition metal alloys is included in the supplementary information. Focused ion beam scanning microscopy was used to analyze the nanostructured interface and the resulting magnetic material, while magnetic force microscopy and magnetic field-induced magnetization were employed to study the material's magnetic properties. In addition to the information provided in the main text, more details about the rare earth transition metal alloys' composition, structure, and magnetic properties, as well as the magnetophotonic device fabrication, are available in the supplementary materials. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is 3 or greater. A detailed examination of the short exact sequences that generate the modules $M(\gl_n)$ also uncovers new information about their underlying structure. The results obtained can be compared to those achieved via a different method, offering additional insights and confirming the validity of the results. The method alternative involves applying the theory of coherent sheaves on the affine space $\mathfrak{g}^\ast$, for the Lie superalgebra $\osp(3,2)$. The construction of the sheaf $\mathcal{M}$ that represents the module $M(\gl_n)$ is a crucial step in determining its lattice structure. The process involves identifying the sheaf $\mathcal{M}$ as coherent, then determining its submodule structure from the exact sequences of the type given by the $\osp(3,2)$-module derivatives, known as the Koszul complex, to finally reconstruct the lattice of submodules of $\mathcal{M}$. The method used also yields information about the cohomology of the sheaf $\mathcal{M}$, which is further examined to determine if the module $M(\gl_n)$ belongs to the category of Harish-Chandra modules. The investigation conducted is then expanded to include modules associated with the superalgebra $\sso(2,2)$, resulting in comparable results for both the lattice structure and the module type. The process developed can be applied to modules for any Lie superalgebra with solvable Lie superalgebra, serving as a model for the process of reconstructing the lattice structure of submodules for modules associated with these superalgebras.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongyuyu/CoIL. Our findings demonstrate the value of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external guidance, offering a novel perspective on reinforcement learning through the cooperation of agents. marked by a constant current. Uncovering the precise conditions under which 
these non-equilibrium steady states are reached in periodically driven open quantum
systems is the focus of our research. We introduce a new method to analyze these
systems and find that their non-equilibrium steady states are actually located at
the intersection of two equilibrium states that are connected by a cyclic path. 
Our novel approach also enables us to determine the exact conditions under which
these systems reach a non-equilibrium steady state and to calculate the current
and the two relevant equilibrium state populations with high precision. As a key 
advantage, our method allows us to combine different driving protocols, transfer

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the complexity and costs associated with transaction recovery, it is crucial to prevent long-running transactions from interfering with other database operations. To address this challenge, we propose two new algorithms: one for detecting when a transaction becomes too large in a standalone deployment, and another for replica set and sharded cluster deployments. These algorithms either limit the size of transactions or terminate them if they exceed a specified size, preventing them from causing database lock-ups. To evaluate our proposed solutions, we conducted a series of experiments involving scalable, distributed transactions and standing alone deployments, and analyzed the results to provide data on performance gains. These experiments revealed a significant reduction in failed transactions and improved overall database performance when employing our size-limited transaction strategy. To further illustrate the benefits of our approach, we created a utility function for database administrators to determine the optimal maximum transaction size that balances the trade-offs between database performance, failed transactions, and data entry speed. To facilitate easy integration of our solutions into existing MongoDB installations, we developed an open-source extension called MongoDB Transaction Size Controller. This controller allows administrators to configure various settings, enables size-limited transaction transactions, and includes the utility function for optimal database performance. To validate our results and ensure consistency across different MongoDB versions, we conducted thorough testing of our extension against the official MongoDB test suite. Finally, we outline possible directions for future development, such as adapting our solutions for MongoDB's latest version and further optimizing our controller to minimize overhead costs. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. These findings are further supported by comparisons made against controlled random network configurations. Additionally, the associated noise spectra demonstrated distinct scaling patterns that are distinct from those observed in both ordered and critical random network configurations. In conclusion, this study reveals how the interplay between magnetic forces and the triangular structure of connected nodes gives rise to robust indicators of self-organization criticality, providing a new understanding of the relationship between geometry, ordering patterns, and the associated noise that occurs within complex networks. This knowledge can be applied to analyzing similar phenomena observed in other triangle-based network assemblies. This research expands on a previous study published in Physical Review Letters 123, 048601 (2019). We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. If we assume the energy flux follows a power law distribution, we estimate the index to be about 1.5 plus or minus 0.3, which is also consistent with earlier results and implies that the total solar wind energy that reaches the surface must be quite small, on the order of 10 to the power of 31 Watts, which is only about 10 times more than the energy required to heat the corona. If we base our calculations on just the proton energy flux, we find that the solar wind energy that reaches the surface must be even smaller, which suggests that the energy that is lost as solar wind is still being produced is very efficiently used to heat the corona. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Through the use of a scanning laser acoustic sensor, our experiments were able to capture these emissions in high definition. A novel approach to applying the correlation dimension and a nonlinear prediction method was then employed to analyze the data, yielding consistent outcomes. This research reveals that a micro-slip event is indicative of a chaotic state and its associated dynamics can be better understood through the lens of fractals and nonlinear analysis. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the distance between these micro-slip events serves as a randomly distributed variable that can aid our comprehension of their collective behavior. A comparative study of two methods for predicting future values from past data has also been conducted, yielding surprising results, as the nonlinear prediction method is shown to yield better outcomes for certain variables than the commonly held ideal of using a random process, despite exhibiting similar performance in other cases. This research paves the way for a deeper analysis of nonlinear dynamics governing the peeling process, which in turn could potentially reveal the underlying causes for tape failure, such as sudden loud sounds or stick-slip motions. This knowledge could then be leveraged to develop predictive models for predicting the remaining lifespan of adhesive tapes during use. This research has the added benefit of introducing a novel approach to extracting information from acoustic emissions, a technique with broader applicability, and providing a nonlinear analysis of stick-slip dynamics despite initial state of chaos. This research further reveals the distribution of the time spent on both micro-slip and stick phases of the process, providing a basis for predictive models of the remaining lifespan of the tape. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Ultimately, the contribution of this research lies in providing a swift and accurate means of calculating hedging costs, an essential consideration for institutions that rely on option delta hedging as a core practice. This approach can be further integrated into existing risk management frameworks to provide a more precise assessment of hedging-related risks. In addition, this new formulation offers substantial computational benefits for financial institutions, given the frequency with which they compute hedging costs, making it an attractive development for the industry as a whole. This research paper originated from a broader study on the optimal pricing of hedging services, with a focus on how hedging costs impact the fair price of services in this context. This fair price is akin to the convenience yield that is a key component of the fair value of an oil option, as discovered through an empirical analysis of oil options prices, or the storage cost that is a significant component of the fair value of Treasury bills with delayed maturity, as found in a study on negative Treasury yields. This research has implications for regulatory bodies, as it highlights the importance of considering hedging costs and costs of delayed settlement in the pricing of financial instruments, and thus the need for clear regulations on hedging costs, in order to prevent institutions from exploiting these costs and distorting market prices. This knowledge can also be applied by financial institutions that manage risks and allocate capital, as well as by investors who trade with these institutions and rely on healthy and transparent financial markets. This research has been conducted with the aim of contributing to the development of risk management frameworks and capital allocation methods that take into account the costs of hedging and delayed settlement, as well as the desire to make hedging services and financial instruments with delayed maturity more attractive to market participants, and thus more widely used. This knowledge can be applied to specific contexts, such as a scenario where a company requires a hedging service but is charged a high cost, in which case this research can help it negotiate

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. Moreover, it facilitates the examination of policy interventions, such as educational systems and fair employment practices, on societal mobility dynamics. The model has a straightforward mathematical expression that can be easily interpreted, making it a valuable tool for understanding the complex interplay between individual status, group affiliation, and societal mobility. The proposed model builds upon the conventional asymmetric experience model by incorporating a learning curve for skill acquisition, thereby accounting for individual differences in ability to rise through socioeconomical levels. The resulting expression for the model's optimal policy reveals its intuitive nature, which can be easily visualized, in addition to providing clear policy-based insights. The introduced model also enables a clear distinction between different types of fair employment practices, offering policy recommendations that can improve socioeconomical mobility in various societal settings. The validity of the proposed model is supported by real-world data from the United States, Canada, and Norway, demonstrating its practical applicability. The result of the model, especially when applied to the mentioned data, reveals a clear and consistent pattern of socioeconomical affirmative action that is in line with the model's predicted outcomes, and it does so while accounting for individual differences in ability to rise through socioeconomical levels. The model's ability to account for individual differences also enables the estimation of these differences from real-world data, offering a quantitative measure of how difficult it is to move up the socioeconomical ladder for certain groups of individuals. The relationship between these differences and various predefined groups, such as gender and ethnicity, can be examined using the proposed model, providing valuable insights into its dynamics. The model-based analysis is complemented by a simulation-based exploration of policy interventions, relying on a simulated dataset with known underlying dynamics. The introduction of new policies or changes in existing ones can be examined in this simulated setting, allowing for a controlled comparison with the actual data

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing all 6 TeV proton beams. This innovation, developed by the LHC experiments, allowed for the precise monitoring of long-term beam dynamics stability and efficient detection of potential issues. As a significant improvement over traditional beam surveys, Emittance Scans provided better time and intensity resolution, and they played a crucial part in maximizing the effectiveness of LHC operations. Furthermore, these scans successfully identified and studied specific beam dynamics phenomena, leading to a better comprehension of long-term beam evolution and allowing for the development of more accurate predictions. This experience has paved the way for future LHC experiments and has implications for other particle accelerators worldwide. As a result of this project, the author was awarded the 2020 Cockcroft-Cocks Award by the European Physical Society. Moreover, the implementation of Emittance Scans has been recognized with the 2020 Stockponder Prize by the American Physical Society. In addition, this achievement led to the author being selected for the 2020 European Physical Society Cockcroft-Cocks Award and the 2020 American Physical Society Stockponder Prize. 

To better understand and predict beam dynamics in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), it is essential to monitor its long-term stability. Previously, this was achieved through beam surveys that utilized fast separation scintillators to determine the beam's emittance and location. However, these surveys had limitations, could be disrupted by certain physics runs, and couldn't be executed continuously. To address these issues, the LHC experiments collaborated to develop a new method called Emittance Scans, which could be used during regular physics production runs. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. The findings highlight the impact of adversarial actions on solution degradation and the benefits of using robust optimization methods in such dynamic environments. The development and evaluation of the proposed algorithm are implemented using MATLAB, and the results show its effectiveness in tackling optimization challenges in multi-agent systems with adversarial behavior. The impact of communication constraints on solution accuracy is also examined in the report. The research presented in the paper has been part of a larger study that was recently published in the journal IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control. The related work section of the paper highlights the differences between its contributions and those of previous studies on the subject. The approach described in the paper is then applied to a scenario involving a power grid, and the results are discussed in the paper's final section. The code and data associated with the paper are available for use by the community, and the paper's results are compared to those of similar studies in the relevant research field. The relationship between the paper and its related work is depicted in a diagram presented in the document. The study discussed in the paper has been funded by a grant from the National Science Foundation, and the paper's findings are relevant to the sustainable development goals related to affordable and clean energy. The research presented in the paper involves the simulation of complex dynamic systems with the help of modeling their interfaces, and the model developed as part of the research is based on optimization algorithms that consider various uncertainties, which are represented as sets of scenarios. The study discussed in the paper involves multiple agents with different goals, and the model includes the simulation of interfaces through the integration of models of individual agents, which are obtained by solving optimization problems that consider the sets of scenarios as uncertainties, which are then solved using gradient-based algorithms that result in algorithms with robust and individual components. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. As the signal of cosmic microwave background anisotropies becomes increasingly precise, the significance of removal of foreground contaminants also needs to be greatly improved. The main obstacle faced by current observations is the bright emission of the galactic plane, which dominates the signal of cosmic microwave background anisotropies by several orders of magnitude. Therefore, it's essential to develop accurate models of foreground radio emission within the galactic plane. A linear model that incorporates 19 components of the galactic foreground is proposed, and a Bayesian method is used to estimate these components from beam-smoothed observations, also taking into consideration their uncertainties. This method is applied to data from the low-frequency, multi-waveband experiments SPICA, BOOMERANG, CMBAnis, SPIPA, ARCADE2, GMAM, DURIP, and VSA at the very same locations observed by these experiments. As a result, detailed maps of the galactic foreground are constructed and used to remove contaminants from the cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Moreover, the estimation method itself is made available for other experiments and can be utilized for a linear model of any source distribution. The present model's limitation is discussed along with possibilities for improving the model by incorporating additional information about the galactic plane's structure and foreground evolution over time. The actual maps and estimates of the galactic foreground are made publicly available at the same website as the model, allowing for the removal of galactic foreground from cosmic microwave background anisotropies. The website address is: https://casa.iayork.org/foregrounds/. The estimated galactic foreground models will be updated in the future as new information becomes available. The model and estimated maps were tested on a small-scale region of the sky observed by the SPICA experiment using a horn beamforming technique, and the results showed that the estimated maps accurately reflected the actual observed values with a slight overestimation of the standard deviation of the estimated galactic foreground components. The main reason for this overestimation was attributed to beamforming being less efficient than expected, especially in regions farthest from the phase center. The galactic foreground models were also applied to a region of the sky observed by the BOOMERANG experiment using a horn beamforming technique, and the results showed that the estimated maps could be corrected by adjusting the standard deviation of the estimated galactic foreground components by a factor of 0.85. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Furthermore, our proposed model exhibits superior performance when applied to real-world datasets, yielding a 9.3\% error rate on the FakeNews Corpus, surpassing existing techniques by an average of 4.5\%. Our code has been made available on GitHub at: \url{https://github.com/zhengfengdu MD-CSD-Net}.

Building on this work, J. R. Kelsus and D. C. Thomas explored its implications within the context of metric and semi-metric spaces. They introduced the term "sun angle" to describe a specific relationship that defines a specific ordering among points in a given space. Through the application of this ordering, Kelsus and Thomas were able to establish various results, including multiple maximum principles for distinct types of functions. Specifically, they demonstrated the existence of a maximum point for the function that achieves the minimum value for a given set, as well as functions that obtain the maximum or minimum value at a specific distance from a given set. Furthermore, they extended these results to different types of functions and spaces, including those with specific topological characteristics. Additionally, the mathematicians proved to obtain specific orderings that result in the attainment of extreme values at specific distances from a given set, often near a particular point within that set. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine a chain of nested lattices within the unit sphere of the field $\mathcal{O}$, whose Minkowski determinant is given by $\Delta(\mathcal{O}) = \lambda_1^2 \cdot \lambda_2^2 \cdots \lambda_{n-1}^2$. In this study, we establish the distribution of the normalized Minkowski determinant, denoted as $\frac{\Delta^{1/n}(\mathcal{O})}{h_K}$ with $h_K$ being the class number times the product of roots of Hecke's function, as approximately normal for a large subset of orders in a given number field, subject to certain conditions on its degree and discriminant. Furthermore, we find that this distribution is governed by an integral involving the characteristic function of a specific family of Gaussian distributions, which is analogous to the Krohn's formula for the distribution of class numbers. This achievement supplements earlier findings by the second author for a limited class of quadratic fields and generalizes the results by Diaz that the normalized Minkowski determinant's variance tends to $n$ for number fields of degree $n$. The proved normality of the Minkowski determinant's distribution also implies that its sequence forms a random sequence in the Kolmogorov sense. The discovered characteristics of its distributional properties can be utilized to derive statistical inferences regarding its components, specifically the distribution of the field's class number. The adopted measure of the unit sphere's volume, defined as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of the embeddings, is a deviation from the conventional measure based on the arithmetic mean, which results in a distinct distribution of the normalized Minkowski determinant. This distinction causes the variance of the class number to be affected by the field's configuration, leading to its dependence on the number of its distinct embeddings rather than their Galois group structure, which was an open question by Diaz. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, we investigate potential links between Forsage and other similar scams utilizing the same hidden backend, which we refer to as the "Pyramid Orchestra." Our research concludes by discussing the implications of our study for the broader cryptocurrency community and the challenges posed by hidden, pyramid-based blockchain applications. Our study's unique access to a normally closed-off pyramid scheme allows us to highlight the difficulties in identifying these schemes and the necessity for greater transparency in cryptocurrency transactions. Through our examination of the Forsage scheme's collapse, we derive valuable insights for developers and users on how to avoid similar disasters and ensure sustainable, fair blockchain applications. Our study's data and analysis are available at our website at https://forsage.science/.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions like Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra, which are adjusted to match the observed Balmer line spectra and the flux of ultraviolet continuum. This approach yields a logarythmic best-fit scaling of 1.00 $\pm$ 0.15 for the total UV continuum flux in the $F_\lambda$ units based on the observed flux in the $r$ band, which is consistent with the findings from previous analyses of UV stellar flares. This updated model also predicts the spectral energy distributions of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  with an rms scatter of 0.15 dex based on the flux in the $r$ band, and demonstrates that a linear relationship holds between the UV continuum flux in different wavelength intervals. This model's predictions are compared with those obtained from state-of-the-art stellar atmosphere models, which show that the UV continuum flux in the $\lambda \approx 2500-3200$ Å\  range is primarily produced in the photospheres of flare ribs, whereas the shorter-wavelength range is dominated by the radiative cooling of chromospheric rib edges. This model has significant implications for future space missions that will observe variability in the near-UV spectral region, as it provides a crucial tool for interpreting future data on low-mass stars and their planets. This model can be utilized to assess UV biosignatures on exoplanets and, combined with radiative hydrodynamic simulations of stellar flares, can be used to assess the habitability of low-mass stars and their planets. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we devise specific methodologies for validating the precision of our security guarantees under different transformation conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the superior precision of our proposed framework compared to the current industry standard, particularly when analyzing a popular point cloud model in 3D object detection known as FCFPN. To accelerate robustness validation, we also introduce a novel technique called inverse normalization, thereby further enhancing its efficiency by approximately 90x. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Analyzing these distinct components has made it possible to identify a large number of previously unobserved RPA poles that were initially broadened to the extent of being undetectable and have since been classified into several distinct categories.
