Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. To support widespread adoption, we open-source the SparseGAN model at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is proposed that takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Furthermore, a relationship between the time it takes for microbial life to migrate between two planetary systems and the distance between them can be predicted, all of which has implications for the search for life beyond our planet. While the proposed model initially suggests that life might be limited to a specific "habitat zone" centered on the Sun, the inclusion of panspermia as a possible mechanism makes the distribution of life more uniform, with consequences for NASA's current and future missions to search for life. The proposed model also highlights the significance of considering the origins of life in relation to the movement of stars and the dispersal of microbial life forms. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method combining capture-recapture and resource usage data that estimates density and usage weights for resources and space, which can be a useful tool for future studies that aim to explore relationships between population density and various environmental factors, including those factors represented by resources.  We apply this method to studies involving black bears and elk.  These studies show that capture-recapture models can be used not only to estimate population density but also to explore the complex spatial behavior of animals, which is a crucial component of conservation planning and management.  We also compare different models and discuss model assumptions, which provide valuable guidelines for future applications.  In addition, we contribute to the development of capture-recapture models that incorporate demographic processes, which is another crucial aspect of animal population research.  These models can produce individual characteristics, including age and sex, which are essential for managing and conserving animal populations.  We conclude that capture-recapture models integrated with capture-location models and resource selection functions can be a powerful tool for conducting comprehensive research on animal populations and can be applied to future studies that aim to explore relationships between population density and various environmental factors, including those represented by resources and space.  We also outline potential future directions for these models, including incorporating behavioral responses into resource selection functions and age and sex structure into capture-recapture models.  We have developed the R package "RCSRFS" to implement these models in R.  This package provides capture-recapture models integrated with capture-location models and resource selection functions, which can be a valuable tool for wildlife researchers worldwide.  We have made "RCSRFS" available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/USGS-WCR/RCSRFS.  We have also created a vignette that can be found at the following address: https://usgs-cr.github.io/RCSRFS/.  This vignette serves as both a user manual and a tutorial for using "RCSRFS" in R.  We have made "RCSRFS" an open-source package

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. Systematic reductions of the multilayer network are also possible, allowing us to map the reduced representation back to the multilayer network, which can be useful in network analysis. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of dynamical systems, including those described by nonlinear equations and those with stochastic components. Moreover, our framework incorporates various interlayer connection configurations, including both weighted and unweighted connections, and can be used to assess the impact of different interlayer connections on a system's dynamics. Our results are further demonstrated through numerical examples presented in the paper's figures. Futhermore, our approach has been utilized to examine the effects of a multilayer network's structure on its synchronization properties in the context of a specific model. Our findings, which are graphically represented in the paper, indicate that a system's synchronization is significantly influenced by its interlayer connections and that these connections can be optimized to achieve higher levels of synchronization. Additionally, our research involves the application of our proposed method to a multilayer network model that incorporates both intra- and interlayer nonlinear interactions, which results in the formation of coexisting phases in the multilayer system. Our analysis of these phases is carried out through a reduced model and involves the examination of the parameter space in the context of the Nishida-Kobayashi theorem. Our findings indicate that there are distinct regions in the parameter space corresponding to different phase coexistences, which can be realized by adjusting the interlayer connections. Our results in this regard are presented in the form of bifurcation diagrams that illustrate the relationships between the multilayer system's parameters, its structure, and its dynamics. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This paper also clarifies the relationship between the Einstein operator, the Cauchy operator, and the $div$ operator on an n-dimensional manifold with respect to its tangent space, identifying key properties such as being a differential operator of order two, having zero trace, and satisfying the Einstein identity when defined on a vector field. Finally, this paper demonstrates how the Einstein operator can be applied to provide a simplified proof of the Einstein equation from the Einstein field equations. Additionally, relationships between the Einstein operator and the Schouten tensor or the Riemann tensor are examined. This paper also introduces the concept of a Ricci operator, which is the result of applying the Einstein operator to the metric tensor of a given manifold and is found to be equivalent to the Ricci operator defined using the Bianchi operator induced from the Einstein operator. This leads to a direct application in deriving the Einstein field equations from the Einstein field equations. This paper further explores its use in a scalar field scenario. Notably, defining the stress operator or the Einstein operator on a manifold is found to be insufficient for parameterizing the Cauchy stress operator; rather, parameterization requires the use of the Einstein operator in conjunction with the Einstein field equations and the metric tensor of the given manifold. Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. This action results in the orbits that are defined as filling in a sphere of radius $\frac{\pi}{3}$ around the point representing the direction of $\delta$. If the field $K$ is infinite, the number of the mentioned orbits is expressed as $\frac{1}{\text{surface area of the sphere}}$, with the surface area defined as $\frac{2^{25}}{3^{5}\pi^2}\sqrt{3}$. If the field $K$ is a finite field with an amount of elements $q$, the number of the mentioned orbits is calculated as $\frac{q^{2l+1}-1}{q^{2}-1}$ for a root system of type $A_l$, and as $\frac{q^{2l+1}-1}{q^{2}-1}$ times $2^{l-1}$ for a root system of type $D_l$. If the field $K$ is a finite field with an amount of elements $q$, and $q$ is not equal to $2$ or $3$, the number of the mentioned orbits can be expressed as $\frac{q^{2l+1}-1}{(q-1)(q^2-1)}$ for a root system of type $A_l$, and as $\frac{q^{2l+1}-1}{(q-1)(q^2-1)}$ times $2^{l-1}$ for a root system of type $D_l$. If the field $K$ is a finite field with an amount of elements $q$, and $q$ is equal to $2$ or $3$, the number of the mentioned orbits can be calculated directly. The mentioned orbits in the root system of type $A_2$ are shown to fill a tetrahedron

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm that provides an accurate estimate of the network's small size, even in the presence of a high number of malicious nodes, with a time complexity of O(log n) and a packet complexity of O(log^2 n), where n is the network size. We developed this algorithm for an undirected and connected wireless network using a limited neighborhood structure, which we call a "tree-like" network. We established its correctness under the assumption that the network's actual size is polynomial in relation to the number of malicious nodes. To establish this validity condition as a general problem statement, we developed a theoretical network with a large number of malicious nodes and a small number of legitimate nodes, showing that determining its size is a #P-complete problem with respect to the number of legitimate nodes. To facilitate efficient algorithm development for network size estimation, we established a crucial but previously unknown property: networks of a specific structure, which we call "tree-like" networks, have sizes that can be counted using #P-complete problems but with a reduced number of necessary bits of precision. To demonstrate the applicability of this property to real-world scenarios, we examined networks defined by two commonly used clustering protocols and determined that they adhere to a specific, scalable variant of tree-like networks. To facilitate further research, we made the source code for our algorithm publicly available. To provide a clear understanding of the conditions necessary for accurate network size estimation, we examined multiple protocols and established precise lower bounds for the maximum allowable network sizes. These bounds range from O(k^3) in the case of a random network to O(k) in the case of a specific structured network, where k represents the maximum number of malicious nodes that can be tolerated. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
This study's results also highlight the importance of considering the drivers'
behavior and queue characteristics to improve traffic state estimation. 
Furthermore, the research reveals that the proposed nonparametric model can be 
used to estimate relevant parameters for the Negative Hypergeometric distribution. 
This knowledge can be applied to situations where more precise parameter estimation is necessary. 
This paper's nonparametric approach and the associated model can be utilized to 
estimate short-term queue lengths in similar traffic scenarios. 
This achievement is made possible by the inherent scalability of the nonparametric approach. 
This study's results are valid for intersections with a single lane per approach, 
but its methodology can be applied to multi-lane approaches in subsequent studies. 
This research contributes to the development of a scalable traffic state estimation framework that is based on nonparametric methods and general traffic knowledge. 
Such a framework's potential to reduce data dependencies and enhance estimation accuracy is demonstrated. 
This accomplishment is shown to facilitate robust traffic state estimation in scenarios with limited or unreliable traffic data. 
This study's outcomes also highlight the significant impact of traffic signal timing on local traffic dynamics and state estimation performance. 
These findings suggest integrating traffic signal control with traffic state estimation can lead to more efficient and precise estimation results. 
This research paves the way for further investigation into integrated traffic management systems that consider various aspects of traffic state estimation and control. 
These systems' potential to better handle non-stationarity and variability in traffic dynamics and state estimation performance is shown. 
This achievement is made possible by the developed nonparametric traffic state estimation approach. 
This approach enables traffic engineers to effectively handle complex real-world traffic conditions and optimize various performance measures that are significantly affected by traffic state estimation errors. 
These performance measures include fuel efficiency, emissions, and journey time, among others. 
Therefore, developing more accurate and robust traffic state estimation methods is crucial for optimizing these performance measures in various application scenarios.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter configurations, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the conformal factor with a new fundamental variable, effectively eliminating the Hamiltonian constraint's impact on the solution's dynamics. Instead, the Hamiltonian constraint is used to solve for the conformal factor after the 2+2 decomposition of the metric and its Christoffel symbols, which are then used to compute the mass-energy density. This method allows for a more direct relation between the initial conditions and the dynamics of the Einstein field, and it has been successfully applied to sample problems involving scalar fields and binary black hole mergers in simulations of scalar perturbations and full three-dimensional simulations of merging black hole configurations. Our results show that the new approach produces the same physical outcomes as the standard method, but with a significant reduction in the computational costs required to generate the same accuracy in the solutions. Specifically, our time-intensive binary black hole merger simulations, which took around 5000 hours to complete on a supercomputer, can now be completed in just 1000 hours using a standard desktop computer. This improvement in efficiency will be crucial for extending current binary black hole merger simulations to include more complex matter configurations that require more intricate resolution scales, as indicated by the subpar success rates of current simulations in resolving fundamental issues of recoil velocities and ejected mass distributions. Our new method has the potential to address these limitations by allowing a significant increase in the number of simulations that can be run in a given time, which will be essential for simulating merging black holes with various mass ratios and spins. Our results also demonstrate the stability and accuracy of this new approach in resolving issues related to constraint violations during long-term evolutions of the Einstein field. In particular, our research shows that the new method yields a $10^4$-fold decrease in the maximum violation of the Hamiltonian constraint during binary black hole mergings, which remains less than $10^{-3}$ times the critical density for an extended period of time, and which remains stable even when considering perturbations of rotating, irregularly shaped black holes, also known as Kerr instabilities. Our new approach has been made available as part of the Numerical Relativity Code, known as NRGrD. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. A comparative study with theoretical models and other materials reveals that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is closely related to the anomalous Hall conductivity and can be effectively controlled by the spin-orbit coupling and magnetic disorder. Our results highlight the anomalous Nernst effect and anomaly in the anomalous Nernst coefficient of Mn$_3$NiN occurring in the high-temperature phase, and also demonstrate the capability to modulate the anomalous Nernst coefficient via the lattice expansion caused by temperature increases. Moreover, our study reveals a positive correlation between the anomalous Nernst coefficient and the anomalous Hall coefficient in materials with the anomalous Hall effect, suggesting that they share a common origin, and also shows that the anomalous Nernst coefficient can be adjusted by varying the spin-orbit coupling and magnetic disorder. Our findings in this study open up new avenues for the investigation and control of the anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials. Our experimental approach can be applied to other materials with the anomalous Hall effect and provides accurate measurements of the anomalous Nernst coefficient, while our theoretical comparison can be used to clarify the underlying mechanisms of the anomalous Nernst effect and anomaly in materials with the anomalous Hall effect. Our discovery of a positive correlation between the anomalous Nernst and Hall coefficients in these materials also suggests future prospects for realizing materials with both extremely large anomalous Hall and Nernst effects. We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$. This achievement comes from a novel way to express the volume's residual contribution as a specific surface residue is mapped onto a shrinking model of a 'blow-up,' effectively revealing its structured, component-based form. This type of analysis yields an equation of a specific surface that represents the minimum perimeter achieved in the 'large volume regime,' a finding that was initially proposed by the mathematicians Giusto and De Philippis. Moreover, our approach enables a systematic analysis of the blow-up model's surface residue, allowing us to distinguish between its intrinsic features and those resulting from the confined object's specific shape. This distinction makes it possible to introduce a new concept of a'minimal surface' that represents the lowest-perimeter surface achievable in the 'large volume regime,' one that is significantly more general than the confined object's specific type known as a 'landscape function.' This newly defined'minimal surface' can be obtained through a process called'sweep,' which combines the confined object's surface with the result of projecting a set of tangent lines perpendicular to the surface, and results in a surface with a specific, pointy structure where the surface residue's features are located. This surface's perimeter is what we seek to minimize in the isoperimetric problem outside a confined object, and we demonstrate that its optimal solution takes the specific form of a sphere if the confined object is also spherical, and the 'large volume regime' scenario is not considered. If the confined object is not a sphere, we discover that the surface that achieves the minimum perimeter in the 'large volume regime' has a particular, complex structure, one that is composed of a main part that is roughly approximated by the confined object itself, along with multiple small surfaces that make up the surface residue's features and are located near the confined object, each with a specific, curved form that is closely related to a particular type of a surface known as a Wulff shape. These small surfaces are what contribute to the surface residue's total area, and we introduce a way to classify them into two distinct categories: those that have a close relation to the confined object's shape and those that do not. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods beyond the traditional methods used on composite materials in project construction phases other than fabrication.
The aim of this research is to explore and develop a novel algorithm for determining deformation in these materials by studying their electrical conductivity changes during bending tests.
A comparative analysis of different self-sensing material models was conducted to develop an equivalent model for a carbon-black-filled polyurethane composite by calculating the dielectric constant and conducting particle size distribution from scattering patterns of individual particles.
The results showed a direct relationship between the conductive phase's size and the material's conductivity, while the aggregate's size primarily influenced the dielectric constant.
The equivalent model accurately predicted both the dielectric and electrical behavior of these materials by effectively accounting for spatial distribution variations of nanofillers.
Utilizing this model's parameters, a novel algorithm was created to calculate local strain from the changes in electrical conductivity during bending tests.
The algorithm's effectiveness was validated by applying it to test data with results that compared favourably to the actual measurements, demonstrating its suitability for use in detecting deformations in self-sensing composite materials. The developed model and algorithm provide a practical tool for predicting and detecting deformations and damage in these materials by analyzing their electrical conductivity changes. The research's findings contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between the self-sensing material's electric and dielectric properties and provide a reliable framework for developing and evaluating these materials. The proposed algorithm's versatility makes it an valuable resource for various engineering applications that utilize these materials in critical safety projects. The study's limitations highlight the need for further research on scaling the developed model for a wider range of loading conditions and different composite material types. The proposed framework can be applied to other material types with similar electric and dielectric property behaviors. The algorithm's precision improves with smaller particle size distributions, emphasizing the importance of accurately controlling the nanofiller's size during the material synthesis process. The developed model accurately predicts the dielectric and electrical behavior of the material for a wide range of loading conditions, ensuring its scalability for various applications. The algorithm's robustness was validated by applying it to different composite materials with diverse loading conditions and different nanofiller distributions, ensuring its versatility for various engineering projects. The study's findings are relevant to a wide range of composite materials with similar electric and dielectric property behaviors

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. This study provides a substantial foundation for utilizing invasive BCIs in recovering more intricate aspects of walking ability in individuals with spinal cord injuries. To achieve this, researchers will need to translate these findings to patients with spinal cord injuries and develop a closed-loop system that incorporates a suitable lower limb prosthetic device. To that end, further research is necessary to establish a direct relationship between recorded cortical signals and actual muscle-based gait parameters in such patients. Nonetheless, the current study demonstrates a significant level of precision in decoding more complex aspects of walking from a direct cortical source and offers a promising avenue for recovering more intricate walking ability in individuals with spinal cord injuries. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios results in subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address these limitations by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our model's capabilities are further highlighted through the creation of personalized recommendations based on dynamic attention graphs from neuroimaging data. DECENNT's efficacy is showcased across multiple tasks and data types, highlighting its versatility. Code availability: https://github.com/ghaith/DECENNT. If applied to larger animals, it could offer insights into minimizing soil compaction, while on a broader scale, it may also provide a new reason why many animals tend to move at specific speeds. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The package provides a reliable prediction for the $\texttt{BR}(\mu\to SS)$ for complex parameters across the $m_{\text{susy}}\ll m_{\text{EW}}$ scenario. The discussion on $\texttt{BR}(\mu\to SS)$ is accompanied by a comprehensive examination of the $\texttt{EW}$ and $\texttt{QCD}$ contributions to the Higgs boson masses and decay widths, with specific examples of decay width variations demonstrated. The development includes a modification to the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code, with the option to employ complex mass parameters. The accuracy of the results is ensured through multiple consistency checks, involving the convergence of different cross-section calculations, the application of the heavy top-quark effective theory, and the use of the $\texttt{OnShellTransfer}$ code to verify the implementation of the $\texttt{RGEs}$. Tempering the evaluation of policies for sequential decision-making under unknown reward distributions is crucial, especially when considering the vast number of possible distributions. When data from a wide range of distributions, both seen and unseen, becomes available during both training and testing phases, our novel efficient policy evaluation method yields superior results. Our approach involves leveraging additional data from testing and validation sets to enhance reward function estimation, thereby improving policy evaluation. In contrast to conventional approaches that utilize separate reward function models for evaluation and parameter tuning, our method employs a unified model to maximize utility under the variance of a sawtooth distribution. Theoretical and empirical studies demonstrate improved policy evaluation when considering a broader range of data distributions. Our framework is particularly effective when data spans multiple contexts and it can be applied when data is limited to a single context but comes from multiple distributions. We evaluate our approach on real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world applications. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/JasonXu1993/ContextBandits.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights rather than developing an algorithm for universal convergence. We establish that in a large network with a significant number of users, the extremal gain from optimal power control compared to binary power control can be substantial, potentially growing exponentially with the number of users. We also find that this gain is not always beneficial, as it may lead to an exponentially large extremal maximum throughput or a significantly longer delay requirement, both of which could indicate a threshold effect where a slight change in parameters results in a drastic change in behavior. To support these findings, we develop a model where the gain and the associated costs are controlled by two independent, independent, and identically distributed (i.i.d.) parameters, both of which are extremely large and follow a specific statistical distribution. We then use these parameters to derive formulas that describe the extremal gain and the associated costs. We also use these parameters to create a new type of extremal network that we call the'monster network', which we then use to demonstrate the applicability and the extremal behavior of our earlier findings. We further investigate the extremal gain in a random multi-path network to demonstrate its independence from the specific choice of user pairing strategy. We also explore the relationship between the extremal gain and the maximum throughput achievable in a random multi-path network. We conclude by examining the limitations of our findings and the potential for extending our research to more complex networks. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested our method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing its results to a standard model that artificially lengthened collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard model while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our algorithm can be further improved by adjusting time steps for particle translations and rotations, and has the potential to be applied to various multiple-step simulations involving interacting particles. System requirements, algorithm details, and potential improvements are also discussed in the paper. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/JiCrime/PTSIC. The underlying open-source flow solver used in this research is OpenFOAM, and the sediment transport model used a modified version of generalPICC. The code was developed using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and compiled using GCC 9.3.0. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, a comparison between monodisperse and bidisperse granular materials showed that the feedback controller enabled the robot to hop on both types of ground with similar success. Ultimately, the developed control system allowed the robot to adjust its hopping frequency to match the natural frequency of the ground, thus avoiding energy loss due to viscous damping. Consequently, the robot was able to increase the desired height by approximately 20% when targeting a height of 50cm. The feedback controller also demonstrated its effectiveness when the target height was set to 60cm, on both monodisperse and bidisperse ground. The findings of this research emphasize the significance of incorporating feedback control into force control systems when interacting with uncertain dynamic environments. Moreover, the resulting controller robustness reduces the difficulty of modeling ground dynamics, enabling the use of less sophisticated models, such as the RFT, for predicting ground reaction forces. The developed model and control system framework are applicable to multiple-degree-of-freedom robots hopping on soft ground. The discrete element method models of the ground have been made available through the LIGGGHTS open-source software, allowing for the simulation of various granular materials. A contact interaction is proposed to describe the dynamics of quarks and mesons in a meson-scattering process. By applying the dressed series expansion, the Bethe-Salpeter equation is utilized to derive a dressed mass formula for quarks and mesons. Utilizing their dressed masses, the meson's composite nature is demonstrated through a straightforward interpretation. The proposed contact interaction's characteristics are examined to determine when the quark and meson masses become tachyonic. The predicted masses are then calculated for various meson types and compared with existing literature. The results indicate that the proposed approach yields comparable outcomes with a larger range of variable spaces, especially for lighter mesons. The derived quark masses also exhibit a linear relationship with the sigma-parameter, which is a characteristic feature of QCD. The proposed model's effectiveness is evaluated using the meson mass variance and the ratio of masses, in addition to the predicted mass range, to determine its confidence level. The majority of the confidence levels are above 99%, indicating that the proposed contact interaction successfully describes meson scattering dynamics. The approach's stability is also examined by investigating the quark and meson mass dependence on the sigma-parameter and coupling constant, which demonstrate that the predicted masses are independent of these parameters. The proposed model's confidence levels are compared with existing literature that employs the Faddeev-Jackiw quantization method, indicating a higher confidence level for the contact interaction approach, especially for lighter mesons. The most stable solution is then selected from the set of predicted masses for each meson type. The resulting masses are then used in various applications, including the investigation of the linear density distribution of heavy meson densities, the study of meson interactions with a constant electric field, and the calculation of meson decay constants. The outcomes of these applications are in agreement with existing literature. The developed code is open-source and can be utilized to derive masses for other hadron systems that are composed of two fundamental particles. The code's versatility is demonstrated by modifying the contact interaction to describe a system of two heavy mesons, for which the predicted masses exhibit a linear relationship with the sigma-parameter. The development of a code to solve the Bethe-Salpeter equation within the RPA framework is also presented. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. These results demonstrate a significant improvement in topic coherence over a key alternative method, while maintaining computational efficiency. A subsequent study using a web search engine's index also yields promising findings, highlighting the potential of HDTM to tackle increasingly large-scale datasets. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, this relationship enables efficient recovery of the annealing gap from post-quench data, facilitating practical quantum annealing simulations. As an example, we apply this approach to quantum annealing on random Ising chains at their critical point, successfully obtaining the annealing gap and related critical exponents through sample 'design' involving quantum quenching. These obtained exponents match their universal classical values, implying that quantum annealing on near-native samples corresponds to a true equilibrium scenario. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that even when the annealing gap cannot be approximated accurately, dynamical data following the quench still yields a wealth of information about the quench-driven post-equilibrium dynamics. This knowledge proves invaluable in revealing the distinct branching processes that underlie quench developments in random critical field theories. As an instance, we clarify the distinction between two quench-driven regimes in random Ising chains - with compact bonds representing 'dead ends' in a star-like structure as opposed to a tree-like structure with link bonds. This distinction manifests as a two-tier branching process, accounting for the absence of the annealing gap and explaining the resulting $t^{-3/2}$ decay of the returned quantum state's overlap with its initial state following the quench. This outcome is further supported by classical analogues, namely the Schramm-Loewner evolution and the Dyson model, both exhibiting dead end branches and analogous $t^{-3/2}$ decay of their returned quantum states' overlap with their initial states following the quench. This overlap decay is attributed to the return quantum state's inability to traverse the 'dead ends' in a random arrangement of branches, in contrast to the equilibrium scenario where all branches are accessible uniformly. This research paves the way for a broader understanding of quantum systems' dynamics in random configurations of the annealing pathway. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, its sound velocity also should rise in accordance with the Le Chatelier principle, which is supported by numerous dense matter models including quantum gravity, modified gravity theories, and certain quark phase scenarios.  By applying the pressure shift rule to various dense matter theories and models, sound velocity's response to density can be broadly classified into two distinct behaviors: it either consistently rises or remains essentially unchanged.  The sound velocity's response, however, can offer additional constraints on the equation of state of compact stars, especially for densities beyond nuclear saturation density.  The project's novel sound velocity relation, expressed as a ratio to the local speed of light, exhibits a robust and essentially density-independent value of approximately 0.58 for the compact star's sound velocity, primarily influenced by the bulk density component rather than surface components.  This new relation is applied to estimate the sound velocity in compact stars based on the $M-R$ relation obtained from recent gravitational wave observations, resulting in a minimum estimated sound velocity of $< 17.3$ km/s with $c$ units for $1.61^{+0.16}_{0.16}$ solar masses stars.  The relationship between the compact star's radius and its sound velocity remains essentially unchanged when considering a range of dense matter equations of state.  The connection between the compact star's radius and its sound velocity also exhibits a bounded and essentially density-independent sound velocity of approximately 0.58, primarily influenced by the bulk rather than surface components.  The introduction of surface components, on the other hand, result in the sound velocity's celeritas curve having a minimum point, located at a density of approximately $0.5$ times nuclear saturation density, where the sound velocity reaches a minimum value of about $15$ km/s.  The application of the new sound velocity relation to a sample of low-mass stars yields a slightly tighter constraint on the minimum sound velocity of $< 16.4$ km/s with $c$ units for $1.49^{+0.16}_{0.16}$ solar masses stars. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's growth rates generally decrease due a decrease in shear velocity difference. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 100-micron particles to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development limits particle-driven VSI similar to how it limits settling, our findings suggest that an outer region of these systems may experience VSI driven by larger particles, further indicating that VSI's dependence on particle size must be considered in modeling disk evolution. As a key observation, all models showed minimal impact from considering particle collisional growth on total particle concentration, indicating that settling dominates over growth in these systems. In a further analysis, we discovered multiple regions in protoplanetary disks susceptible to another instability, the Greshbach-Davis shear instabilities, but only in models featuring small particle sizes and specific shear velocity differences. As a result, dust development may also hinder these instabilities' growth in these systems. As an outcome of this research, we observed how particle behavior is crucial for modeling VSI and other shear-driven instabilities in protoplanetary disks, and in a broader context, how these systems' evolution are interconnected and how each component affects the others. As an example, particle development is influenced by heat dissipation from these systems, which in turn is impacted by VSI's ability to drive turbulence. In a model that incorporates all these interactions, we refer to the interconnection of these processes as "coupled disk evolution". As a next step in this research effort, we propose developing models of protoplanetary disk evolution that incorporate coupled disk evolution, with a focus on modeling VSI-driven turbulence and the resulting dust development and its feedback on the surrounding environment. Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network initialization that is unconventional. Through a systematic investigation, it was discovered that random initialization of neural networks could lead to dynamic backdoors, even in models that have a high degree of integrity, thus providing valuable insights into how to develop robust machine learning securely. A straightforward solution to this problem is proposed, where a new algorithm that dynamically updates neural network initialization is used, resulting in a robust model that has a low tendency to exhibit hidden functionalities when operating in different environments. Through extensive testing, it was demonstrated that this solution significantly reduces the likelihood of dynamic backdoors manifesting in various machine learning models, particularly those that utilize neural networks. What is notable about this solution is that it does not compromise the efficiency of these models nor can it be considered a form of robust machine learning, but rather a novel approach to securely initializing machine learning models. A thorough examination of various unconventional neural network initialization methods revealed that many of them are prone to leading models to hidden functionalities that are embedded, even in models that have a high degree of integrity, despite some of these methods being widely accepted by the machine learning community. Through the development of a testing framework, it was discovered that a vast majority of these initialization methods are susceptible to leading models to dynamic backdoors that are embedded, thus providing valuable insights into how to design robust machine learning securely. A novel perspective on the problem of hidden functionalities that are embedded is presented from the viewpoint of machine learning model reliability, thus distilling the development of a robust model that has a low tendency to exhibit different forms of embedded functionalities that are dynamic, such as backdoors, adversarial examples, and out-of-distribution data, into a binary classification problem. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable $\gamma$'s effect on measured parallax were conducted for several astronomical phenomena. These effects were found to be significant for some observations and could potentially introduce an additional astrometric uncertainty of up to 3.6 $\mu$arcsec, which is comparable with the predicted errors for Gaia's parallax measurements. Furthermore, a small deviation in $\gamma$ from 1 or variations in this parameter over time may also affect the measurements and should be considered in future missions with similar precision. A relativistic model that accounts for the Earth's motion around the Sun was applied, and the effects of variable $\gamma$ were found to be significant enough to be detected by a mission like Gaia, with an estimated uncertainty of around 0.0003 for this parameter based on a combination of astrometric and geometric considerations. Therefore, both variable $\gamma$ and its possible change over time should be factored into the design of future high-precision astronomical missions. The impact of variable $\gamma$ on measurements of other astronomical parameters, such as positions, distances, and masses, was also assessed in this study. The developed post-Newtonian model can be used to predict effects of possible distortions in general relativity on future high-precision astronomical measurements, allowing for a more accurate assessment of their potential impact. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Additionally, the knowledge acquisition process is analyzed to better understand what knowledge is deemed essential for answering specific questions. A subsequent examination of the knowledge's semantic value reveals insights into the nature of the knowledge itself. KnowQA's superiority is also shown to extend to other datasets like the TREC DeepQA collection. The code and models associated with this research are available at: https://github.com/ghrua/KnowQA. KnowQA's knowledge acquisition process and analysis of semantic value can be accessed at: https://knowqa.cs.uic.edu/. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution and cometary neutral gas composition. It also highlights potential for future spaceborne and ground-based observations to fill these gaps. Knowing where Cometary Secondary Emission Spectra End and Solar Induced Fluorescence Begin can aid in developing a more comprehensive model of the cometary environment. Furthermore, a lack of spectral information about some low-energy electronic transitions may indicate a missed opportunity for a mission that could potentially observe it. Such a mission could provide a clearer comprehension of a significant aspect of the cometary environment and could be a future low-cost space mission, perhaps using a currently operational platform. It is also essential to consider the electron energy levels of molecules and their relation to each other as well as how they behave in plasma and the cometary environment in order to correctly interpret spectra. This involves understanding both the temporary and permanent electronic states of cometary molecules as well as their respective abundance. It is, however, crucial to utilize a consistent and accurate nomenclature to avoid confusion in these designations. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle is the necessity to communicate encrypted model updates among nodes, complicating conventional optimization techniques. We present a novel method that adapts the Network Gradient Descent algorithm to tackle this issue, enabling efficient model learning while minimizing communication between nodes. Theoretical convergence time estimates for this method are also derived, considering both smooth and non-smooth model scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive synthetic data experiments and a real-world example using a healthcare dataset. This leads to a model with high accuracy in a healthcare classification task, showing the versatility of this FedNetGD algorithm. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A broader analysis considering the value of saved lives as well as the monetary value of crimes prevented reveals substantial economic benefits of offering mental health treatment within the criminal justice system.  An examination of different mental health treatment durations discovered that treatments lasting seven months or less have the highest likelihood of success.  An examination of different court branches found the reduction in future crimes is greater in superior courts.  An examination of different judges found some have a much higher success rate with mental health treatment than others.  An examination of different counties found that urban counties have lower reduction in future crimes than rural counties. An examination of different crime types found that mental health treatment reduces both violent and property crimes although property crimes are reduced more significantly. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new consistent medical image segmentation metric called the Consistent Curve-based F-score (CcFScore). The CcFScore statistic assesses segmentation consistency through a relatedness measure, capturing the relationship between adjacent pixels. This consistency assessment is a critical component in evaluating segmentation accuracy, given the limited available annotation data. The paper also presents The Consistent Curve-based F-Score (CcFScore) in a comparative analysis with established metrics such as the Jaccard-FC, DSC, and Hausdorff Distance (HD). Evaluations using real-world datasets for both head MRI cerebral segmentation and chest CT lung segmentation reveal that the new CcFScore statistic consistently ranks higher than the established metrics in accordance with clinical expert assessments. The research demonstrates the utility of CcFScore in evaluating medical image segmentation tasks, particularly those involving small annotated datasets. The associated code can be found in a public repository. The CcFScore metric has been integrated into the MedNAG evaluation package, which is also publicly available. The study's findings highlight the importance of considering the spatial coherence of medical images in segmentation tasks, showing that the existing global metrics fail to account for this aspect, and thus often misrank valid segmentations. The paper's contributions are reflected in the following code repositories: https://github.com/zhongyuan8410/ConsistentCCF and https://github.com/zhongyuan8410/MedNAG. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by a single parameter, where the distribution depends on an additional unknown variable. Suppose the available data consists of a single observation from a mixture of distributions, with the mixing variable being a count variable with an unknown positive integer. The goal is to estimate the parameters of the distribution family using an efficient method of moments estimation. To accomplish this, Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators are employed to estimate the parameters of the mixing variable's distribution. This results in a system of equations whose solutions yield the method of moments estimators. The procedure is applicable even when the mixing variable's distribution is not identified. The properties of the estimators are examined, including consistency and asymptotic normality. The method is utilized to estimate the parameters of a specific distribution family, obtaining results that compare with existing literature. Additionally, the method is applied to estimate the parameters of a Weibull distribution, with one of the distribution's shape parameters being unknown, using a limited number of mixture distribution observations. The resulting model is scalable and efficiently estimates the specified distribution parameters through the method of moments, with results that surpass the efficiency of Maximum Likelihood Estimation when the distribution is partially identified. The purpose of employing GMLSE is two-fold: it serves as a parameter estimation method for its own sake and also provides a necessary step in solving the system of equations that yields the method of moments estimators. The procedure is particularly useful when the moment equations fail to yield a solution, offering an alternative path to obtaining consistent estimators. The GMLSE approach is particularly advantageous when the mixing variable's distribution is not fully identified, offering a straightforward means of handling such cases. The purpose of employing GMLSE prior to method of moments estimation is illustrated through a simulation demonstrating its superior performance over the direct method of moments estimation, even in situations where the distribution is fully identified. The simulation demonstrates that the additional step of employing GMLSE results in a significant reduction in bias of the method of moments estimators, with the added benefit of being a more efficient estimation procedure when the distribution is partially identified. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical results alongside model comparison through rigorous statistical analysis are presented in the report accompanying PyKT. The findings highlight both promising performance and unpredictable behavior across different datasets. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. This investigation yields a stronger form of Helmholtz decomposition, referred to as the $\mathfrak{A}$-decomposition, which is obtainable on any manifold $M$. This paper also provides a weaker form of Helmholtz decomposition on manifolds with noncompact components. This weaker form is identical to the original Helmholtz decomposition achieved through the use of Coulomb fields. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this concept with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training approach. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). These gains were achieved with both the pre-trained English model and the adapted model on its own. Our top results showed a 14% WER decrease on the standard Czech dataset GirafTTS in comparison to the baseline transfer learning results. Additionally, our findings provided a basis for additional research opportunities, for example the study of transfer learning among Czech and Polish languages. We also contributed our Czech ASR data preprocessing guidelines to the community. Our ASR models have been made available on the Model Hub of Hugging Face.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater by utilizing TD learning with approximate value function updates, which we've enhanced with Gaussian Process regression.  As a result, our method yields a significant boost in efficiency compared to conventional TD learning, allowing it to efficiently navigate underwater environments.  By approximating the action-value function using GP-SARSA, our algorithm achieves a notable reduction in computational expenses and approximate value function updates, which in turn enables greater exploration and a faster convergence rate in approximately Markov decision processes. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. Utilizing these theorems, four previously known single-fluid solutions are identified as specific two-fluid solutions. The mass-radius relationships and compactness bounds are calculated for these four-fluid solutions. The two-fluid generalizations were found to maintain the same compactness bound as the corresponding single-fluid solutions. The mass-radius relationships for the two-fluid cases exhibit similar curves to their respective single-fluid counterparts. However, the two-fluid solutions yield a slightly higher maximum mass when the boundary condition $\bar{r}_+ = 6$ is fixed. The research also involves a comparison with certain known relativistic stars composed of a single fluid with anisotropic pressure. The findings demonstrate that two-fluid descriptions generally result in larger allowed masses for specific types of stars, with some deviations observable in certain types of anisotropic distributions. The compactness bounds of the two-fluid stars mirror those of their single-fluid counterparts. The approach introduced in this study can be further applied to seek two-fluid solutions for dynamic and asymmetric stars. The method developed also highlights the significance of choosing a particular covariant semi-tetrad and the necessity of 1+1+2 as opposed to 1+2 or 2+2 for describing two-fluid stars in general relativity. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. Yet, creating pseudo data is often impractical due to limited resources in real-world applications. This paper explores a more cost-effective approach for few-shot domain adaptation, drawing on the idea of learning a flexible grammar framework through meta-learning theory. Our proposed method, a hierarchical context encoder based on recurrent neural networks, leverages context encoders to obtain a domain-specific context vector, which is employed in a finder network to determine a parameter vector for the flexible grammar framework. To achieve few-shot domain adaptation, we employ a finder network to locate a parameter vector for the target domain, with the flexible grammar framework serving as a shared prototype. Theories on meta-learning are utilized to derive a cost function for finding the parameter vector, with results from large-scale, fully supervised GEC datasets at the task level and specific domain level indicating improved performance over current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our proposed approach demonstrates viable performance on even more constrained datasets, showing minimal decline when moving from large-scale baselines. Our code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengfengdu/MetaGEC.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we demonstrated the existence of a mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good for three or more agents, although this is based on an arbitrary, rather than polynomial, time complexity. In our investigation of mechanisms with the property of inducing pure Nash equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, a condition of agents' valuation functions adding up without the possibility of monetary transactions was assumed. However, we also examined mechanisms with this property for sets of agents where values can add up and there is the possibility of making monetary transactions, and derived analogous results involving the relaxed envy-free allocations. In addition to this, we established that for any mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to one good for two agents, a condition equivalent to being approximately strategy-free is satisfied.
