Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it establishes that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup of approximately the same size. Additionally, it is demonstrated that groups with a polynomially bounded diameter contain a solvable subgroup of a similar size, and this result is used to derive an innovative proof of Pyber's length problem for infinite groups. An analysis of specific groups, including algebraic groups and Cayley graphs, is also performed to gain insight into the broad classes of groups that possess a polynomial diameter. This research builds upon previous findings by Breuillard, Conlon, and Helfgott, as well as the recent work by O'Nan and Saltstone. An examination of the proposed diameter metric's behavior with different generating sets is also conducted. This is accomplished by establishing an infinite sequence of groups with increasingly large diameter values, as well as discovering groups with specific properties that maintain a constant diameter for varying generating sets. This research is further expanded to investigate groups with a bounded diameter in a specific dimension, which leads to a generalization of Pyber's length problem and new infinite sequences of finite and infinite groups. A comprehensive analysis of these groups reveals intriguing differences between their finite and infinite counterparts. This research is also used to develop innovative bounds for groups with a polynomially bounded diameter, which are applied to derive new results for specific groups and include an improvement on previous diameter dimension bounds from the works of Breuillard, Conlon, and Helfgott, as well as Breuillard and Conlon. This research is also applied to a wide range of finite groups, which are shown to have a polynomially bounded diameter, including the solvable, nilpotent, and groups of Lie type, as well as the symmetric and alternating groups and the braid groups. A key aspect of this research is the development of a new metric called the weak diameter, which is used to extend the polynomial diameter property to groups with infinite generating sets. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by calculating the mean of the two frequencies, yielding an accurate reading with minimal variance. The temperature sensor was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, occupying an area of 0.036mm^2, and demonstrated a 0.03°C resolution at 65°C, a -0.075°C/°F sensitivity, and an operating voltage range of 0.4V to 0.7V. Moreover, it exhibits a wide temperature measurement range from -20°C to 110°C. By incorporating a dynamic voltage supply, the energy consumption of the temperature sensor is adaptable to different temperature ranges and systems, thereby achieving a minimum energy consumption of 1.57nJ/°C. A working temperature sensor circuit was fabricated and the data obtained meets the simulation results, validating the effectiveness of the proposed design. Furthermore, it complies with industry standards, making it suitable for various applications in modern electronics. This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant result derived in this research establishes that the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids can be viewed as a natural transformation between gerbes. This interpretation extends the existing relationship between the Chern-Weil map and gerbe isomorphisms to the realm of Lie groupoids. Moreover, this result enables the extension of certain constructions from [arXiv:1907.00375] to the context of smooth stacks. A key aspect of this research is the introduction of a concept called "smooth stack gerbes" which is an expansion of the existing theory of stack gerbes. This development is made possible by the application of the Chern-Weil map to the universal bundle over a smooth stack. A significant finding in this research reveals that the Chern-Weil map produces a natural isomorphism between the gerbe obtained from the universal bundle over a smooth stack and the original stack. This achievement allows for the extension of various results developed in [arXiv:1907.00375] to the realm of smooth stacks. A key aspect of this research is also the demonstration that the space of connections for smooth stack gerbes can be viewed as the quotient of the space of connections for a related bundle gerbe by the action of character gerbes. This finding expands on a similar result presented in [arXiv:2012.08447] which was limited to dynamic stacks. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  It is, however, worth noting that this observation aligns with previous findings from the TMC-1 and Cygnus X-2 clouds, pointing to a possible universal pattern among massive starless cores, with masses typically ranging between 10 to 30 solar masses.  This study's results are also relevant to the theory that massive star formation is often facilitated by turbulent flow and density fluctuations, which would favor the growth of more massive cores at the expense of less massive ones.  Ultimately, further investigation of the cores within the Dragon cloud will be essential to better understand their dynamics and the role of turbulence in the region.  In the meantime, we have discovered one notable protostellar core with a massive outflow, suggesting that it could be a key site for examining the relationship between massive star formation and its surrounding environment.  This core's unique characteristics make it an ideal candidate for future, in-depth studies, with possible areas of focus including a detailed analysis of its outflow, as well as a search for a central protostar and the core's mass function through millimeter spectroscopy. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The resulting impact on the Gegenbauer expansion coefficients is a modified polynomial, which the paper explicitly defines. The connection between these operators and the Recard-Diamond integral is explored, along with the application to dimension increase in the context of radial positive definite functions. The paper also examines the cases where the original and modified polynomials coincide, which include instances of polynomial nature and specific parameter ranges. A relevant example is provided to demonstrate the application of these operators in the context of the Recard-Diamond integral. The paper's contributions are highlighted by its novel introduction of the beta-Hermite polynomials and the resulting connection to the Gegenbauer polynomials, along with the derivation of their explicit expression. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The study's findings are relevant to various applications involving the flow of complex liquids and could be useful in optimizing these flows by reducing surface roughness. The discovery of the stationary soap film regime, which we propose as a new "superstick-slip" state, also provides a new outlook on the physics governing these flows. The impact of surface roughness on the stress exerted during the collapse of a liquid film is significant, with stresses achieved in the "superstick-slip" regime reaching up to 1.5 times the value obtained in smooth surface conditions. The study's results have important implications for various real-world scenarios, such as foam flows in the paper and dairy industries, as well as for improving our understanding of the stress exerted during the collapse of a liquid film, a phenomenon with significant consequences during events like tsunami waves crashing on shore. The newly proposed "leverage rule" also offers insights into the stress distribution in stick-slip regimes, with stresses concentrated at the surface asperity contacts, and could serve as a fundamental basis for future simulations of these regimes. The study's findings on the relationship between surface roughness and the curvature of Plateau borders could be valuable for developing models that predict the behavior of complex liquids over time, as well as for optimizing surface roughness to minimize stress and improve foam flows. The newly observed "superstick-slip" regime could serve as a new research topic for exploring the physics governing this distinct state of the liquid interface. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The code and models developed during the challenge are available online.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene. However, the observed ethynyl benzene abundance is approximately one order of magnitude greater than expected, which could indicate this compound has a distinct or additional formation pathway, perhaps related to benzene's greater stability and ability to react with atomic carbon. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also on previously generated words in the target sentence. Our analysis shows that standard decoding order is crucial for maintaining translation accuracy and that certain words are more likely to be influenced by previously generated words than others. We have developed a novel look-ahead neural machine translation model that takes into account the dependence of target word generation on previous words by incorporating a conditional attention mechanism. Experimental results indicate significant improvements in translating highly dependent datasets, while showing no loss in performance on datasets with minimal dependence. Our model achieves these gains without the need for order-dependent decoding or specialized training data. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. Our best model achieves a translation quality of 46.69 in the NIST metric for the IWSLT 2015 en->de dataset. Our results also demonstrate that replacing the standard attention model with our conditional model leads to performance increases in a variety of translation tasks. Our model's versatility allows it to be combined with other improvements, such as learning attention weights or employing recurrent decoders, resulting in further quality enhancements. Our analysis of word dependence can be applied to other attention-based models and our model has the added benefit of reducing the degree of attention weights learned from training data, resulting in a 50% reduction in the number of weights to be learned in certain cases. Our model has the added benefit of producing attention weights that more accurately reflect the structure of the target language. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in software development and its practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the creation and dissemination of map-reduce-type frameworks. By applying the principles of translational science, we propose a simple, efficient, and widely applicable variety of frameworks, whose varieties include Hadoop, Terracota, and Google's Street View Streaming Map API. A key contribution of this study involves developing specific metrics to measure the ease with which code may be modified to use these frameworks, as well as the difficulty of using them. Furthermore, we propose these metrics be made part of an open source project to facilitate widespread adoption. This initiative, known as TCS, would provide educational resources, benchmark problems, and a scoring system for frameworks based on the ease with which code may be modified to use them. As a testament to the simplicity of one of the variants of TCS frameworks, we detail the experience of teaching undergraduate computer science students using it. The results show that students who use this variant complete a task that is significantly more complex in less time than those who use other variants of the TCS frameworks, which include Hadoop. The code for TCS frameworks, which includes Hadoop, Terracota, and Google's Street View Streaming Map API, as well as the variants of TCS frameworks, may be found at https://github.com/robparashar/TCS. The TCS project website is located at https://tcs.cs.rmit.edu.au/. The educational materials that are part of the TCS project, which include the variants of TCS frameworks, may be found at https://tcs.cs.rmit.edu.au/teaching/. The evaluation metrics for TCS frameworks, which include the ease with which code may be modified to use them, as well as the scores for Hadoop, Terracota, and Google's Street View Streaming Map API, may be found at https://tcs.cs.rmit.edu.au/metrics/. The paper related to this project was presented at the 2020 ACM Conference on Fair, Secure and Transparent AI to be found at https://fairai2020.acm.org/. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient under these conditions leads to a cosmologically interesting and constant deceleration parameter. The model is capable of describing the evolution of the universe from its present state back to a point where the Hubble parameter was approximately 20 times greater than its current value. The model's ability to asymptotically approach a state with constant viscosity also allows it to effectively model the universe's evolution during the epochs of inflation and quintessence. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. Assessing constraints from J/ψ decay depth variables, we find certain neutrino combinations are already firmly established as being unlikely, with additional limitations imposed by branching fractions and other J/ψ decay depths. These constraints significantly narrow down the possible parameter spaces for neutrino masses and effective coupling constants. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that certain effective operators could be highly restrictive for masses as low as 20 MeV, given current neutrino physics knowledge. We also observe that existing constraints already preclude the presence of a small number of sub-GeV dark matter particles with a certain interaction strength. Combining all constraints, we find that future J/ψ depth and neutrino experiments have the potential to explore new parameter spaces, with some areas being accessible with upgraded or new facilities, depending on the experiment's sensitivity. For instance, a 10-fold improvement in the JΨ charmonium decay branching fraction measurement could allow for a 10-fold reduction in the product of the neutrino mass and effective coupling constant. Similarly, a 5 GeV upgrade in the J/ψ energy spectrum search range could enable the exploration of a 5-fold larger parameter space for light sterile neutrinos with masses up to 50 MeV. Our study also highlights potential for other experiments, either existing or in development, such as the BESIII, LHCb, and DZero experiments, as well as the PANDA and Drell-Yan experiments at the future Chinese accelerator facilities. Our findings suggest that J/ψ decay depth variables offer a promising avenue for discovering light, GeV-scale sterile neutrinos, and could potentially reveal a neutrino mass region previously inaccessible due to the limited range of available experiments. Our research initializes this line of inquiry but acknowledges the need for further, more detailed theoretical and experimental analyses of J/ψ effective operators in the neutrino sector. Our results are also relevant to other experiments that can search for similar neutrino interactions with charm or light quarks. To facilitate this research, we have made our effective field theory code public, enabling the calculation of various J/ψ depth variables from effective neutrino interactions. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. The benefits of MFSSA are highlighted through a comparative analysis with other state-of-the-the-art methods, including a detailed examination of its computational impact. A real-world application exploring the use of MFSSA for reconstructing missing data components in multivariate functional time series signals is also demonstrated. Furthermore, the stability and optimal choice of parameters are investigated through a set of constructed examples and synthetic datasets. A real-world case study involving the analysis of temperature curves in multiple cities across China reveals striking patterns of seasonal fluctuations and periodic variations in differences between these curves. The implementation of MFSSA is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/Chen-Yi-Hong/MFSSA. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This allowed it to produce plasma with a 2.5 times higher density than initially possible, and with a 2 times longer plasma column than initially available. This improved plasma source can now support higher power RF waves, and has a similar plasma density to other European test facilities. It is now capable of supporting the widest range of RF power studies in Europe. It is also similar to the plasma sources used in the ASDEX Upgrade and JET tokamaks. It was also observed that in helicon mode, a significant amount of plasma is lost to the ends of the source, and it is assumed this plasma is lost when tokamaks use this plasma source. A study was also conducted to investigate how plasma interacts with the antenna, and it was found that it causes significant erosion of the antenna, and it leads to the formation of a plasma shield that reduces the plasma density in the center of the device. It was also found that increasing the magnetic field strength reduces the plasma density, but it also causes a significant increase in the size of the plasma plenum, which means more material needs to be replaced after each experiment. It was also found that increasing the RF power increases the plasma density, but it also causes the plasma to interact more strongly with the walls of the device, leading to the formation of filaments that can cause uneven distribution of plasma density. It was also found that the plasma plenum can be divided into two parts: a central region with a low density, surrounded by a high-density region, and it was found that this distribution remains unchanged even when the magnetic field strength or RF power is changed. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In a comparison with the current state-of-the-art method, U-Net, the proposed approach delivers a substantial improvement in detection performance, as validated by both quantitative and qualitative results. Furthermore, the proposed approach outperforms the state of the art in terms of F-score, achieving a score of 0.83 or higher when modeling various types of cancerous and non-cancerous cell images. To support widespread adoption, the code for the proposed approach has been made publicly available on GitHub. 

To evaluate the proposed approach's performance in a real-world cancer diagnosis context, researchers conducted an experiment where they applied the model to a large set of non-cancerous breast cell images with minimal impact on accuracy, as discovered in a follow-up experiment. Moreover, the paper explores the relationship between model performance and the size of input images, revealing that the proposed approach can accurately detect small nuclei in images scaled down by as much as 3 times, before a noticeable decline in performance occurs. 

In order to facilitate widespread adoption of the proposed approach in real-world cancer diagnosis settings, the code has been made available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/aliotori/wsh_nucleus_detection. 

To ensure reproducibility of the research, in addition to the code, the paper's authors have made the following artifacts available: standardized evaluation metrics for performance assessment, pre-trained models on various image datasets, and sample pathological image datasets for cancer types including breast, colon, and liver. These artifacts can be found at https://aliotori.github.io/artifacts/.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic if the equality of their gamma factors holds for all s with sufficient negative magnitude. Our proof relies on an inductive approach by transforming the problem into a system of equations involving the gamma factors of the automorphic representations of the symplectic group Sp(2r+1+2) or a specific group of orthogonal matrices with 2r+3 dimensions, denoted as $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{std}}(s)$ or $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{ext}}(s)$ respectively, which are known to have a specific relationship according to the Langlands recursion formula. By utilizing the properties of these relationships, especially the fact that only the standard $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{std}}(s)$ results in a non-trivial solution for a system of equations, we conclude the proof of our claim. This result was initially proven for the special orthogonal group in a prior work by the authors, while the case for the symplectic group represents new findings. In the process, we also establish the local converse theorem for the representation of the special orthogonal group with an even number of dimensions, denoted as SO(2r)(F), which represents another important aspect of this paper. In this version of the paper, we consider the case for the symplectic group and the special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions, while a separate paper deals with the case for the special orthogonal group with an even number of dimensions. Additionally, we employ the result for the special case of the symplectic group and the special orthogonal group with an even number of dimensions in another separate paper. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A subsequent section delves into the derivation of GCNN learning rules, with the result showing that GCNNs embody both CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as distinct subcases. A systematic exploration of non-equilibrium Markov processes is also introduced as a broader framework for understanding the dynamics of both GCNNs and recurrent Neural Networks. A concluding section explores the relation of these results to existing literature and highlights the potential for further study in this domain. A comprehensive overview of the paper's findings is provided in the appendix section. Code for the paper is available at this link https://github.com/strawberry-cs/gcnn-analysis. In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit those of standard Chern-Simons theory. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic paths, while in rotating hairy black holes cases, the theory allows recovery of the temperature and chemical potential. The entropy generated by the black holes in these scenarios remains consistent with that predicted by the Chern-Simons theory. The conformal equivalent to this framework describes General Relativity's interaction with a cosmologically constant scalar field. The redefinition of the Chern-Simons form for this system, incorporating a Weyl field, enables the derivation of a nonlinear equivalent to conformal Weyl gravity. The addition of a conformally transformed Chern-Simons form for another group of symmetries leads to a new sector with a massless graviton and a massless scalar field, whose behavior is self-sustaining through a feedback mechanism, defined by a non-trivial holonomy constraint. The redefinition of this Chern-Simons form form also results in a Fock-type particle interpretation of this massless scalar field, indicating its soliton state as a coherent state with a specific number of photons. The connection between this Chern-Simons form and the Einstein-Hilbert action suggests that Einstein's gravity theory can be viewed as a consequence of this self-sustaining feedback mechanism, defined by a non-trivial holonomic constraint, which in turn implies that the scalar field's self-correction mechanism originates from the gravitational interaction itself. The holonomic constraint is essential in restricting the space of possible solutions to only those that are conformally flat, determining the role of the Chern-Simons form's complex degree of freedom as the driving force of this self-sustaining feedback mechanism, which in turn defines the spacetime in which the Chern-Simons form exists. The relationship between the Chern-Simons form and the Einstein-Hilbert action also enables the derivation of Einstein's gravity

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Consequently, the proposed VSSA-based elastography technique exhibits a substantial advantage in multiple directions over conventional SA elastography. Specifically, the increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction directly translate to improved estimation of lateral tissue displacement, thereby facilitating more accurate determination of tissue mechanical properties. Consequently, the VSSA-based elastography technique proves capable of accurately determining tissue mechanical properties across various orientations, thereby broadening the scope of SA-based elastography for examining complex tissues with diverse mechanical properties. The proposed method's versatility is demonstrated by applying it to both ex vivo and in vivo subjects, incorporating regional segmentation of tissues with distinct mechanical properties, and calculating PR at different depth levels. Overall, the introduction of VSSA enhances SA elastography's imaging depth, permits increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction, and empowers accurate estimation of lateral tissue displacement, thereby facilitating a better understanding of tissue deformability behavior in multiple directions. As a result, this technique has the potential to improve the diagnostic accuracy of various diseases, including cancers and cardiovascular diseases, by offering a more precise and accurate assessment of tissue mechanical properties across various orientations. The developed framework is presented as BEAMWIN, a comprehensive toolbox that incorporates VSSA beamforming in conjunction with OVERWIND elastography, enabling easy application to various subjects and allowing for different tissue segmentation based on depth levels. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic program, where each rule represents a type of step that can be taken. This development offers a novel, proof-based understanding of logical pseudocodes and sheds light on the relationship between the steps of natural deduction and the execution of a program in logical pseudocodes. Furthermore, this relationship provides a theoretical basis for innovative debugging techniques that leverage the insight gained from this connection. Specifically, it enables the diagnosis of errors by analyzing the underlying natural deduction proof that led to an execution error. This diagnosis can be achieved without access to the source code of the original program. As an illustration of these new debugging techniques, we will demonstrate their application to a specific type of execution error that results from the inclusion of certain unjustified steps in a natural deduction derivation. This example showcases the capabilities of these techniques in a concrete manner. Additionally, these techniques can be combined with other methods of debugging, allowing the application of any previously developed technique to the "purer" form of the natural deduction derivation that led to the error. This pure form represents the minimal subset of the original program responsible for the execution error. As a natural extension to this research, future developments could involve the creation of compilers that convert logical pseudocodes into a form analogous to assembly codes, facilitating the discovery of the minimal source code contributing to specific execution errors. This achievement would, in turn, facilitate a deeper investigation of the relationship between the steps of natural deduction and the execution of a program in logical pseudocodes. This investigation is essential for unlocking the full potential of these new debugging techniques. This research was initially presented at the 10th International Conference on Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS 2012). A more detailed account of these developments can be found in the associated document. This document also presents additional related research mentioned in the AAMAS 2012 conference proceedings. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We achieve this improvement by introducing a new technique that leverages a novel partitioning method, and our result applies when the optimal center distribution is bounded by a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$. By combining our approach with existing results, we significantly narrow the gap between the upper and lower bounds for the space complexity of the $k$-means clustering problem in dynamic streams. Specifically, we establish that there exists an integer $p(d,\log\Delta)$, where $p(3,10) = 17$ for example, such that for any dimension $d \geq p$ and scale $\Delta \geq 2$ there is a data set with $n$ points in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, mean squared error at least $\Omega(kd^{-p(d,\log\Delta)})$ from the optimal, and a way to generate it in a one-pass stream. We can solve this problem with a coreset of $\poly(k,d,\log\Delta)$ size while maintaining a mean squared error comparable to the optimal. If the dimension is sufficiently high, we can reduce the required storage to approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $\log\Delta$. We also show that upper and lower bounds for the space complexity of the $k$-means clustering problem in dynamic streams are at least an order of magnitude apart if the data has an unbounded dimension. We further investigate a variant of the problem where we aim to find the optimal center distribution for a given set of predefined centers, and obtain more general results applicable to various coreset algorithms. We also explore the variant where we consider a stream of points in a single-dimensional Euclidean space. In this case, we find an explicit data set and Euclidean space dimension such that the lower bound for the space complexity of the $k$-means clustering problem in dynamic streams is at least an order of magnitude greater than the corresponding upper bound, demonstrating a significant gap that needs further research. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Specifically, it yields significant reductions in computation time for significant grid scales, with a notable scaling advantage over flat policies as the grid size increases. Additionally, it offers a scalable and general framework suitable for application in diverse grid configurations.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based methods. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks does not generally lead to a significant gain in performance, and in some cases may even result in a loss of efficacy. To overcome this limitation, we show that isolating distinct sub-structures within the learned dynamics model can be beneficial for tasks with varying observation spaces, and we propose a novel solution, task-observable structure learning, to automatically determine these sub-structures. Our proposed method, which identifies observation-specific sub-structures, enables the learned dynamics model to accurately handle different observation spaces for each task, resulting in a significant improvement. We further demonstrate the benefits of our approach in multiple scenarios of multi-task reinforcement learning. Our proposed technique is compared to alternative methods of addressing different observation spaces, including the use of common encoders, which shows its superior performance. Our research and proposed solution can be applied to various domains of multi-task reinforcement learning, including domain-independent action selection and value function multi-task learning. Our code is available at: \url{https://github.com/haotianzhang123/tree-based-rom}.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. This examination reveals how a compact formulation of the relevant logical principles can yield the incompleteness theorems as a direct consequence, offering an alternative derivation of these theorems that provides additional insights into their underlying structure and logical requirements. This analysis also clarries the relationship between type theory and the incompleteness theorems, demonstrating how the essential features of the latter can be obtained from just a limited version of type theory. This version excludes the capacity for a system to express the notion of being part of a system's proof theory, yet still enables us to establish both the undefinability of truth and the incompleteness of the system. This examination is not merely a historical or technical review, but rather an exploration of the underlying logical principles that give rise to the incompleteness theorems, and it paves the way for a broader discussion on the fundamental limitations of formal systems in mathematics. This examination is also notable for its use of a novel formulation of the relevant logical principles that are a part of the standard metalanguage about formal systems, yet are not part of the systems themselves. This distinction is crucial in understanding the relationship between the limitations of formal systems and the standards of the metalanguage used to describe them. This examination has significant implications for various areas in the philosophy of mathematics, and it offers a fresh perspective on some of the long-standing debates within this field of study. This examination also clarries the relationship between type theory and the incompleteness theorems in a way that provides a viable explanation for why some formal systems are incomplete, yet others are not. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples from the posterior distribution for any given measurement, without significantly increasing the computational burden. This allows for the creation of more accurate training data for neural networks, enabling them to produce high-quality solutions even in cases where the prior assumptions have limited applicability. We achieved this by introducing a new neural network component that generates a Markov chain consistent with the posterior distribution, without the need for expensive reconfiguration for each new observation. We applied this method to various inverse problems including MRI reconstruction and image deblurring, and the results demonstrate substantial gains over current methods. Code available at: \url{https://github.com/Hengs123/inverse-probability-mapping}.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of how to identify and analyze the dynamics of systems confined to invariant sets within their state space using local stability techniques for specific dimensions. A series of illustrative examples highlight how this approach can be applied, and we also review some key theorems related to the conditions under which a subset of the state space remains stable over time. Furthermore, this report reviews the relevant mathematical frameworks, including the Invariance Principle, the Continuous Stability Theorem, and the Hopf Bifurcation Theorem. By integrating these concepts, we provide a framework for investigating how changes in system parameters influence the evolution of its underlying dynamics. This report is designed to serve as a primer for researchers and students seeking to understand the applications of invariant sets in the analysis of complex dynamical systems. Some of the discussed topics, such as the Global Manifold Theorem and the Dynamic Transition Diagram, are particularly useful for studying non-linear systems characterized by multiple stable states and their associated transitions. Some renowned examples, including the Lotka-Volterra model, May-Leen population dynamics, and the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction, are used to demonstrate the practical utility of these theoretical concepts. This report is intended for readers with a basic understanding of differential equations and linear algebra, and it should facilitate their entry into the study of nonlinear dynamical systems from a stability-focused perspective. Some of the discussed theories and associated theorems are also applicable to a broad range of nonlinear systems, and this report aims to provide a stability-oriented framework that can be applied across various scientific disciplines. Some of the discussed concepts, such as the conditions for a set to remain invariant over time and the associated stability theorems, are fundamental to a wide range of nonlinear systems and can be found in various nonlinear dynamical system textbooks. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Another screen, responsible for significant scintillation, is located about 7.5 parsecs away but is not linked to any evident void. Both screens were found to occupy fixed positions in space, unlike some screens discovered in other observations that moved relative to the Earth. This study reveals the possibility that screens in the interstellar medium, even those found in regions like the Local Bubble, can persist for a long time and points to the potential for future investigations into the relationship between screens and the surrounding medium. Additionally, the analysis of the void associated with one screen may hint at the screen's own influence on the local interstellar medium. The observed timescales for the formation of faint patterns are much shorter than previously recorded and suggest that smaller screens or screens at greater distances are more difficult to detect and may be more common. The paper also presents a model for estimating screen sizes based on the duration of specific scintillation patterns and alkaline earth element abundances in the surrounding interstellar medium. Two screens were found to exhibit different rotation periods and might be linked to the varying rotation rates observed in the surrounding stars, whereas no direct correlation was found between screen distances and rotation periods. The analysis of the void associated with one screen reveals a shape that could be indicative of a screen's own influence on the local interstellar medium rather than a pre-existing void. The study suggests that screens can persist for a long time and are likely embedded within the interstellar medium rather than being situated at its surface. The paper also examines the distribution of screen distances in the solar neighborhood and presents a model that could be useful for future observations and element diffusion research. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, a quasi-periodic WaveNet model is presented, showing promising results in controlling pitch over a wider input range compared to standard WN. In the speech synthesis domain, F0-constrained QPNet yields a lower error rate than several state-of-the-art methods, indicating its potential applications in professional voice editing. Experiment codes and pre-trained models are available at: https://github.com/zwang84/qpnet.

Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. The discussion also delves into the characteristics of shadows applied to categories, thereby connecting them to the principles of THH and its relation to the K-theory of categories. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training a separate classifier to distinguish between foreground objects and their surroundings using a classifier that has been trained to recognize various categories of objects. This leads to a surprise finding where the classifier incorrectly identifying parts of the image as background often corresponds to the source of the sound. To further this research, we develop a novel algorithm that first extracts features from a learned sound source localization model, and then employs these features to localize the sound source in videos. Notably, our algorithm succeeds in circumventing the need to annotate data, and it achieves this without any compromise on accuracy. To validate our approach, we created two new datasets - one for evaluating sound source localization in videos (SsLVi) and another for assessing the effectiveness of our algorithm on these new datasets (AdSsL). SsLVi stands out as a comprehensive, publicly available dataset in this domain, thoroughly tested to ensure its efficacy. Our algorithm has been found to perform exceptionally well on these newly developed datasets, surpassing existing methods even when employed on extracted features from a model trained using manually labeled data. Our source code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/kuanghysoundsource/AdSsLVi.git. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent with hyperbolic geometry. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN achieves the highest accuracy on CORA-T and CORA-S, and it outperforms the current best results by $12.34\%$ and $15.32\%$ on CORA-T and CORA-S respectively. LGCN's distortion-minimizing capability also enables the successful representation of large datasets like CORA-T and Pubmed. The code for LGCN is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/zhongjuan-vector/LGCN}.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness and stability result are obtained by employing a single measurement to establish an operator's smoothness, which is then utilized to apply a Carleman estimate and produce an appropriate weight for achieving the desired stability estimate. An alternative approach to demonstrate the desired stability estimate is also presented, based on a log-regularity result obtained through the use of boundary observations in the case of a single observation, and the use of a regularity result combined with a boundary observability inequality in the multi-observation scenario. An existing result from [J. Sesti, Inverse Problems, 2020] concerning the source term's uniqueness is leveraged from a different argument based on the energy inequality property. An approximate method for recovering the source term is also introduced and tested numerically. This research builds upon a previous study presented in [J. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model is comparable to the standard
exponential delay discounting model, enabling a direct assessment of its
validity. Utilizing our model, we re-analyzed previous data and obtained a
significantly higher average impulsivity than what was previously found, and our
results also indicate that impulsivity rather than delay discounting itself is
the primary driver of decision-making variability. Hence, our findings support the
notion that impulsivity, a key component of personality, exerts a substantial
effect on economic decision-making. Our delay discounting model, coupled with
Tsallis' statistical framework, offers a versatile tool that can be applied to
investigate other psychological and socioeconomic phenomena governed by the

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The resulting theory also exhibits a covariant version of the "degenerate metric" approach.  Furthermore, when the choice of harmonic gauge is made, the true physical degree of freedom can be unambiguously identified, allowing for a consistent application of the Hamiltonian constraint to obtain a linearized Hamiltonian constraint that matches the 2nd order time derivative of the true degree of freedom.  This outcome occurs regardless of the specific choice of harmonic gauge.  We have previously established that the harmonic gauge appears as a class in both the linearized f(Weyl) gravity theory and massive bradyon gravity, suggesting that this feature has a broader significance within the context of linearized metric theories of gravity.  The issue of the harmonic gauge appearing as a class also raises the question of how the true physical degree of freedom is distinguished from the other two gauge degrees of freedom in a generally covariant theory of gravity.  This problem becomes particularly pertinent when applying the Hamiltonian constraint to derive a linearized Hamiltonian, as the standard procedure fails to identify the true degree of freedom unambiguously in these types of theories.  Nevertheless, we have demonstrated that despite this issue, a consistent application of the Hamiltonian constraint is possible in the harmonic gauge version of the Fierz-Pauli theory and massive gravity, leading to a covariant time evolution of the true physical degree of freedom.  This feature is absent, however, in the fundamental Higgs model. By contrast, the canonical Hamiltonian formalism fails to yield a consistent covariant time evolution in the harmonic gauge version of the fundamental Higgs model, the scalar Minimos, and massless bradyon gravity. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of differentiating this notion from its oft-confused counterpart, negative temperature in the context of classical thermodynamics. A brief overview of its applications follows, including in the study of atomic and molecular physics, as well as in the behavior of certain quantum systems undergoing interactions and decoherence. A notable example of the latter is found in the dynamics of a two-level system as a result of its interaction with an environment, or in other words, noise. A simulation of this scenario is also presented. A significant amount of research has been conducted on open two-level systems, however, a novel finding presented here shows that despite often being overlooked, closed two-level systems with non-equilibrium conditions also exhibit a negative temperature phase, which is not solely a feature of open systems. A comprehensive review of both the theory and relevant phenomena is provided. A key aspect of this review is the introduction of a new, simplified model that demonstrates the possibility of achieving negative absolute temperature without the need for any dissipation, in addition to the standard characteristics of its corresponding phase equation. A crucial distinction of this model when compared to existing ones is that it employs only the most fundamental parameters while still exhibiting all possible temporal evolution scenarios of a two-level system. A particular highlight of this model is that it allows for the direct adjustment of its parameters to replicate the results obtained from other systems, as becomes evident from the subsequent numerical examples presented. A notable aspect of these examples is that they were derived from real-world experiments and simulations conducted on various two-level systems, including both atomic and molecular systems, as well as quantum systems comprising multiple two-level systems that interact with each other. A key aspect that makes this model distinct from the existing literature is that it is highly versatile and its corresponding equations can be applied to a wide range of two-level systems and their respective conditions of operation. A notable limitation of this review is that the negative temperature phase is identified solely by means of its temporal evolution, whereas a direct measurement of negative temperature itself is not considered. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it reveals that the relative I-functions can be used to compute I-functions for combined configurations. Moreover, it shows that combined FJRW invariants can be calculated using the relative I-functions. This research also establishes relationships between these invariants and the invariants of the individual components. Finally, it presents an example of computing invariants for combined FJRW theories. This research was initially presented as part of the author's PhD thesis at the University of Pennsylvania. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept is demonstrated where a pre-trained StyleGAN model can be used to create synthetic images of an ideal patient population with a specific health characteristic, allowing researchers to produce artificial chest X-rays. When paired with a decoder neural network, a set of encoded latent factors can be converted into detailed medical images, filling existing gaps in machine learning datasets. A critical finding showed that a model trained only on real chest X-rays can accurately identify pneumonia, with an impressive performance of 0.997 AUC, even surpassing the results achieved with traditional deep learning techniques. This study also explored models' performance on outcome prediction, revealing that a GAN-based model, when provided with artificial images representing severe COVID-19, can predict a 26.3% higher 30-day mortality rate compared to a model using real images, demonstrating the utility of disease-aware image editing in healthcare field tasks. As proof of this technique's versatility, a StyleGAN model trained to detect lung nodules was successfully applied to create artificial FUlL-CHEST images from partial ones, achieving a 0.763 AUC score in nodule outcome prediction, a level on par with models trained on complete images. This innovative approach opens up a range of possibilities, including creating artificial medical images for a machine learning model, refining a model's ability to recognize specific diseases, and producing artificial images from partial ones, all without the need for explicit nodule or disease annotation. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to K
means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. This report outlines the application's
features and delves into a specific use case where it was employed to analyze
near-infrared reflectance spectra, efficiently identifying key peaks following
the application of elastic mapping. Furthermore, sample code is provided for
feature extraction from such spectra where the desired peaks are known in
advance. The complete ViDaExpert project, along with its documentation, is
available through GitHub at the address indicated in the text. ViDaExpert can
be downloaded from the same address following installation instructions
presented herein. The address is https://github.com/GeoscienceSoftwareVision/ViDaExpert. A related project, ViDa, is also available at the address:
